findings.summary: Verbal manipulation was named in distinct waves, and each wave redefined what manipulation IS. The sophists (c. 460-380 BCE) experienced it as raw force — Gorgias's Encomium of Helen calls logos a "powerful lord" and a drug (pharmakon) on the soul; Protagoras taught "making the weaker argument the stronger" (dissoi logoi). Plato named it from outside as counterfeit: rhetoric is kolakeia (flattery), a knack (empeiria) like cookery, not an art (Gorgias, c. 380 BCE), later redeemable as psychagogia, soul-leading (Phaedrus). Aristotle made it analyzable: the Rhetoric's three pisteis (ethos/pathos/logos) and the enthymeme as "the body of persuasion," plus the Sophistical Refutations' first fallacy catalog — exactly 13 fallacies split 6 "in language" / 7 "outside language," defined by the appearance condition (seeming-valid-but-not). Rome turned it into teachable craft: the Rhetorica ad Herennium (c. 86-82 BCE) gave the first systematic Latin figure catalog (~64 figures of diction and thought) and openly taught insinuatio for "discreditable causes"; Quintilian (c. 95 CE) cataloged occultatio/paralipsis, paradiastole, and hyperbole ("an elegant straining of the truth") while relocating ethics into the speaker (vir bonus dicendi peritus). The medieval trivium made the whole thing a school subject — Peter of Spain's fallacy tract (c. 1230-45) was THE university textbook for 400 years, recasting manipulation as rule-violation in formal disputation. Renaissance manuals inflated the figure count (Peacham's Garden of Eloquence 1577/1593: ~191-200 figures, each with definition, species, examples) and Puttenham (1589) gave figures brutally honest English nicknames — Allegoria is "the figure of false semblant," which "no man can pleasantly utter and persuade without." Schopenhauer's 38 eristic stratagems (c. 1831) is the first catalog written from the manipulator's point of view. The modern fallacy lists descend by continuous forking (Port-Royal 1662 → Locke's three ad-arguments 1690 → Bentham's ~30 political fallacies 1824 → Whately 1826 → Copi's 18, 1961 → Hamblin's 1970 demolition → Walton and pragma-dialectics' "fallacy = dialogue-rule violation"). Five of captioneer's six families have deep classical names (hedging≈aporia/dubitatio; deflection≈ignoratio elenchi/apoplanesis; loaded framing≈paradiastole; overclaim≈hyperbole/secundum quid; minimizing≈meiosis/litotes/euphemismos) — but deleted-subject/passive-voice has NO classical name: grammatical concealment was invisible to catalogs built for conspicuous ornament and was only named by 20th-century critical linguistics. The 2,400-year through-line is Aristotle's appearance condition: manipulation is identified by how language APPEARS, not by reading minds — direct ancestry for captioneer's charter.

key_findings.claim: The earliest surviving theory of verbal manipulation treats it as quasi-physical force, not technique
key_findings.detail: Gorgias of Leontini's Encomium of Helen (late 5th c. BCE) calls logos a 'powerful lord' (dynastes megas) that 'with the smallest and most invisible body' accomplishes divine works, and compares speech acting on the soul to drugs (pharmaka) acting on the body — toxic or healing by turns. Manipulation is a force one is subjected to; there is no taxonomy yet, only awe.

key_findings.claim: The sophists were the first paid teachers of persuasion, and their slogan became the first accusation
key_findings.detail: Protagoras (c. 490-420 BCE) is the likely source of the claim to 'make the weaker argument the stronger' (ton hetto logon kreitto poiein) and of dissoi logoi — paired opposing speeches on every question. Aristophanes' Clouds (423 BCE) personifies the 'Weaker/Unjust Argument' on stage: the first popular satire of technique-teaching, predating any technical catalog.

key_findings.claim: Plato coined the first pejorative names for manipulation: flattery, knack, cookery
key_findings.detail: In the Gorgias (c. 380 BCE) Socrates argues oratory is not a techne (art) but an empeiria (mere knack) and a species of kolakeia (flattery), standing to justice as cookery stands to medicine and cosmetics to gymnastics — producing belief (pistis) without knowledge. In the Phaedrus he offers the redeemable name psychagogia ('soul-leading'). Plato's move: manipulation = a counterfeit of a true art, defined by what it lacks (knowledge, concern for the good).

key_findings.claim: Aristotle's Rhetoric is the first neutral engineering analysis of persuasion
key_findings.detail: Rhetoric defined as 'the capacity to observe the available means of persuasion in each case.' Three technical pisteis: ethos (perceived character: practical wisdom, virtue, goodwill), pathos (emotion altering judgment), logos (argument). The enthymeme — a deduction from accepted opinions, adapted to public audiences — is 'the body of persuasion.' Crucially, Aristotle says rhetorician and sophist differ not in technique but in purpose/moral choice (prohairesis): the same toolkit, two uses. Rhetoric II.24 catalogs 'apparent enthymemes' — fallacious arguments that persuade if undetected — making counter-manipulation literacy part of the art itself.

key_findings.claim: The first fallacy catalog contains exactly 13 fallacies, and its top-level split is a language/non-language architecture decision
key_findings.detail: Aristotle's Sophistical Refutations (c. 350 BCE): 6 fallacies dependent on language (in dictione): equivocation, amphiboly, composition, division, accent, form of expression; 7 outside language (extra dictionem): accident, secundum quid (dropping qualifications), ignoratio elenchi (irrelevant refutation), consequent, begging the question, non-cause as cause, many questions. His definition — 'arguments which appear to be refutations but are really fallacies' — establishes the APPEARANCE CONDITION that anchors the whole tradition: a fallacy is identified by how it looks in language, not by intent.

key_findings.claim: Rome's oldest complete rhetoric manual openly teaches a named manipulation technique for 'discreditable causes'
key_findings.detail: The anonymous Rhetorica ad Herennium (c. 86-82 BCE, long misattributed to Cicero) distinguishes the direct opening (principium) from insinuatio, the 'subtle approach' via dissimulation, prescribed when your cause is discreditable or the audience is hostile. Its Book IV is the first systematic Latin figure catalog (~64 figures by the standard count: figures of diction including 10 tropes, plus figures of thought) — 'the first text to compile them and discuss the effects they have on an audience.' Cicero (De Inventione c. 87 BCE; De Oratore 55 BCE) added stasis theory and the three officia oratoris: docere, delectare, movere (teach, delight, move).

key_findings.claim: Quintilian cataloged the spin figures while relocating ethics into the speaker, not the technique
key_findings.detail: Institutio Oratoria (c. 95 CE, 12 books) treats occultatio/praeteritio (= paralipsis/apophasis: introducing prejudicial matter 'as if by accident' while professing to pass over it, IX.3.98), paradiastole, and defines hyperbole (VIII.6.67) as 'an elegant straining of the truth' — a virtue when used with taste. His resolution of the manipulation problem is the vir bonus dicendi peritus: the good man skilled in speaking. The devices are neutral; only the speaker's character makes them corrupt. This is the strongest classical precedent for not hard-coding 'manipulative' as a property of a technique.

key_findings.claim: Medieval Europe made manipulation-detection a compulsory school subject for 400+ years
key_findings.detail: The trivium (grammar, logic, rhetoric) was the lower division of the seven liberal arts, taught in monastic and cathedral schools and, from the 12th century, in universities. Peter of Spain's Tractatus/Summulae Logicales (c. 1230-45) — with Tract 7 devoted to fallacies and stocked with sophismata (deliberately tricky puzzle-sentences) — remained the standard university logic textbook into the 17th century. The disputation culture (obligationes) recast manipulation as rule-violation inside a formal game, anticipating modern pragma-dialectics by 750 years.

key_findings.claim: Renaissance figure-manuals exploded the catalog and gave techniques frank English 'manipulation' nicknames
key_findings.detail: Erasmus's De Copia (1512, 11+ printings), Susenbrotus's Epitome troporum ac schematum (1541, 20+ printings — the standard schoolbook), Sherry's Treatise of Schemes and Tropes (1550, first English figure-manual), Henry Peacham's Garden of Eloquence (1577; 1593 edition ~191-200 figures, each given definition, division into species, and examples from the Bible and classics). George Puttenham's Arte of English Poesie (1589) renamed figures in English with startling candor: Allegoria is 'the figure of false semblant or dissimulation' ('when we speake one thing and thinke another'), Ironia 'the Dry Mock,' Sarcasmus 'the Bitter Taunt' — and he concedes 'no man can pleasantly utter and persuade without' false semblant, princes and counsellors included.

key_findings.claim: Paradiastole is the classical-Renaissance name for 'spin' — the direct ancestor of captioneer's loaded-framing family
key_findings.detail: Quintilian treats it as forensic redescription (recasting events with alternative motive-words to change their moral weight); Peacham (1577) defines it as 'when by a mannerly interpretation, we doe excuse our own vices... by calling them vertues' (prodigality becomes generosity, cowardice becomes caution). Quentin Skinner's scholarship names this 'rhetorical redescription' and traces its use and exposure through Hobbes and Shakespeare — an unbroken 2,000-year lineage for evaluative reframing as a NAMED, detectable move.

key_findings.claim: Schopenhauer's 38 stratagems (c. 1831) is the first catalog written from the manipulator's own point of view
key_findings.detail: Eristische Dialektik: Die Kunst, Recht zu behalten (published posthumously 1864) sarcastically lists 38 ways to win regardless of truth. Directly mappable to captioneer families: #1 Extension (stretch the claim beyond its natural limits → overclaim), #12 choose favorable metaphors and names ('every wight praises his own wares' — the founding analysis of loaded language/euphemism), #18 interrupt and divert the dispute + #29 diversion (→ deflection), #23 provoke exaggeration (→ manufacturing overclaim in the opponent), #26 turn the tables (retorsio), #32 file the thesis under an odious category (→ loaded framing by label), #36 bewilder with senseless bombast, #38 become personal (argumentum ad personam). Its inversion of stance — how-to rather than how-to-detect — proved that detection catalogs and manipulation playbooks are the same data read in two directions.

key_findings.claim: Modern fallacy lists descend from Aristotle by continuous forking, with each fork redefining what a fallacy IS
key_findings.detail: Bacon's Idols (1620) shifted to psychological bias; Port-Royal Logic (1662) kept 8 of Aristotle's 13 and added post hoc and hasty generalization; Locke (1690) named three ad-arguments (ad verecundiam, ad ignorantiam, ad hominem) WITHOUT calling them fallacies; Watts (1724) added ad fidem, ad passiones, ad populum; Bentham's Handbook of Political Fallacies (1824) cataloged ~30 fallacies of political deception in four classes (authority, danger, delay, confusion); Whately (1826) split logical vs material; Mill (1843) went inductive/epistemic; Copi (1961) fixed the '18 informal fallacies' textbook canon; Hamblin's Fallacies (1970) demolished this 'standard treatment' as 'debased, worn-out and dogmatic'; Walton and pragma-dialectics (van Eemeren & Grootendorst, 10 rules of critical discussion) redefined fallacy as any violation of dialogue rules — abandoning 'invalid argument' entirely.

key_findings.claim: Five of captioneer's six families have deep classical names; deleted-subject/passive-voice has none
key_findings.detail: hedging ≈ aporia/dubitatio (staged doubt); deflection ≈ ignoratio elenchi (Aristotle's 13) and apoplanesis (Peacham: evading by digression); loaded framing ≈ paradiastole + Schopenhauer #12/#32 + Aristotle's Rhetoric III.2 on slanted epithets; overclaim ≈ hyperbole (Quintilian's 'straining of the truth') + secundum quid (dropping qualifiers) + Schopenhauer #1; minimizing ≈ meiosis/tapinosis/litotes + euphemismos. But agent-deletion via passive voice appears in NO classical, medieval, or Renaissance catalog — those traditions cataloged conspicuous ornament, and grammar-level concealment was only named by 20th-century critical linguistics (Fowler, Hodge, Kress & Trew, Language and Control, 1979). The classical corpus both validates captioneer's families and exposes where the tradition was blind.

key_findings.claim: Each era's answer to 'what IS verbal manipulation' forms a coherent sequence the framework can present as its origin story
key_findings.detail: Force/drug acting on the soul (sophists) → counterfeit of a true art, flattery (Plato) → apparent-but-invalid reasoning, same tools as honest rhetoric but different purpose (Aristotle) → neutral craft taught openly, ethics located in the speaker (Rome) → rule-violation inside a formal disputation game (medieval) → courtly dissimulation no persuader can do without (Renaissance) → the manipulator's own playbook (Schopenhauer) → invalid argument that appears valid (Copi's standard treatment) → violation of the norms of rational dialogue (Hamblin/Walton/pragma-dialectics). Note the spiral: the newest definition (dialogue-rule violation) is the medieval one rediscovered.

key_findings.claim: The primary texts are nearly all open: the framework can legally embed 2,400 years of source material
key_findings.detail: Perseus Digital Library releases its Greek/Latin/English texts and XML under CC BY-SA 4.0; Project Gutenberg hosts public-domain full texts of Sherry's Treatise of Schemes and Tropes (1550), Puttenham's Arte of English Poesie, and T. Bailey Saunders's translation of Schopenhauer's Art of Controversy; LacusCurtius and the Internet Archive carry Quintilian and Peacham facsimiles. Exception: Silva Rhetoricae (rhetoric.byu.edu, Gideon Burton, BYU) — the best existing map of the hundreds of figure-terms — is conventional copyright (1996-2002, citation requested), so it can guide the taxonomy but its entry text cannot be copied; definitions must be rewritten from primary sources.

techniques.name: Psychagogia (soul-leading)
techniques.definition: Plato's name in the Phaedrus for rhetoric's real nature: the art of leading souls through words — manipulative when done without knowledge of truth and of soul-types, legitimate when grounded in both.
techniques.origin: Plato, Phaedrus, c. 370 BCE
techniques.example: Any persuasion tuned to the hearer's psychology rather than to the matter itself.

techniques.name: Kolakeia (flattery-rhetoric)
techniques.definition: Plato's category for oratory as a knack (empeiria) of gratification that imitates a true art: cookery imitating medicine, cosmetics imitating gymnastics — producing belief without knowledge.
techniques.origin: Plato, Gorgias, c. 380 BCE
techniques.example: Telling an audience what pleases them in the form of what informs them.

techniques.name: Dissoi logoi / antilogic
techniques.definition: Composing equally persuasive opposing speeches on the same question; the sophistic training method behind the charge of 'making the weaker argument the stronger.'
techniques.origin: Protagoras, 5th c. BCE; anonymous treatise Dissoi Logoi c. 400 BCE; satirized in Aristophanes' Clouds, 423 BCE
techniques.example: A debate coach's drill: argue both sides of the same case with equal conviction.

techniques.name: Enthymeme (and apparent enthymeme)
techniques.definition: Aristotle's rhetorical deduction from premises the audience already accepts — 'the body of persuasion'; the apparent enthymeme (Rhetoric II.24) mimics this form while resting on faulty inference, persuading if undetected.
techniques.origin: Aristotle, Rhetoric, c. 350 BCE
techniques.example: 'He's a family man, so he wouldn't do this' — persuasive shape, unearned inference.

techniques.name: Equivocation (homonymia)
techniques.definition: Using one word in two senses across an argument; first of Aristotle's six language-dependent fallacies.
techniques.origin: Aristotle, Sophistical Refutations ch. 4, c. 350 BCE
techniques.example: 'Light' as color in the premise, weight in the conclusion.

techniques.name: Amphiboly (amphibolia)
techniques.definition: Exploiting ambiguous sentence structure rather than ambiguous words; second language-dependent fallacy.
techniques.origin: Aristotle, Sophistical Refutations, c. 350 BCE
techniques.example: 'I shot an elephant in my pajamas' — the structure supports two readings.

techniques.name: Secundum quid (dropping the qualifier)
techniques.definition: Sliding between a qualified and an unqualified claim — the classical ancestor of overclaim and hasty generalization.
techniques.origin: Aristotle, Sophistical Refutations, c. 350 BCE (extra dictionem group)
techniques.languages: Greek para to pe, Latin secundum quid
techniques.example: 'The study found a small effect in one cohort' becomes 'science proves it works.'

techniques.name: Ignoratio elenchi (irrelevant refutation)
techniques.definition: Proving something other than what is at issue while appearing to answer it — the classical root of captioneer's deflection family and of the later 'red herring.'
techniques.origin: Aristotle, Sophistical Refutations, c. 350 BCE
techniques.example: Asked about the missing funds, the official proves at length that the program is popular.

techniques.name: Many questions (complex question)
techniques.definition: Packing a contestable presupposition inside a question so any direct answer concedes it.
techniques.origin: Aristotle, Sophistical Refutations, c. 350 BCE
techniques.example: 'Have you stopped falsifying the reports?'

techniques.name: Insinuatio (the subtle approach)
techniques.definition: The dissimulated opening prescribed when your cause is discreditable or the audience hostile: win goodwill obliquely before revealing what you are actually arguing.
techniques.origin: Rhetorica ad Herennium I, c. 86-82 BCE; Greek antecedent ephodos
techniques.example: Beginning a defense of an unpopular client with a story that first wins laughter and sympathy.

techniques.name: Paralipsis / apophasis / occultatio / praeteritio
techniques.definition: Emphasizing a point by professing to pass over it — smuggling prejudicial content in under a show of restraint; Quintilian classes it as a figure of thought that plants matter 'as if by accident.'
techniques.origin: Greek paraleipsis; Latin occultatio in Rhetorica ad Herennium IV; Quintilian, Institutio IX.3.98, c. 95 CE
techniques.example: 'I won't even mention my opponent's bankruptcy.'

techniques.name: Paradiastole (rhetorical redescription)
techniques.definition: Redescribing a vice as its neighboring virtue (or vice versa) to change its moral weight — Skinner's 'rhetorical redescription,' the named classical ancestor of spin and loaded framing.
techniques.origin: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria (forensic redescription); named and moralized in Peacham, Garden of Eloquence 1577, and Puttenham 1589
techniques.languages: Greek name, Latin theory, English Renaissance elaboration
techniques.example: Prodigality praised as 'generosity'; recklessness as 'boldness'; cowardice excused as 'caution.'

techniques.name: Hyperbole
techniques.definition: Overstatement beyond literal truth; Quintilian defines it as 'an elegant straining of the truth' (decens veri superiectio) — a virtue in ornament, an overclaim when passed off as measurement.
techniques.origin: Greek rhetoric; codified Quintilian, Institutio VIII.6.67, c. 95 CE
techniques.example: 'Everyone agrees'; 'the greatest crisis in history.'

techniques.name: Meiosis / tapinosis / litotes
techniques.definition: The family of belittling figures: understatement that shrinks the significance of a thing (meiosis), degrades it by a base name (tapinosis), or affirms by weak double negative (litotes) — the classical minimizing toolkit.
techniques.origin: Greek rhetoric; cataloged in Rhetorica ad Herennium, Quintilian, and the Renaissance manuals
techniques.example: Calling a scandal 'a bit of a mix-up'; 'mistakes were not unheard of.'

techniques.name: Euphemismos (euphemism)
techniques.definition: Substituting a milder or fairer-sounding word for a harsh reality; the figure-level mechanism of minimizing and of paradiastole.
techniques.origin: Greek rhetorical term; standard in Renaissance figure-manuals (Peacham, Puttenham)
techniques.example: 'Collateral damage' for killed civilians; 'let go' for fired.

techniques.name: Aporia / dubitatio (staged doubt)
techniques.definition: Professing uncertainty or deliberating aloud — genuine when honest, a hedging device when the doubt is performed to avoid commitment or to disarm.
techniques.origin: Greek aporia; Latin dubitatio in Rhetorica ad Herennium IV and Quintilian IX
techniques.example: 'I hardly know how to describe my opponent's conduct...' (then describing it at length).

techniques.name: Apoplanesis (evasive digression)
techniques.definition: Leading the hearer away from the point at issue by digressing to another matter — a named Renaissance figure for deflection.
techniques.origin: Greek term cataloged in Peacham, Garden of Eloquence, 1577
techniques.example: Answering a question about the budget with a tour of the company's founding story.

techniques.name: Allegoria as 'false semblant'
techniques.definition: Puttenham's English renaming of sustained saying-one-thing-meaning-another: 'the figure of false semblant or dissimulation... when our wordes and our meanings meete not' — which he says no persuader, courtier, counsellor, or prince can do without.
techniques.origin: George Puttenham, The Arte of English Poesie, Book III 'Of Ornament', 1589
techniques.languages: English nicknames for Greek/Latin figures (also Ironia 'the Dry Mock', Sarcasmus 'the Bitter Taunt')
techniques.example: Courtly speech praising a rival in terms every hearer understands as damning.

techniques.name: Schopenhauer stratagem 1: The Extension
techniques.definition: Stretch the opponent's statement beyond its natural limits, then refute the exaggerated version — manufacturing overclaim to attack it.
techniques.origin: Schopenhauer, Eristische Dialektik, c. 1831 (publ. 1864)
techniques.languages: German original; English trans. T. Bailey Saunders 1896 (public domain)
techniques.example: 'You said the policy has costs — so you think we should do nothing at all?'

techniques.name: Schopenhauer stratagem 12: favorable names and metaphors
techniques.definition: Pre-load the conclusion by the choice of words: pick the metaphor or label that flatters your thesis — his examples are exactly modern loaded language ('religion' vs 'bigotry', 'protection' vs 'control').
techniques.origin: Schopenhauer, Eristische Dialektik, c. 1831
techniques.example: 'Reform' vs 'gutting'; 'job creators' vs 'the wealthy.'

techniques.name: Schopenhauer stratagems 18 & 29: interruption and diversion
techniques.definition: When losing, break the thread — interrupt, change the subject, start a new dispute; the codified playbook form of deflection (mutatio controversiae).
techniques.origin: Schopenhauer, Eristische Dialektik, c. 1831
techniques.example: 'Before we get lost in numbers, the real question is character.'

techniques.name: Schopenhauer stratagem 32: the odious category
techniques.definition: Dispose of a claim by filing it under a hated label rather than engaging it — loaded framing by classification.
techniques.origin: Schopenhauer, Eristische Dialektik, c. 1831
techniques.example: 'That's just Manichaeism / socialism / conspiracy talk.'

techniques.name: Schopenhauer stratagem 38: argumentum ad personam
techniques.definition: The last resort: abandon the subject and attack the person — which Schopenhauer distinguishes from ad hominem (arguing from the opponent's own concessions).
techniques.origin: Schopenhauer, Eristische Dialektik, c. 1831
techniques.example: 'Coming from someone with your record, this is rich.'

techniques.name: Locke's ad-arguments
techniques.definition: Three named pressure-moves that bypass evidence: argumentum ad verecundiam (authority/modesty), ad ignorantiam (demand the opponent disprove), ad hominem (press a man with his own concessions) — contrasted with ad judicium (proof proper). Locke named them without calling them fallacies; the fallacy label came later.
techniques.origin: John Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, 1690; extended by Watts 1724 (ad fidem, ad passiones, ad populum)
techniques.example: 'Are you really going to contradict the entire profession?'

techniques.name: Sophismata (medieval puzzle-sentences)
techniques.definition: Deliberately treacherous sentences used in university teaching to train students to spot how language misleads — the medieval pedagogical form of fallacy training inside the trivium.
techniques.origin: 13th-c. terminist logic; Peter of Spain, Tractatus (Summulae Logicales) Tract 7, c. 1230-45
techniques.example: 'All men are donkeys or men and donkeys are donkeys' — parse it and find the trap.

framework_implications: Data model — techniques need many-named identity: model each technique as a stable slug plus a set of dated NAMING EVENTS (name, language, namer, work, year, quoted definition). One record must hold paraleipsis/apophasis/occultatio/praeteritio/'passing over' as attestations of one technique. The naming timeline is not metadata decoration; it IS the 'origin and evolution' content the owner wants, and it falls directly out of this schema.

Two ontological layers, kept separate in the engine: FIGURES (surface patterns visible in a text span — the Ad Herennium/Quintilian/Peacham lineage) vs MOVES (dialogical stratagems — Aristotle's fallacies, Schopenhauer's 38, pragma-dialectic rule violations). Captioneer's six families are figure-level and text-anchored; keep the detector there. Moves require dialogue context and inferred purpose, so ship them as a distinct, clearly-labeled taxonomy layer (useful for analyzing exchanges/threads later) rather than mixing them into span-highlighting.

Charter has 2,400 years of precedent — encode it: Aristotle's appearance condition ('appears to be a refutation but is not') through Whately and Copi defines manipulation by how language APPEARS, never by the speaker's mind; and Aristotle explicitly says sophist and rhetorician share techniques and differ only in purpose. Put this lineage in the framework's founding document as the scholarly justification for 'reads the language, never the mind' — it preempts the 'lie detector' misreading with authority.

Never hard-code valence on a technique: every era shows the same device serving honest and manipulative ends (Quintilian calls hyperbole a virtue; Puttenham says no one persuades without 'false semblant'; Schopenhauer's stratagems are Aristotle's tools inverted). Severity/valence must be a per-instance annotation on the marked span, not a property of the technique record. The technique table stays descriptive; judgment lives in the reading.

Record 'first named' metadata and mine the gaps in both directions: deleted-subject/passive-voice was never named classically (only by 1970s critical linguistics), proving the framework must include grammar-level concealment the old catalogs missed; conversely the classical catalogs offer ready-made, well-documented candidate families beyond the current six — paradiastole (redescription), paralipsis (mention-by-denial), apoplanesis (evasive digression), aporia (staged doubt), complex question (smuggled presupposition) — each already text-anchored and hence detectable under the existing design.

Adopt the Renaissance manual as the entry schema: Peacham's format (name → definition → division into species → curated positive and abusive examples) sustained a mass 'learnable lens' curriculum for centuries, and the trivium proves ordinary students can be taught this. Every technique entry in the open-source repo should ship name(s), definition, species, honest-use example, manipulative-use example, and a spot-it exercise — a curriculum object, not just a detector rule.

Scope discipline from catalog history: lists that survived were small and structured (Aristotle's 13, Locke's 3, Schopenhauer's 38, Copi's 18); the 200-figure Renaissance gardens became unteachable ornament inventories. Keep a small canonical core (the six families, maybe growing to ~10) as the product surface, with the long tail of hundreds of named figures living in the reference layer that core families link out to.

Version the taxonomy and expect forks — that IS the tradition: from Aristotle to pragma-dialectics, every generation reorganized the same material under a new theory (Whately, Mill, Copi, Hamblin, Walton each reclassified). Store technique identity separately from classification so reclassification is a cheap versioned overlay; publish the taxonomy with semver and treat competing classifications (logical, dialogical, linguistic) as parallel views over one technique table.

Corpus and licensing plan: seed the historical layer from Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0 — Aristotle, Quintilian in XML), Project Gutenberg public-domain texts (Sherry 1550, Puttenham 1589, Saunders's 1896 Schopenhauer translation), and Internet Archive facsimiles (Peacham 1577); treat Silva Rhetoricae as a copyrighted reference map — follow its term coverage but write all definitions fresh from primary sources. Release the framework's own technique database under CC BY-SA to stay license-compatible with Perseus-derived content.

factChecks.claim: Gorgias of Leontini's Encomium of Helen (late 5th c. BCE) calls logos a 'powerful lord' (dynastes megas) that 'with the smallest and most invisible body' accomplishes divine works, and compares speech acting on the soul to drugs (pharmaka) acting on the body.
factChecks.evidence: Multiple independent sources quote the famous passage (DK 82B11 sec. 8): 'Speech is a powerful lord, which with the smallest and most invisible body accomplishes the most godlike works,' and sec. 14's comparison of speech on the soul to drugs (pharmaka) on the body ('some cause sorrow, some pleasure, some fear...'). Late-5th-c. BCE dating is standard (often c. 414 BCE). Caveat: the claimed source URL (individual.utoronto.ca/rbarney/Helen.pdf, Rachel Barney's translation) failed to load over HTTPS (SSL error) when fetched, so I verified the content via other sources including a De Gruyter chapter 'Drugs and Psychotropic Words in Gorgias' Encomium of Helen' and standard translations. The framing 'earliest surviving theory... no taxonomy yet, only awe' is interpretive, not a checkable fact (note Helen sec. 13 does distinguish kinds of persuasive discourse, so 'only awe' is a slight overstatement, but the quasi-physical-force reading is mainstream).

factChecks.claim: Protagoras (c. 490-420 BCE) is the likely source of 'make the weaker argument the stronger' and of paired opposing arguments (dissoi logoi); sophists were the first paid teachers of persuasion; Aristophanes' Clouds (423 BCE) personifies the Weaker/Unjust Argument on stage.
factChecks.evidence: IEP (iep.utm.edu/protagor/): 'born in approximately 490 B.C.E. ... died c. 420 B.C.E.'; he 'could make the worse (or weaker) argument appear the better (or stronger)'; 'probably the first Greek to earn money in higher education... notorious for the extremely high fees.' SEP (plato.stanford.edu/entries/sophists/): 'Protagoras of Abdera (ca. 490-420 BC)'; Aristotle attributes the weaker-logos claim to him; per Diogenes Laertius he 'was the first to maintain that on any matter there are two theses... opposed to one another.' Wikipedia (The Clouds): 'originally produced at the City Dionysia in 423 BC' featuring 'the personified arguments Superior (Right) and Inferior (Wrong)' debating on stage (agon at lines 949-1104). Minor nuance: 'dissoi logoi' as a title strictly names an anonymous later treatise (c. 400 BCE) exemplifying the Protagorean doctrine; attributing the doctrine (two opposed logoi on every question) to Protagoras is correct. 'First popular satire of technique-teaching' is interpretive but chronologically sound (423 BCE predates all surviving technical catalogs).

factChecks.claim: In the Gorgias (c. 380 BCE) Socrates argues oratory is not a techne but an empeiria (knack) and a species of kolakeia (flattery), standing to justice as cookery to medicine and cosmetics to gymnastics, producing belief (pistis) without knowledge; in the Phaedrus Plato offers psychagogia ('soul-leading').
factChecks.evidence: SEP 'Plato on Rhetoric and Poetry' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/plato-rhetoric/) confirms every element: rhetoric is 'a mere knack (empeiria, or experience)' aimed at gratification; the proportion 'As medicine stands to cookery, so justice to rhetoric; as gymnastics to cosmetics, so legislation to sophistry' (Gorgias 464b-466a); rhetoric 'instills beliefs merely' without knowledge (cf. 454e-455a); and Phaedrus 261a8: rhetoric as 'the art of directing the soul by means of speech' (psychagogia). Wikipedia dates the Gorgias 'around 380 BC.' The claimed source (cyprusconferences.org PDF) turned out to be a Wikipedia-derived summary of the dialogue, whose extracted text confirms the flattery/pastry-baking/cosmetics/gymnastics/medicine analogies — a weak citation, but the content is right. 'Coined' is loose (kolakeia was an existing Greek word; Plato's innovation was applying the classification to rhetoric), but the substance stands.

factChecks.claim: Aristotle's Rhetoric defines rhetoric as the capacity to observe the available means of persuasion in each case; three pisteis (ethos = practical wisdom, virtue, goodwill; pathos; logos); the enthymeme is 'the body of persuasion,' a deduction from accepted opinions adapted to public audiences; rhetorician and sophist differ in prohairesis (moral purpose), not technique; Rhetoric II.24 catalogs apparent/fallacious enthymemes.
factChecks.evidence: SEP 'Aristotle's Rhetoric' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/aristotle-rhetoric/) confirms: rhetoric 'defined as the ability to see what is possibly persuasive in every given case' (Rhet. I.2, 1355b26f); persuasion through ethos/pathos/logos with ethos requiring 'practical intelligence (phronesis), a virtuous character, and good will'; 'Aristotle calls the enthymeme the body of persuasion,' deducing from accepted opinions (endoxa) with brevity for public audiences; and Rhet. II.24 as topoi 'for the construction of merely apparent (i.e. fallacious) enthymemes.' The prohairesis point is NOT in the SEP entry but is directly in Aristotle, Rhetoric I.1 1355b17-21 (verified via Perseus text at perseus.tufts.edu): 'what makes a man a sophist is not his faculty, but his moral purpose' — in dialectic the moral purpose (prohairesis) makes the sophist, the faculty (dynamis) the dialectician. So the sub-claim is true; only its attachment to the SEP citation is imprecise.

factChecks.claim: Aristotle's Sophistical Refutations (c. 350 BCE) contains exactly 13 fallacies: 6 dependent on language (equivocation, amphiboly, composition, division, accent, form of expression) and 7 outside language (accident, secundum quid, ignoratio elenchi, consequent, begging the question, non-cause, many questions); his definition 'arguments which appear to be refutations but are really fallacies' establishes the appearance condition.
factChecks.evidence: SEP 'Fallacies' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/fallacies/) states Aristotle identifies thirteen fallacies, 6 in dictione (equivocation, amphiboly, combination [= composition], division, accent, form of expression) and 7 extra dictionem (accident, secundum quid, consequent, non-cause, begging the question, ignoratio elenchi, many questions) — an exact match to the claim's lists. Definition quoted verbatim in SEP: 'arguments which appear to be refutations but are really fallacies and not refutations' (SR 1 164a20), and SEP explicitly discusses the appearance condition ('appear to be real owing to men's inexperience'). Wikipedia dates the work c. 350 BC. Two minor hedges: Wikipedia says 'twelve or thirteen' (some scholars merge two), though 13 is the standard and SEP count; and the gloss 'identified by how it looks in language, not by intent' slightly compresses the appearance condition, which is about appearing to be a genuine refutation — Aristotle classifies by source of illusion, not intent, so the spirit is right.

factChecks.claim: Rhetorica ad Herennium (c. 86-82 BCE, anonymous, long misattributed to Cicero) is Rome's oldest complete rhetoric manual; it distinguishes principium from insinuatio (subtle approach via dissimulation, prescribed for discreditable causes or hostile audiences); Book IV is the first systematic Latin figure catalog (~64 figures: figures of diction incl. 10 tropes, plus figures of thought); Cicero (De Inventione c. 87 BCE; De Oratore 55 BCE) added stasis theory and the three officia oratoris docere, delectare, movere.
factChecks.correction: The ad Herennium core is fully confirmed; the Cicero tail has three errors. (1) De Inventione is standardly dated c. 91-88 BCE (Cicero's youth), not c. 87 BCE — meaning it likely PREDATES the ad Herennium (the ad Herennium remains the oldest COMPLETE Latin manual, since De Inventione covers only invention). (2) Cicero did not 'add' stasis theory: it originated with Hermagoras of Temnos (2nd c. BCE), and the ad Herennium itself already contains stasis doctrine (the constitutiones in Books I-II); De Inventione transmitted/refined Hermagorean stasis in Latin. (3) The exact triad docere/delectare/movere is not from De Oratore (55 BCE), where the formulation is probare/conciliare/movere (or docere/conciliare/movere); the delectare formulations appear in the later Orator (46 BCE: probare/delectare/flectere) and De Optimum Genere Oratorum (46 BCE: docere/delectare/permovere). The triad is genuinely Ciceronian but the work-and-date attribution is wrong.
factChecks.evidence: Confirmed via Caplan's Loeb introduction (penelope.uchicago.edu): dated 'c. 86-82 B.C.'; 'from Jerome's time on, as a work by Cicero'; 'the oldest Latin Art preserved entire.' Book I text (penelope.uchicago.edu) quotes: 'two kinds of Introduction: the Direct Opening... and the Subtle Approach,' used when 'our cause is discreditable,' when 'the hearer has apparently been won over by the previous speakers of the opposition,' or when wearied — achieved 'covertly, through dissimulation.' Silva Rhetoricae's Book IV outline (rhetoric.byu.edu) lists 45 figures of diction (the last 10 explicitly tropes: nominatio through permutatio) + 19 figures of thought = 64. Wikipedia carries the exact quote 'the first text to compile them and discuss the effects they have on an audience.' Corrections sourced from: multiple scholarly summaries dating De Inventione c. 91-88 BCE and attributing stasis theory to Hermagoras of Temnos ('developed primarily by Hermagoras... Cicero refined and expanded'); and sources on the officia noting docere/delectare/movere is 'actually defined in Cicero's Orator (46 BC),' with De Oratore II using probare/conciliare/movere.

findings.summary: Between 1900 and 2000 manipulation went from a craft performed by an orator in a room to an industrial product: WWI's Creel Committee (1917-19) mass-produced messaging through 75,000 "Four Minute Men," Lippmann named the "manufacture of consent" (1919/1922) and located its mechanism in the stereotype-built "pseudo-environment," Bernays professionalized it as PR ("engineering of consent," the staged Torches of Freedom event of 1929), and by century's end Luntz was selecting words like drugs by dial-testing ("death tax" beat "estate tax" by 20-30 points). The counter-tradition industrialized too: the Institute for Propaganda Analysis (1937-42) published the first public technique taxonomy — Name Calling, Glittering Generalities, Transfer, Testimonial, Plain Folks, Card Stacking, Bandwagon — taught it to about a million schoolchildren, and then died of exactly the pressures an open framework must design against (single-funder collapse, wartime demand that analysis go one-sided, HUAC flak); Orwell (1946/1949), the NCTE doublespeak committee and Lutz (1972-2000), Herman & Chomsky's five structural filters (1988), and Pinker's euphemism treadmill (1994) each added a distinct analytical layer — textual devices, channel economics, and diachronic laws of word decay. The through-line for the framework: when the medium changed, techniques mutated predictably (broadcast selected for compressed, repeatable symbol-association, deleted authorship, and empirically tested wording), the manufacturing side outgrew the checking side ~2:1→6:1 PR-to-journalist by 2018, and the IPA's device list has already been reborn machine-readable (Da San Martino et al. 2019 / SemEval-2020 Task 11 span-level annotation of 18 techniques) — which is precisely captioneer's phrase-anchored shape, and predicts the algorithmic/LLM era as per-user dial-testing plus fully synthetic authorship inside Ellul's "integration propaganda" total environment.

key_findings.claim: "Manufacture of consent" was coined by Lippmann as diagnosis, not accusation
key_findings.detail: Walter Lippmann first used the phrase in Liberty and the News (1919) and elaborated it in Public Opinion (1922): citizens act not on the world but on a "pseudo-environment" assembled from stereotypes — "the pictures in our heads" — so consent will inevitably be manufactured by whoever controls the pictures; the press, dependent on private interests, cannot carry the truth-telling burden democracy assigns it.

key_findings.claim: WWI's CPI is the hinge between oratory and mass media
key_findings.detail: The Committee on Public Information (1917-19, George Creel) used every available medium — newspapers, pamphlets, ads, film — and its Four Minute Men program (~75,000 volunteer speakers delivering centrally scripted 4-minute talks, advised to avoid "hymns of hate") is the exact transitional form: centrally mass-produced content still delivered by local oratory. Its excesses became the cautionary blueprint for WWII's Office of War Information.

key_findings.claim: Bernays turned manipulation into an engineering profession with manufactured events and hidden authorship
key_findings.detail: Propaganda (1928) opens by calling "the conscious and intelligent manipulation of the organized habits and opinions of the masses" an "important element in democratic society." His Torches of Freedom stunt (Easter Parade, March 31, 1929: ~10 debutantes smoking Lucky Strikes as staged "protest") combined a manufactured news event, psychoanalytic consulting (A. A. Brill supplied the "torches of freedom" symbol), and third-party voices concealing the tobacco client. His 1947 essay "The Engineering of Consent" (Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science 250:113-120) formalized the method as applied science.

key_findings.claim: The Institute for Propaganda Analysis (1937-42) was the first public "lens of clarity" project
key_findings.detail: Founded by Clyde R. Miller at Columbia Teachers College with a $10,000 grant from philanthropist Edward Filene. Its bulletin Propaganda Analysis reached ~10,000 subscribers at $2/year, it corresponded with ~2,500 teachers, and its school series "What Makes You Think So?" reached roughly 1 million students — mass media-literacy education a full 80 years before the modern misinformation panic.

key_findings.claim: The IPA's seven devices, exactly: Name Calling, Glittering Generalities, Transfer, Testimonial, Plain Folks, Card Stacking, Bandwagon
key_findings.detail: First published in the bulletin article "How to Detect Propaganda" (Propaganda Analysis, November 1937), drafted principally by Clyde Miller with Violet Edwards; Sproule's research note traces their intellectual origins to older rhetoric and fallacy traditions repackaged for ordinary citizens. This list is the direct ancestor of nearly every later technique taxonomy, including captioneer's six families.

key_findings.claim: The IPA died of three compounding causes — and each is a governance lesson
key_findings.detail: Its farewell issue (January 9, 1942) said dispassionate analysis of all propaganda, "good" and "bad," would be "misunderstood" and could be misused during the war emergency; simultaneously its funding collapsed after Filene's death, and it drew political flak — Hearst papers attacked Miller, and HUAC later labeled the IPA a Communist front (1947). A neutral lens pointed at one's own side's propaganda during a crisis got defunded and smeared.

key_findings.claim: Orwell named four prose vices and then wrote the design document for weaponized vocabulary
key_findings.detail: "Politics and the English Language" (1946) catalogs dying metaphors, operators/verbal false limbs, pretentious diction, and meaningless words, arguing political language is "the defense of the indefensible" — euphemism and agent-deletion at scale. The Newspeak appendix to Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949) inverts language growth: a shrinking lexicon (A/B/C vocabularies, compounds like goodthink/crimestop/bellyfeel, "duckspeak") engineered so heresy becomes literally unthinkable.

key_findings.claim: Lutz institutionalized the Orwell watchdog role for three decades
key_findings.detail: NCTE formed the Committee on Public Doublespeak in 1972 out of Vietnam-era euphemism (first Doublespeak Award, 1974, went to a USAF colonel insisting bombing be called "air support"); Lutz edited the Quarterly Review of Doublespeak (1980-2000) and in Doublespeak (1989) fixed the four-type taxonomy — euphemism, jargon, gobbledygook/bureaucratese, inflated language — defining doublespeak as "the language of non-responsibility," constructed to appear to communicate while not communicating.

key_findings.claim: Herman & Chomsky moved the analysis from the sentence to the channel
key_findings.detail: Manufacturing Consent (1988) argues media bias needs no conspiracy: five structural filters — (1) concentrated ownership and profit orientation, (2) advertising as primary revenue, (3) sourcing dependence on government/business information providers, (4) flak as discipline, (5) anticommunism (later generalized to fear ideology) — pre-shape what becomes news. Manipulation here is invisible in any individual sentence; it lives in the economics of the pipe.

key_findings.claim: Luntz closed the century by making word-choice an empirical manufacturing process
key_findings.detail: Over 2,500 dial sessions plus focus groups: "death tax" generated 20-30% higher opposition than "estate tax" (he advised GOP lawmakers to hold press conferences "at your local mortuary"); his 2002 memo urged "climate change" over "global warming" as "less frightening." His thesis — "It's not what you say, it's what people hear" (Words That Work, 2007) — is Bernays' engineering completed: vocabulary selected by measurement, not composed by rhetors.

key_findings.claim: Pinker's euphemism treadmill is a discovered LAW of manipulation-vocabulary evolution
key_findings.detail: Coined in a April 3, 1994 New York Times piece: euphemisms re-acquire the taint of their referent (water closet→toilet→bathroom→rest room→lavatory; shell shock→battle fatigue→operational exhaustion→PTSD), because "concepts, not words, are in charge." Consequence: every engineered term has a half-life, so any framework tracking manipulative language must be diachronic — a static lexicon rots on schedule.

key_findings.claim: The manufacturing side outgrew the checking side by an order of magnitude
key_findings.detail: PR practitioners outnumbered US journalists roughly 2:1 in 1980, 3:1 by 2008, and over 6:1 by 2018 (BLS data; newsroom employment fell 23% 2008-2017 while PR kept growing). The asymmetry itself is a century-scale finding: professionally engineered language is now the default input to public discourse, not the exception.

key_findings.claim: Ellul diagnosed the deepest mass-media mutation: propaganda as environment, not message
key_findings.detail: Propaganda: The Formation of Men's Attitudes (French 1962, English 1965) taxonomizes in pairs — political/sociological, agitation/integration, vertical/horizontal, rational/irrational — and argues modern integration propaganda is a continuous total environment the individual comes to need, building on Lasswell's Propaganda Technique in the World War (1927), which had defined propaganda as management of collective attitudes by "manipulation of significant symbols" and founded quantitative content analysis.

key_findings.claim: The medium-change mutation pattern is consistent and therefore predictive
key_findings.detail: Oratory-era technique lived in performance and argument (delivery, audience, enthymeme). Broadcast selected for what survives compression and repetition (symbol-association devices: transfer, glittering generality, slogans), for deleted authorship (press releases laundered into news voice, Bernays' front groups — the industrial-scale passive voice), and for feedback-tested wording (Bernays' engineering → Luntz's dials). The algorithmic/LLM era amplifies each: dial-testing becomes per-user real-time engagement optimization, deleted authorship becomes fully synthetic authorship, one-message-to-millions inverts into millions of personalized messages, and Ellul's integration propaganda becomes the feed itself.

key_findings.claim: The IPA's 1937 device list has already been reborn as machine-readable annotation — captioneer's exact shape
key_findings.detail: Da San Martino et al. (2019) built a corpus of ~550 news articles with professional span-level annotations against 18 propaganda techniques largely descended from the IPA list; SemEval-2020 Task 11 formalized two subtasks — Span Identification (find the manipulative fragment) and Technique Classification (name the device) — which is structurally identical to captioneer's "every mark points at a visible phrase" rule, meaning interoperability with existing corpora and models is available off the shelf.

techniques.name: Name Calling
techniques.definition: Attaching a bad label to a person or idea so the audience rejects it without examining evidence.
techniques.example: "terrorist," "radical," "un-American" applied in place of argument
techniques.origin: IPA, "How to Detect Propaganda," Propaganda Analysis bulletin, November 1937 (Clyde Miller with Violet Edwards)
techniques.languages: Language-universal; the labels themselves are culture-specific

techniques.name: Glittering Generalities
techniques.definition: Binding a program to virtue words (freedom, progress, justice) so vague and positively charged that assent is given without inspection — the mirror image of name calling.
techniques.example: "a common-sense plan for working families"
techniques.origin: IPA, November 1937
techniques.languages: Universal; each language has its own halo lexicon

techniques.name: Transfer
techniques.definition: Carrying the authority or prestige of a respected symbol or institution over to something unrelated so it is accepted by association.
techniques.example: flag, cross, or lab coat behind a product or policy; Bernays' cigarettes as feminist "torches of freedom"
techniques.origin: IPA, November 1937

techniques.name: Testimonial
techniques.definition: Having a loved or hated figure endorse or condemn an idea so the audience adopts the attitude toward the figure as a verdict on the idea.
techniques.example: celebrity endorsements; "doctors recommend" advertising
techniques.origin: IPA, November 1937

techniques.name: Plain Folks
techniques.definition: A speaker presents themselves and their ideas as "of the people" to borrow the trust given to ordinary folk.
techniques.example: politician in work clothes at a diner; folksy register in speeches
techniques.origin: IPA, November 1937
techniques.languages: Universal; the plain-register markers are language-specific (dialect, colloquialism choice)

techniques.name: Card Stacking
techniques.definition: Selective use of facts, half-truths, and favorable framings — over- and under-emphasis — to give the best or worst possible case; ancestor of modern "cherry-picking."
techniques.example: citing only trials where the drug worked; quoting a report's one favorable line
techniques.origin: IPA, November 1937
techniques.languages: Universal; the only IPA device that is about content selection rather than surface wording

techniques.name: Bandwagon
techniques.definition: Claiming everyone (in the audience's group) is doing or believing it, exploiting conformity: "jump aboard or be left behind."
techniques.example: "Americans agree..."; "the fastest-growing movement"
techniques.origin: IPA, November 1937

techniques.name: Dying metaphors
techniques.definition: Worn-out metaphors used because they save the writer inventing a phrase; they no longer evoke an image and often get mixed, signaling the writer isn't visualizing what they say.
techniques.example: toe the line, Achilles' heel, no axe to grind, swansong
techniques.origin: Orwell, "Politics and the English Language," Horizon, April 1946
techniques.languages: Every language has its own stock; the diagnostic (mixed/dead imagery) transfers

techniques.name: Operators / verbal false limbs
techniques.definition: Padding simple verbs into vague noun-phrase constructions that add syllables and symmetry while blurring agency.
techniques.example: "render inoperative," "make contact with," "be subjected to" instead of break, contact, suffer
techniques.origin: Orwell, 1946
techniques.languages: Strongest in English/European bureaucratic registers; analogous light-verb padding exists widely (e.g., suru-nominal constructions in Japanese officialese)

techniques.name: Pretentious diction
techniques.definition: Latinate/foreign/scientific-sounding vocabulary used to dress bias as objectivity and dignify shabby judgments.
techniques.example: "epoch-making, inexorable, veritable"; "liquidate" for kill
techniques.origin: Orwell, 1946
techniques.languages: English-specific realization (Latinate register); most languages have an analogous prestige register (Sanskritized Hindi, Sino-Japanese kango, Arabic fusha officialese)

techniques.name: Meaningless words
techniques.definition: Words with no agreed referent deployed for their emotional charge; often consciously used dishonestly because speaker and hearer hold different private definitions.
techniques.example: "fascism" as generic insult; "democracy," "freedom," "realistic" in political prose
techniques.origin: Orwell, 1946
techniques.languages: Universal; the specific hollow words differ per political culture

techniques.name: Newspeak vocabulary engineering
techniques.definition: Fictional crystallization of real techniques: shrink the lexicon so dissent lacks words (A vocabulary stripped of ambiguity, B vocabulary of politically loaded compounds like goodthink/crimestop/bellyfeel, C vocabulary compartmentalizing science), producing "duckspeak" — speech without thought.
techniques.example: "doubleplusgood"; abolishing "free" in the political sense
techniques.origin: Orwell, "The Principles of Newspeak," appendix to Nineteen Eighty-Four, 1949
techniques.languages: A thought experiment in English, but modeled on real controlled vocabularies and totalitarian language (LTI: Klemperer's Nazi German)

techniques.name: Euphemism (as doublespeak)
techniques.definition: A word or phrase deployed to avoid a harsh reality and mislead — distinguished by Lutz from tactful euphemism by its intent to shield the speaker from responsibility.
techniques.example: "pacification" for village destruction; "downsizing" for firing; "collateral damage" for civilian deaths
techniques.origin: William Lutz, Doublespeak, 1989 (building on NCTE Committee on Public Doublespeak, 1972-74)
techniques.languages: Universal mechanism; Lutz's corpus is American English

techniques.name: Jargon (as doublespeak)
techniques.definition: Specialist in-group language used on out-group audiences to overwhelm and impress rather than inform.
techniques.example: "involuntary conversion of a 727" for a plane crash (airline report)
techniques.origin: Lutz, 1989
techniques.languages: Universal; every profession in every language grows one

techniques.name: Gobbledygook / bureaucratese
techniques.definition: Sheer volume of complex, stacked language that buries meaning; the reader assumes their own inadequacy rather than the text's emptiness.
techniques.example: multi-clause regulatory prose that resolves to "we may cancel anytime"
techniques.origin: Lutz, 1989 (term "gobbledygook" coined by US Rep. Maury Maverick, 1944)

techniques.name: Inflated language
techniques.definition: Making the ordinary seem extraordinary — grandiose titles and descriptions that upgrade status without changing substance.
techniques.example: "automotive internist" for mechanic; "vertical transportation corps" for elevator operators
techniques.origin: Lutz, 1989

techniques.name: Manufactured event (created news)
techniques.definition: Staging an occurrence whose only purpose is to be reported, so the medium's news-voice launders advocacy into fact.
techniques.example: Torches of Freedom march, Easter Parade, March 31, 1929 — debutantes hired to smoke Lucky Strikes as "protest"
techniques.origin: Edward Bernays, 1929 (theorized later as the "pseudo-event," Boorstin 1961)

techniques.name: Third-party technique / front groups
techniques.definition: Routing a message through apparently independent voices (experts, institutes, citizens' groups) so the true author — and their interest — is deleted; the industrial-scale analogue of the passive voice.
techniques.example: tobacco-funded "research institutes"; Bernays' physician endorsements of bacon breakfasts
techniques.origin: Bernays, practice from 1920s; named in PR literature
techniques.languages: Language-independent; leaves textual tells in sourcing and attribution

techniques.name: Engineered lexical substitution
techniques.definition: Replacing a term with a tested alternative whose measured emotional response better serves the client; the pair is decided by dial-session data, not etymology or accuracy.
techniques.example: "death tax" for estate tax (20-30% higher opposition in dial tests); "climate change" for global warming ("less frightening," 2002 memo); "exploring for energy" for drilling for oil
techniques.origin: Frank Luntz, 1990s-2000s; Words That Work, 2007
techniques.languages: Method is language-independent; documented pairs are American English

techniques.name: Euphemism treadmill
techniques.definition: A diachronic law, not a device: each euphemism absorbs the stigma of its referent and must be replaced, because "concepts, not words, are in charge" — predicting a decaying succession of terms around any taboo.
techniques.example: shell shock → battle fatigue → operational exhaustion → PTSD; water closet → toilet → bathroom → rest room → lavatory
techniques.origin: Steven Pinker, New York Times, April 3, 1994; expanded in The Blank Slate (2002)
techniques.languages: Attested cross-linguistically wherever taboo domains exist

techniques.name: The five filters (structural manipulation)
techniques.definition: Channel-level, not text-level: concentrated ownership, advertising revenue, official-source dependence, flak, and fear ideology (originally anticommunism) filter what becomes news, producing propaganda without any conspirator or detectable sentence-level tell.
techniques.example: a story dropped because it threatens advertisers; flak campaigns disciplining outlets
techniques.origin: Edward S. Herman & Noam Chomsky, Manufacturing Consent, 1988

techniques.name: Agitation vs integration propaganda
techniques.definition: Ellul's central pair: agitation propaganda mobilizes for episodic action (wars, revolutions); integration propaganda is continuous, ambient conformity-maintenance that the modern individual comes to need — propaganda as environment rather than message.
techniques.example: wartime hate campaigns (agitation) vs advertising + civic ritual + news rhythm as a whole (integration)
techniques.origin: Jacques Ellul, Propagandes, 1962 (Eng. Propaganda: The Formation of Men's Attitudes, 1965)

techniques.name: Manipulation of significant symbols
techniques.definition: Lasswell's founding definition of propaganda technique — managing collective attitudes by manipulating culturally charged symbols (flags, atrocity stories, sacred words); also the root of quantitative content analysis as the counter-method.
techniques.example: WWI atrocity narratives; symbol counts in wartime press analysis
techniques.origin: Harold Lasswell, Propaganda Technique in the World War, 1927

framework_implications: Adopt span-anchored annotation as the interchange format: captioneer's 'every mark points at a visible phrase' is structurally identical to SemEval-2020 Task 11's Span Identification + Technique Classification, so define the framework's data model as (text, span offsets, technique ID, evidence note) and publish a crosswalk from captioneer's six families to the PTC 18-technique taxonomy — this buys instant interoperability with existing corpora, models, and evaluation benchmarks.

Model the technique taxonomy as a versioned genealogy graph, not a flat list: every technique record carries origin (author, publication, exact date), lineage edges (IPA 'Name Calling' 1937 → SemEval 'Name calling/Labeling' 2019), and cross-scheme aliases (Lutz euphemism vs IPA glittering generality overlaps). This makes the charter's 'origin and evolution of techniques' first-class queryable data instead of prose.

Enforce a three-layer separation with different engine claims: Layer 1 textual devices (IPA/Orwell/Lutz families — detectable in a pasted statement, captioneer's current scope); Layer 2 structural filters (Herman-Chomsky — properties of channel economics, encyclopedia/education content, never claimed as text detection); Layer 3 diachronic laws (euphemism treadmill, engineered substitution — require historical term data, surfaced as cited annotations). The century's credibility failures came from blurring these layers.

Build two contribution-friendly datasets that only an open project can maintain: (a) a term-succession table for euphemism-treadmill chains (term, predecessor, date range, domain, citation — e.g., shell shock→battle fatigue→operational exhaustion→PTSD), and (b) an engineered-pair registry (death tax/estate tax; climate change/global warming) with memo-level provenance. Detection is then lexicon lookup + citation — 'this term is a documented engineered substitution' — which stays inside the reads-the-language-never-the-mind charter because the claim is about the word's documented history, not the speaker's intent.

Add a medium-affordances field to every technique record (oratory / print / radio / TV / feed / LLM) documenting how it manifests per medium, because the 1900-2000 record shows mutation is predictable: broadcast selected for compression + repetition + deleted authorship + tested wording; algorithmic media select for arousal, personalization, and convergent tested phrasing. This field is what lets the framework predict rather than chase.

Governance must be designed against the IPA failure mode: the first lens-of-clarity project died in 5 years from a single funder's collapse, wartime pressure to exempt 'our side,' and political flak (Hearst, HUAC). Concretely: open license and forkable data so no board vote can kill the corpus, multi-institution stewardship, diversified funding with a public cap on any single source, a structurally enforced symmetry rule (analyses must run on all political sides, audited), and a documented expectation that flak (Herman-Chomsky filter 4) will target the project itself.

Write the lineage into the charter: IPA analyzed devices not truth, Orwell attacked language not persons, Lutz judged the function of words not the hearts of speakers, and Pinker's treadmill proves words can't be permanently sanitized or condemned. Present 'reads the language, never the mind' as a 90-year-old disciplinary norm with citations, not a novel legal disclaimer — it is the framework's strongest defense against both misuse and flak.

Position the truth caption as pedagogy with provenance: the plain-meaning first-person rewrite is the direct heir of the IPA's classroom method ('What Makes You Think So?', ~1M students) — restate the message stripped of device so the reader learns to do it unaided. Add a 'show your work' mode linking each change in the rewrite back to a marked span, turning the LLM feature into a teachable, auditable transformation rather than an oracle.

For the LLM era, detect optimization artifacts instead of trying to detect machines or lies: the tell of industrial language has always been testedness and convergence (Luntz slogans repeated verbatim across speakers, engineered pairs, high-arousal loaded framing). These are measurable against corpora — verbatim-phrase propagation, known-pair lookup, register anomalies — and they generalize from the PR century to synthetic authorship without ever requiring a claim about any mind, human or model.

factChecks.claim: Lippmann first used 'manufacture of consent' in Liberty and the News (1919), elaborated in Public Opinion (1922); pseudo-environment, 'pictures in our heads', press cannot carry democracy's truth-telling burden
factChecks.correction: Liberty and the News was published in 1920, not 1919 (its constituent essays ran in The Atlantic Monthly in 1919, but the book — where the phrase appears — is 1920). All other elements are confirmed.
factChecks.evidence: Liberty and the News (Harcourt, Brace & Howe) asks whether 'government by consent [can] survive... in a time when the manufacture of consent is an unregulated private enterprise' — Google Books and the Princeton UP reissue date the original to 1920. Gutenberg full text of Public Opinion (1922) confirms: Chapter I is 'The World Outside and the Pictures in Our Heads'; 'the insertion between man and his environment of a pseudo-environment. To that pseudo-environment his behavior is a response'; 'That the manufacture of consent is capable of great refinements no one, I think, denies'; and the press 'is too frail to carry' the burden democratic theory assigns it. Note: many secondary sources (e.g. Aeon) credit the coinage to Public Opinion; the 1920 usage predates it, supporting the 'first used' claim once redated.

factChecks.claim: CPI (1917-19, George Creel) used all media; Four Minute Men: ~75,000 volunteers delivering centrally scripted 4-minute talks, advised to avoid 'hymns of hate'; its excesses were the cautionary blueprint for WWII's OWI
factChecks.correction: 'Centrally scripted' overstates it: the CPI centrally supplied topics and talking points (Four Minute Men Bulletins), but per the claimed source itself, speakers were 'advised to keep their message positive, always use their own words and avoid hymns of hate.' All other facts stand.
factChecks.evidence: Wikipedia (the claimed source) confirms: CPI operated April 13, 1917 - August 21, 1919 under chairman George Creel; used newsprint, posters, radio, telegraph, movies, pamphlets and a daily Official Bulletin; ~75,000 volunteers delivered (per Creel) 7.5 million four-minute orations; the 'hymns of hate' advice is quoted verbatim. The OWI framing is broadly supported — the OWI Wikipedia article says CPI/Creel Committee propaganda 'were viewed as a failure,' feeding Congressional and public fear of a propaganda machine — though the CPI article itself credits the Office of Censorship (not OWI) with explicitly rejecting the CPI precedent.

factChecks.claim: Bernays' Propaganda (1928) opens with the 'conscious and intelligent manipulation... important element in democratic society' line; Torches of Freedom (Easter Parade March 31, 1929, ~10 debutantes, Lucky Strikes, Brill's symbol, concealed client); 'The Engineering of Consent' in Annals 250:113-120 (1947)
factChecks.evidence: Wikipedia's Propaganda (book) article quotes the opening thesis verbatim: 'The conscious and intelligent manipulation of the organized habits and opinions of the masses is an important element in democratic society' (the famous first sentence of ch. 1, 'Organizing Chaos'). Torches of Freedom (Wikipedia + multiple histories): 31 March 1929 Easter parade; George Washington Hill of American Tobacco hired Bernays; Bernays' secretary Bertha Hunt posed as a feminist activist and telegraphed debutantes (30 invited, ~10 marched smoking Lucky Strikes — '~10' is fair); psychoanalyst A. A. Brill supplied the symbol ('Cigarettes, which are equated with men, become torches of freedom'); the tobacco client was concealed behind the staged feminist protest. Citation exact per RePEc/SAGE: Bernays, 'The Engineering of Consent,' The Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science, vol. 250(1), pp. 113-120, March 1947.

factChecks.claim: IPA (founded 1937 by Clyde R. Miller at Columbia Teachers College, $10,000 Filene grant); bulletin ~10,000 subscribers at $2/year; corresponded with ~2,500 teachers; 'What Makes You Think So?' school series reached ~1 million students
factChecks.evidence: The claimed CJR source confirms every figure: Miller founded the IPA in 1937 at Columbia's Teachers College with a $10,000 grant from Edward A. Filene; 'Some 10,000 people subscribed to the Bulletin, which cost $2.00 a year'; it 'corresponded with some 2,500 teachers'; the series 'What Makes You Think So?...' was distributed through Scholastic in 1939-40, and 'By the late 1930s, 1 million school children were using IPA's methods.' Minor nuances: the 1M figure is for IPA methods broadly rather than the series alone, and Wikipedia lists Kirtley Mather and Filene as co-founders (incorporated September 23, 1937).

factChecks.claim: IPA's seven devices (Name Calling, Glittering Generalities, Transfer, Testimonial, Plain Folks, Card Stacking, Bandwagon) first published in 'How to Detect Propaganda' (Propaganda Analysis, Nov 1937), drafted principally by Clyde Miller with Violet Edwards; Sproule traces origins to older rhetoric/fallacy traditions
factChecks.correction: Sproule's research note attributes the seven-devices format ENTIRELY to Clyde R. Miller, not 'Miller with Violet Edwards' — Violet Edwards Lavine herself 'attributed the seven devices format entirely to her mentor, Miller,' and Sproule concludes 'it is possible now to give Clyde R. Miller full credit.' Edwards only co-authored a 1936 precursor application (Miller & Edwards, 'The Intelligent Teacher's Guide Through Campaign Propaganda,' The Clearing House, Oct 1936).
factChecks.evidence: Extracted the full text of the claimed source (Sproule, 'Authorship and Origins of the Seven Propaganda Devices: A Research Note,' Rhetoric & Public Affairs 4(1), 2001, 135-143). Device list matches exactly (name calling, glittering generalities, transfer, testimonial, plain folks, card stacking, band wagon); first publication confirmed as the unsigned article 'How to Detect Propaganda,' Propaganda Analysis 1, no. 2 (November 1937): 5-7 (Sproule's note 3). The fallacy-tradition link is only lightly supported — Sproule quotes Edgar Dale that the format 'takes a number of very complicated fallacies in logic and reduces them to terms that a fourteen year old child can understand,' but the note's thesis is Miller's sole authorship from his Teachers College lecture materials, not a genealogy of older rhetorical traditions.

factChecks.claim: IPA died of three compounding causes: farewell issue (Jan 9, 1942) saying dispassionate analysis of 'good' and 'bad' propaganda would be 'misunderstood'/misused in the war emergency; funding collapsed after Filene's death; Hearst papers attacked Miller and HUAC labeled the IPA a Communist front (1947)
factChecks.evidence: Farewell issue: CJR and Schiffrin (IJoC 16, 2022) both confirm the January 9, 1942 'We Say Au Revoir' issue stating that 'dispassionate analysis of all kinds of propaganda, good and bad, is easily misunderstood during a war emergency' and could be 'misused for undesirable purposes.' Funding: IJoC — 'Running low on funding, the IPA stopped publishing the Bulletin in 1942'; Filene died September 26, 1937, his Good Will Fund committed only three years, and the IPA then patched together AJC/Whitney Foundation/subscription money — so the collapse followed Filene's death but by ~4 years, not proximately. Hearst: CJR — 'Hearst had complained to Teachers College about Miller, saying he should lay off'; IJoC documents Hearst-press red-baiting of Miller (largely via his Methodist Federation ties). HUAC: CJR — 'The House Unamerican Activities Committee in 1947 also attacked the IPA calling it a Communist front organization.' Caveat: the claimed source (Wikipedia's IPA article) contains only the farewell quote and January 1942 date — the Filene, Hearst, and HUAC details are supported by CJR and IJoC instead.

findings.summary: Between 2000 and 2026 the field converged on a workable answer to "can manipulation be cataloged machine-readably?": yes for rhetoric, no for lies. The strongest lineage is the QCRI/Padova propaganda-technique line — Da San Martino et al. (EMNLP 2019) defined 18 span-level techniques on the PTC corpus (CC BY 4.0), SemEval-2020 Task 11 ran it with 14, SemEval-2023 Task 3 matured it into a 2-level taxonomy of 6 families and 23 persuasion techniques annotated at paragraph level across 9 languages (EN/FR/DE/IT/PL/RU + surprise ES/EL/KA), and SemEval-2024 Task 4 recast the same 22 techniques as a hierarchical DAG for multimodal memes in EN/AR/BG/MK — proving the taxonomy transfers across languages, genres, and modalities. Parallel catalogs converge on nearly the same objects: MAFALDA (NAACL 2024, CC BY-SA) unified Argotario/LOGIC/COVID/ElecDeb-style fallacy datasets into Aristotle's pathos/ethos/logos over 23 fine-grained fallacies; Cambridge's Bad News game teaches 6 techniques and Jigsaw's Science-Advances-validated prebunking videos teach 5 — all subsets of the SemEval families. DISARM (CC BY-SA 4.0, v1.6.1 2026) covers the complementary campaign-behavior layer (150+ ATT&CK-style TTPs). Meanwhile the deception-detection literature is a hard negative result: verbal lie cues have median d≈0.10 (DePaulo 2003), humans hit 54% accuracy (Bond & DePaulo 2006), and SCAN is experimentally indistinguishable from chance — vindicating captioneer's "reads the language, never the mind" charter as the scientifically correct scope. The LLM era raises stakes: GPT-3 propaganda matches real foreign propagandists (PNAS Nexus 2024), personalized GPT-4 beats human debaters 64% of the time (Nature Human Behaviour 2025), and post-training/prompting — not scale — drive persuasion while the most persuasive models are the least accurate (Science 2025); yet the same machinery durably cuts conspiracy belief ~20% (Science 2024). The framework's clearest move: adopt the SemEval-2023 taxonomy as its open spine (the taxonomy is freely reusable even though the 2023-24 corpora are research-restricted), crosswalk it to MAFALDA/DISARM/captioneer's six families, seed gold data only from CC-licensed corpora (PTC, MAFALDA), avoid LIWC's proprietary dictionaries, and build the teaching layer on inoculation-theory evidence.

key_findings.claim: The 18-technique PTC taxonomy (2019) is the root of the whole computational lineage, and its corpus is CC BY 4.0
key_findings.detail: Da San Martino, Yu, Barrón-Cedeño, Petrov, Nakov, 'Fine-Grained Analysis of Propaganda in News Articles' (EMNLP 2019) introduced span-level annotation of 18 propaganda techniques in news (loaded language, name calling, repetition, exaggeration/minimisation, doubt, appeal to fear/prejudice, flag-waving, causal oversimplification, slogans, appeal to authority, black-and-white fallacy, thought-terminating cliché, whataboutism, reductio ad Hitlerum, red herring, bandwagon, obfuscation/intentional-vagueness/confusion, straw man). SemEval-2020 Task 11 (250 teams registered, 44 submitted) ran two subtasks — Span Identification and Technique Classification — on the PTC-SemEval20 corpus with 14 techniques: it merged red herring + straw man into whataboutism, bandwagon into reductio ad Hitlerum, and dropped obfuscation for sparsity. The corpus is openly downloadable from Zenodo under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0.

key_findings.claim: SemEval-2023 Task 3 is the mature, multilingual, hierarchical version: 6 families, 23 techniques, 9 languages — but its corpus is NOT freely redistributable
key_findings.detail: Piskorski, Stefanovitch, Da San Martino, Nakov (ACL 2023): subtask 3 annotates every paragraph of news articles with a 2-level taxonomy — Attack on Reputation (name calling/labeling, guilt by association, casting doubt, appeal to hypocrisy, questioning the reputation), Justification (flag waving, appeal to authority, appeal to popularity, appeal to values, appeal to fear/prejudice), Distraction (straw man, red herring, whataboutism), Simplification (causal oversimplification, false dilemma/no choice, consequential oversimplification), Call (slogans, conversation killer, appeal to time), Manipulative Wording (loaded language, obfuscation/vagueness/confusion, exaggeration or minimisation, repetition). Data in English, French, German, Italian, Polish, Russian plus surprise-test Spanish, Greek, Georgian; 181 teams registered, 41 submitted; XLM-RoBERTa-class multilingual fine-tuning won. Crucially, the dataset terms permit use 'only in the context of this shared task, and only for scientific research purposes' with redistribution prohibited — the taxonomy is open (published in CC BY 4.0 ACL papers), the corpus is not.

key_findings.claim: SemEval-2024 Task 4 proved the taxonomy works as a hierarchy across modalities and new languages
key_findings.detail: 'Multilingual Detection of Persuasion Techniques in Memes' organized the 22 persuasion techniques into a multi-level hierarchy (DAG) with hierarchy-aware scoring (partial credit for predicting an ancestor); ~10,000 memes in English plus surprise Bulgarian, North Macedonian, and Arabic; three subtasks spanning text-only and multimodal (text+image); 153 teams registered, 48 submitted. Lesson: technique catalogs should be trees/DAGs with coarse-to-fine credit, not flat label lists.

key_findings.claim: DISARM is the open, ATT&CK-style standard for the campaign-behavior layer, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0
key_findings.detail: DISARM Foundation's Red framework (v1.6.1, March 2026) catalogs disinformation-operation TTPs across tactic stages TA01–TA18 (Plan Strategy, Plan Objectives, Microtarget, Develop Content ... Drive Online Harms) with 150+ techniques and sub-techniques carrying stable IDs (e.g., T0016 Create Clickbait, T0046 Search Engine Optimization, T0097 Present Persona with sub-techniques T0097.100 Individual Persona etc.); a Blue framework catalogs countermeasures. STIX templates (DISARM_CTI) enable TAXII interchange; used by EU/EDMO/ENISA FIMI analysts. It describes operations (accounts, amplification, personas), not text spans — complementary to, not competitive with, SemEval-style rhetoric taxonomies.

key_findings.claim: MAFALDA unified the fragmented fallacy datasets into a 3-level Aristotle-rooted taxonomy of 23 fallacies, CC BY-SA
