key_findings.detail: Helwe, Calamai, Paris, Clavel, Suchanek (NAACL 2024): Level 0 = fallacious/not; Level 1 = pathos (Appeal to Emotion), ethos (Fallacy of Credibility), logos (Fallacy of Logic); Level 2 = 23 fine-grained types — Credibility: abusive ad hominem, ad populum, appeal to false authority, appeal to nature, appeal to tradition, guilt by association, tu quoque; Logic: causal oversimplification, circular reasoning, equivocation, false analogy, false causality, false dilemma, hasty generalization, slippery slope, straw man, fallacy of division; Emotion: appeal to positive emotion, anger, fear, pity, ridicule, worse problem. Corpus: 9,545 unannotated texts merged from prior datasets + 200 gold texts with 260 manually annotated fallacy spans, each with a written justification; introduces a subjectivity-tolerant evaluation. Code and data public under CC BY-SA (copyleft imposed by the Goffredo et al. source dataset). Predecessors it aligns: Argotario (Habernal et al. 2017, gamified, 5 fallacy types), LOGIC/LogicClimate (Jin et al. 2022, 13 types from educational materials and climate news), COVID-19 fallacy annotations (Musi et al./Alhindi et al. 2022, 10 types).

key_findings.claim: ElecDeb60to16 grounds fallacy detection in real political debate with argumentative structure
key_findings.detail: Goffredo et al. (IJCAI 2022; EMNLP 2023 extension ElecDeb60to20 adding Trump-Biden) annotate US presidential debates 1960-2020 with six fallacy categories — ad hominem, appeal to authority, appeal to emotion, false cause, slippery slope, slogans — layered on claims/premises and support/attack relations, showing fallacy labels can sit on top of argument mining. Its license terms propagated CC BY-SA copyleft into MAFALDA.

key_findings.claim: LIWC is the dominant psycholinguistic lexicon but is proprietary and cannot be embedded in an open framework
key_findings.detail: LIWC-22 (Pennebaker et al., UT Austin) scores text on 100+ validated psychological dimensions (the Receptiviti API exposes 94 LIWC categories: pronouns, negations, emotion, cognitive processes, certainty/tentativeness — the classic home of hedging measurement). It is owned by Pennebaker Conglomerates; academic licenses are restricted to university research, and Receptiviti Inc. holds exclusive commercial distribution rights. Its dictionaries may not be redistributed — an open framework must build or adopt open lexicons (and hedging/certainty is exactly the dimension the SemEval taxonomies lack).

key_findings.claim: The deception-detection meta-analyses are a decisive negative result: verbal cues to lying are faint and human accuracy is near chance
key_findings.detail: DePaulo et al. 2003 (Psych. Bulletin, 158 cues across 120 samples): of 50 cues examined in 5+ studies only 14 (28%) related significantly to deception, median effect d≈0.10, mean of significant cues d=0.25. Bond & DePaulo 2006: across ~24,500 judges, average truth/lie classification accuracy is 54% vs 50% chance. Luke et al. 2023 survey and Vrij's reviews confirm no reliable verbal or nonverbal 'Pinocchio's nose'. Any system that outputs 'this text is a lie' from linguistic features is claiming something the evidence base cannot support.

key_findings.claim: SCAN (Scientific Content Analysis) is used by police worldwide and is pseudoscience
key_findings.detail: Bogaard, Meijer, Vrij, Merckelbach (Frontiers in Psychology, 2016): SCAN could not distinguish truthful from fabricated accounts of a negative event; it lacks a defined criteria list and standardized scoring; only ~6 validity studies exist (4 peer-reviewed), none supportive. In a survey of scholars, 88% qualified SCAN as pseudoscience and 96% said it should not be taught to law enforcement. This is the cautionary tale for 'statement analysis' products — and the scientific backing for captioneer's explicit NOT-a-lie-detector charter.

key_findings.claim: Inoculation theory supplies the validated 'teaching layer': small technique lists, measurable recognition gains
key_findings.detail: Cambridge's Bad News game (Roozenbeek & van der Linden, 2018+) has players wield 6 misinformation techniques — impersonation, emotional exploitation, polarization, conspiracy, discrediting, trolling — and improves misinformation identification post-gameplay across cultures (with caveats: an Indian replication found no discrimination improvement, and some effects reflect response bias). Google Jigsaw + Cambridge (Roozenbeek et al., Science Advances 2022) ran 90-second prebunking videos as YouTube ads teaching 5 techniques — emotionally manipulative language, incoherence, false dichotomies, scapegoating, ad hominem — yielding 5-10% better technique recognition in randomized field tests on ~millions of users; Jigsaw then deployed a scapegoating campaign in Poland/Czechia/Slovakia. Effects held across ideology, education, and personality. Every technique they teach maps onto the SemEval-2023 families.

key_findings.claim: AI-generated propaganda already matches professional human propagandists
key_findings.detail: Goldstein, Chao, Grossman, Stamos, Tomz (PNAS Nexus, Feb 2024): in a preregistered experiment, GPT-3-davinci articles seeded from real covert foreign propaganda were nearly as persuasive as the originals at moving US respondents to agree with the propaganda theses, and light human curation closed the gap. A 2025 PNAS Nexus follow-up documents measurable AI impact in an actual state-backed campaign ('Generative propaganda').

key_findings.claim: Personalized conversational LLMs out-persuade humans in debate
key_findings.detail: Salvi, Horta Ribeiro, Gallotti, West, 'On the conversational persuasiveness of GPT-4' (Nature Human Behaviour 9:1645-1653, 2025): in preregistered multi-round debates, GPT-4 with access to basic sociodemographic data about its opponent had 81.2% higher odds of shifting post-debate agreement than a human persuader, winning 64% of the time — microtargeting works conversationally with trivial personal data.

key_findings.claim: What makes AI persuasive is post-training and information density — and the most persuasive configurations are the least accurate
key_findings.detail: Hackenburg et al., 'The levers of political persuasion with conversational AI' (Science, 2025; UK AISI collaboration): 19 LLMs, 707 political issues, 76,977 responses from 42,357 participants. Persuasion post-training boosted persuasiveness up to +51% and prompting up to +27%, dwarfing model scale and personalization; prompting models to pack in facts/evidence ('information density') was the strongest lever, yet the most information-dense, most persuasive outputs contained the most inaccurate claims. Detection frameworks should therefore treat confident factual barrage as a manipulation surface, not only emotional rhetoric.

key_findings.claim: The same conversational machinery works for de-manipulation: durable ~20% reduction in conspiracy belief
key_findings.detail: Costello, Pennycook, Rand (Science, Sept 2024): 2,190 conspiracy believers held personalized evidence-based dialogues with GPT-4 Turbo; conspiracy belief fell ~20%, the effect persisted at 2 months, generalized across conspiracy types, and worked even for entrenched believers. Persuasion taxonomies can power counter-speech, not just detection — the scientific warrant for captioneer's opt-in truth caption growing into an evidence-dialogue feature.

key_findings.claim: License terrain is asymmetric: taxonomies are open, several key corpora are not
key_findings.detail: Freely reusable: PTC-SemEval20 corpus (CC BY 4.0, Zenodo), DISARM frameworks (CC BY-SA 4.0), MAFALDA code+data (CC BY-SA), all ACL taxonomy papers (CC BY 4.0). Restricted: SemEval-2023 Task 3 and SemEval-2024 Task 4 corpora (shared-task scientific research only, no redistribution, passcode-gated), LIWC dictionaries (proprietary, commercial rights exclusive to Receptiviti). An open framework can adopt the 23-technique taxonomy wholesale but must assemble its own redistributable example corpus from PTC + MAFALDA + newly annotated community data.

techniques.name: Name Calling or Labeling
techniques.definition: Attaching a loaded positive or negative label to a person/idea so the audience judges the label instead of the argument.
techniques.example: 'the radical left', 'globalists', 'fake news media'
techniques.languages: Annotated in EN/FR/DE/IT/PL/RU (+ES/EL/KA test) in SemEval-2023; EN in PTC
techniques.origin: IPA 1937 'name calling' → PTC-18 (2019) → SemEval-2023 family: Attack on Reputation

techniques.name: Guilt by Association
techniques.definition: Discrediting a target by linking it to a hated person or group (absorbs reductio ad Hitlerum).
techniques.example: 'This policy is exactly what the Nazis did'
techniques.origin: PTC-18 reductio ad Hitlerum → generalized in SemEval-2023

techniques.name: Casting Doubt
techniques.definition: Undermining credibility of a person or institution by questioning it, without disproving anything.
techniques.example: 'Can we really trust the election officials?'
techniques.origin: PTC-18 'Doubt' → SemEval-2023 Attack on Reputation

techniques.name: Appeal to Hypocrisy (Tu Quoque)
techniques.definition: Answering an accusation by accusing the accuser of the same or worse, instead of addressing the charge.
techniques.example: 'You lecture us on emissions while flying private jets'
techniques.origin: Classical tu quoque fallacy; added as fine class in SemEval-2023

techniques.name: Questioning the Reputation
techniques.definition: Preemptively smearing a target's character with negative claims unrelated to the argument at hand.
techniques.example: 'Remember, this senator was once investigated for fraud'
techniques.origin: New in SemEval-2023 Attack on Reputation family

techniques.name: Flag Waving
techniques.definition: Justifying a position by appeal to national, group, or patriotic identity rather than evidence.
techniques.example: 'Real Americans support this bill'
techniques.origin: IPA-era propaganda device → PTC-18 → SemEval-2023 Justification

techniques.name: Appeal to Authority
techniques.definition: Using an authority's endorsement as the sole support for a claim, including false or irrelevant authorities.
techniques.example: 'A Nobel laureate says the vaccine is dangerous'
techniques.languages: 9 SemEval-2023 languages; MAFALDA 'appeal to false authority'; ElecDeb60to16
techniques.origin: Classical argumentum ad verecundiam → PTC-18 → SemEval-2023 Justification

techniques.name: Appeal to Popularity (Bandwagon)
techniques.definition: Arguing something is true or right because everyone (or the majority) believes or does it.
techniques.example: 'Millions have already switched — what are you waiting for?'
techniques.origin: PTC-18 'Bandwagon' → SemEval-2023 Justification

techniques.name: Appeal to Values
techniques.definition: Anchoring a claim to sacred or widely shared values (freedom, family, tradition) so rejecting the claim feels like rejecting the value.
techniques.example: 'This law is an attack on family values'
techniques.origin: New in SemEval-2023 Justification family

techniques.name: Appeal to Fear or Prejudice
techniques.definition: Building support by cultivating anxiety, panic, or prejudice toward the alternative.
techniques.example: 'Without this wall, criminals will flood our towns'
techniques.languages: 9 SemEval-2023 languages; MAFALDA pathos 'appeal to fear'; Jigsaw prebunk 'fearmongering'
techniques.origin: Classical ad metum; IPA → PTC-18 → SemEval-2023; also a Jigsaw 2022 prebunking video topic

techniques.name: Straw Man
techniques.definition: Misrepresenting the opponent's position into an easier-to-attack distortion, then refuting the distortion.
techniques.example: 'They want open borders and no country at all'
techniques.origin: Classical; PTC-18 → merged 2020 → restored as own class in SemEval-2023 Distraction

techniques.name: Red Herring
techniques.definition: Introducing irrelevant material to divert attention from the actual issue.
techniques.example: Asked about the deficit, answering about the opponent's emails
techniques.origin: Classical ignoratio elenchi; PTC-18 → SemEval-2023 Distraction

techniques.name: Whataboutism
techniques.definition: Deflecting a charge by pointing at the accuser's (or a third party's) alleged wrongdoing instead of answering.
techniques.example: 'What about the wars YOUR country started?'
techniques.languages: 9 SemEval-2023 languages; salient in RU-related corpora
techniques.origin: Cold-War Soviet rhetoric ('and you are lynching Negroes') → PTC-18 → SemEval-2023 Distraction

techniques.name: Causal Oversimplification
techniques.definition: Attributing a complex outcome to a single cause.
techniques.example: 'Crime rose because of immigration, period'
techniques.origin: PTC-18 → SemEval-2023 Simplification; also MAFALDA

techniques.name: False Dilemma or No Choice
techniques.definition: Presenting only two options (or only one 'inevitable' course) when more exist; black-and-white framing.
techniques.example: 'You're either with us or with the terrorists'
techniques.languages: 9 SemEval-2023 languages; MAFALDA logos; Jigsaw 'false dichotomies' video
techniques.origin: Classical false dilemma; PTC-18 'black-and-white fallacy' → SemEval-2023 Simplification; Jigsaw Science Advances 2022 prebunk

techniques.name: Consequential Oversimplification (Slippery Slope)
techniques.definition: Asserting an improbable inevitable chain of events from a first step to catastrophe.
techniques.example: 'Legalize this and next they'll ban all cars'
techniques.origin: Classical slippery slope → SemEval-2023 Simplification

techniques.name: Slogans
techniques.definition: Brief, striking, emotionally charged phrases substituting for argument.
techniques.example: 'Build back better', 'Take back control'
techniques.origin: PTC-18 → SemEval-2023 Call family

techniques.name: Conversation Killer (Thought-Terminating Cliché)
techniques.definition: Stock phrases deployed to shut down discussion and critical thought.
techniques.example: 'It is what it is', 'You can't argue with that'
techniques.origin: Lifton 1961 'thought-terminating cliché' → PTC-18 → SemEval-2023 Call

techniques.name: Appeal to Time (Kairos)
techniques.definition: Arguing that NOW is the uniquely right moment to act, using urgency in place of justification.
techniques.example: 'History will not give us another chance — act today'
techniques.origin: Classical kairos; new fine class in SemEval-2023 Call

techniques.name: Loaded Language
techniques.definition: Emotionally charged word choice designed to steer the audience's attitude; the single most frequent technique in every PTC-lineage corpus.
techniques.example: 'the regime's brutal crackdown' vs 'the government's response'
techniques.languages: 9 SemEval-2023 languages; EN PTC; memes EN/AR/BG/MK
techniques.origin: IPA-era → PTC-18 → SemEval-2023 Manipulative Wording; overlaps Jigsaw 'emotionally manipulative language'

techniques.name: Obfuscation / Intentional Vagueness / Confusion
techniques.definition: Deliberately unclear, ambiguous, or agentless wording so the audience can't pin down the claim (the taxonomy's nearest cousin to captioneer's deleted-subject/passive-voice family).
techniques.example: 'Mistakes were made and processes will be reviewed'
techniques.languages: 9 SemEval-2023 languages (restored after being dropped in 2020 for sparsity)
techniques.origin: PTC-18 → dropped SemEval-2020 → restored SemEval-2023 Manipulative Wording

techniques.name: Exaggeration or Minimisation
techniques.definition: Representing something as far better/worse, larger/smaller than it is (covers both captioneer's 'overclaim' and 'minimizing').
techniques.example: 'the greatest economy in history' / 'just a few isolated incidents'
techniques.origin: PTC-18 → SemEval-2023 Manipulative Wording

techniques.name: Repetition
techniques.definition: Repeating the same message or phrase until it is accepted (illusory-truth exploitation).
techniques.example: Repeating 'rigged election' across every paragraph
techniques.origin: IPA-era → PTC-18 → SemEval-2023 Manipulative Wording

techniques.name: Impersonation
techniques.definition: Mimicking a trusted person, brand, or institution (fake accounts, spoofed outlets) to borrow credibility.
techniques.example: A tweet styled as an official health-agency account
techniques.languages: Taught in Bad News (EN + ~a dozen localizations); behavior-level analog DISARM T0097 Present Persona
techniques.origin: Bad News game technique #1 (Roozenbeek & van der Linden 2018); DISARM Red

techniques.name: Polarization
techniques.definition: Deliberately widening the gap between groups, amplifying us-vs-them hostility to make audiences receptive.
techniques.example: Running pages for both extremes of one issue
techniques.languages: Bad News localizations; measured in cross-cultural inoculation replications
techniques.origin: Bad News technique; studied in inoculation literature (Traberg, Roozenbeek, van der Linden 2022)

techniques.name: Conspiracy
techniques.definition: Framing events as the work of a secret malevolent plot, immune to disconfirming evidence.
techniques.example: 'They don't want you to know what's in the vaccines'
techniques.languages: Bad News; Costello et al. 2024 shows GPT-4 dialogue reduces such beliefs ~20%
techniques.origin: Bad News technique; conspiracy-belief literature (van der Linden; Costello/Pennycook/Rand Science 2024)

techniques.name: Discrediting / Deflection
techniques.definition: Deflecting criticism by attacking the critic or source ('the media is lying about us') rather than the content.
techniques.example: 'Don't believe the fact-checkers — they're bought'
techniques.languages: Bad News; overlaps SemEval Casting Doubt + Ad Hominem
techniques.origin: Bad News technique #5

techniques.name: Trolling
techniques.definition: Deliberately provoking emotional reactions to derail discourse and farm engagement.
techniques.example: Bait posts designed to enrage a community
techniques.languages: Bad News; behavior-level analog in DISARM harassment techniques
techniques.origin: Bad News technique #6

techniques.name: Incoherence
techniques.definition: Using mutually contradictory claims in support of one conclusion, exploiting that audiences rarely check consistency.
techniques.example: 'Climate has always changed, and also it's cooling, and scientists fake the warming'
techniques.languages: Jigsaw prebunking video (EN; campaigns in PL/CZ/SK)
techniques.origin: Jigsaw/Cambridge Science Advances 2022 prebunk technique; 'techniques of science denial' literature

techniques.name: Scapegoating
techniques.definition: Blaming a person or group for a complex problem they did not cause.
techniques.example: 'Migrants are why your rent went up'
techniques.languages: Jigsaw video; deployed as ad campaign in Poland, Czechia, Slovakia
techniques.origin: Jigsaw Science Advances 2022; classical propaganda studies

techniques.name: Ad Hominem (family)
techniques.definition: Attacking the arguer instead of the argument; MAFALDA splits abusive ad hominem, tu quoque, guilt by association; ElecDeb60to16 uses one Ad Hominem class.
techniques.example: 'Only an idiot would propose this budget'
techniques.languages: EN (MAFALDA, ElecDeb, Jigsaw video); mapped into SemEval Attack on Reputation
techniques.origin: Aristotle/Locke; formalized in every 2020s fallacy dataset

techniques.name: MAFALDA-distinct fallacies (aggregate)
techniques.definition: Fine-grained fallacy types in MAFALDA Level 2 not individually present in SemEval-2023: appeal to nature, appeal to tradition, circular reasoning, equivocation, false analogy, false causality, hasty generalization, fallacy of division, appeal to pity, appeal to ridicule, appeal to positive emotion, appeal to anger, appeal to worse problem.
techniques.example: 'It's natural, so it's safe' (appeal to nature); 'We've always done it this way' (tradition)
techniques.languages: EN (CC BY-SA gold set: 200 texts, 260 spans)
techniques.origin: MAFALDA taxonomy (Helwe et al., NAACL 2024) unifying Argotario/LOGIC/COVID/debate datasets under pathos-ethos-logos

techniques.name: DISARM Red TTPs (aggregate, campaign level)
techniques.definition: 150+ behavior-level techniques with stable IDs across 18 tactic stages describing how operations are planned, produced, and amplified — e.g., T0016 Create Clickbait, T0046 Search Engine Optimization, T0085 Develop Text-Based Content, T0097 Present Persona (with sub-techniques), T0151 Digital Community Hosting Asset.
techniques.example: A campaign entry: microtarget veterans (TA05) + create clickbait (T0016) + persona spoofing (T0097.101 Local Persona)
techniques.origin: AMITT (Credibility Coalition/CogSec Collab, 2019) → DISARM Foundation, modeled on MITRE ATT&CK; v1.6.1 March 2026

techniques.name: Hedging / certainty markers (gap)
techniques.definition: Tentativeness vs certainty language (LIWC's 'tentat'/'certain' categories are the standard proprietary operationalization); notably ABSENT as a technique in all SemEval/MAFALDA taxonomies — captioneer's hedging family is a genuine extension, but note meta-analyses find hedging is NOT a reliable deception cue.
techniques.example: 'It seems, perhaps, one might argue…' vs 'undeniably, everyone knows'
techniques.languages: LIWC-22 dictionaries exist for EN + translations (proprietary)
techniques.origin: Pennebaker's LIWC (2001→LIWC-22); pragmatics literature on hedges (Lakoff 1973)

framework_implications: Adopt the SemEval-2023 Task 3 taxonomy (6 families → 23 techniques) as the framework's spine: it is the most battle-tested (2019-2025 shared-task lineage, 9+ languages, news + memes + Slavic follow-ons), hierarchical, and freely reusable as a taxonomy even though the 2023/2024 corpora are not redistributable. Publish an explicit crosswalk from captioneer's six families: deflection → Distraction; loaded framing → Manipulative Wording/Loaded Language; overclaim + minimizing → Exaggeration-or-Minimisation (consider keeping them split as sub-techniques — a legitimate refinement); deleted-subject/passive → Obfuscation-Vagueness; hedging → new framework-native family (no SemEval equivalent; ground it in pragmatics, not LIWC's proprietary lists).

Data model: make every technique a versioned, stable-ID object in a DAG (MITRE/DISARM style — id, name, definition, family, aliases, crosswalk IDs to PTC-18/SemEval-14/SemEval-23/MAFALDA/DISARM/Bad-News, per-language surface-realization notes, origin/history field for the framework's etymology dimension, example spans). Score and evaluate hierarchy-aware (ancestor credit), as SemEval-2024 proved necessary. Serialize to JSON with an optional STIX mapping so FIMI/fact-checking orgs (EDMO, EEAS ecosystems already speak DISARM) can consume it.

Two-layer architecture, explicitly separated but linkable: a text-span rhetoric layer (SemEval/MAFALDA style — every mark points at a visible phrase, captioneer's existing invariant) and a campaign-behavior layer (DISARM crosswalk for impersonation, amplification, persona TTPs). Don't flatten them: span techniques describe language; TTPs describe operations. Captioneer's close-reader is the span layer; the framework can document the behavior layer without detecting it.

Codify 'no deception verdicts' in the schema itself, not just the charter: the meta-analytic record (median d≈0.10 verbal cues, 54% human accuracy, SCAN experimentally worthless) means any truth-value output field would be pseudoscience. The engine's claims must always be of the form 'technique X present in span Y' — a claim annotators demonstrably CAN agree on and that inoculation research shows people can learn to see. This is also the framework's differentiation from SCAN-style 'statement analysis' products.

Licensing strategy: taxonomy, lexicons, and annotated data under CC BY-SA 4.0 (compatible with DISARM and MAFALDA, and copyleft blocks proprietary enclosure of community annotations); engine code under a permissive OSI license (MIT/Apache-2.0). Seed the gold corpus from PTC-SemEval20 (CC BY 4.0, Zenodo) and MAFALDA (CC BY-SA); never bundle SemEval-2023/2024 corpora (shared-task-only terms) or any LIWC dictionary (proprietary, Receptiviti-exclusive commercially). Build framework-native open lexicons for hedging/certainty since the standard tool (LIWC) is closed.

Build the teaching layer on inoculation theory's evidence base: for each detected technique, ship a 90-second-lesson equivalent (definition + weakened-dose synthetic example + 'spot it' micro-quiz), mirroring Bad News (6 techniques) and Jigsaw's videos (5 techniques, 5-10% recognition gains in randomized YouTube field tests). This converts detections into the 'lens everyone can learn' and is the only intervention style with large-scale causal field evidence. Be honest about limits: cite the failed Indian replication; effects are on technique recognition, not belief change.

Design multilingual from the schema up: keep technique definitions language-agnostic, store per-language trigger lexicons and localized examples as separate attachable resources (SemEval-2023 proved technique labels transfer across 9 languages including zero-shot Georgian/Greek/Spanish with multilingual encoders, so a shared label space is viable); reserve a field for language-specific strategies that don't transfer, which is exactly the framework's cross-language research dimension.

Treat LLM-generated persuasion as a first-class threat model and benchmark: include AI-generated propaganda (Goldstein-style GPT-articles) in evaluation sets; add 'confident factual barrage / information density' as a monitored register since Science 2025 shows it is the strongest persuasion lever and correlates with inaccuracy — this argues for a future evidence-linking hook, distinct from span-marking. Conversely, model the opt-in truth caption's growth path on Costello 2024: personalized, evidence-based dialogue demonstrably and durably reduces false beliefs, giving the 'caption' feature a scientific north star.

Governance: run the project like a shared task + ATT&CK hybrid — versioned taxonomy releases with changelogs (DISARM ships ~quarterly, v1.6.1 current), a public benchmark with hierarchy-aware leaderboard, and an RFC process for adding/merging techniques (the 18→14→23 history shows taxonomies must merge sparse classes and split overloaded ones over time; the framework should record those lineage edges rather than erase them).

findings.summary: The tricks work because human comprehension runs on Grice's Cooperative Principle: hearers assume speakers are being adequately informative, truthful, relevant, and clear, and they automatically compute implicatures, accommodate presuppositions, and fill in deleted agents — so a manipulator can install a false belief while never asserting a falsehood. This gives the framework a precise, defensible spine: a commitment hierarchy (asserted > presupposed > implicated > insinuated) in which each step down buys the speaker more deniability, formalized by Saul's lying/misleading distinction, Camp's off-record insinuation, and Pinker's strategic-speaker game theory, and validated empirically by the paltering literature (Rogers/Zeckhauser et al., JPSP 2017 — the exact scholarly anchor for the owner's "verisleight"), Fausey & Boroditsky's replicated finding that non-agentive framing cuts blame and 30–50% of requested damages, and the DARVO studies showing both that the pattern measurably shifts credibility toward perpetrators and that teaching people to name it inoculates them. Equally important is the negative floor: text-based lie DETECTION is pseudoscience-adjacent — humans hit 54% (Bond & DePaulo, 24,483 judges), SCAN performs at chance yet is sold to police worldwide, and the best linguistic classifiers (LIWC 61–67%, CBCA/RM ~70% lab ceiling) are nowhere near forensic reliability — so the charter "reads the language, never the mind" is not just an ethical stance, it is exactly where the science draws the line: marking manipulation-affording structures in text is solid linguistics; inferring deception from them is not.

key_findings.claim: Grice's Cooperative Principle (1975) is the causal mechanism behind nearly every manipulation family the product already marks
key_findings.detail: Grice's 'Logic and Conversation' posits that hearers interpret utterances assuming the speaker follows four maxims — Quantity (informative enough), Quality (truthful/justified), Relation (relevant), Manner (clear, unambiguous, orderly). Implicatures are computed from this presumption of cooperation. Deception-by-implicature works by covertly VIOLATING a maxim while appearing to observe it: under-informativeness (Quantity) yields misleading half-truths, irrelevant true answers (Relation) yield deflection, obscurity (Manner) yields evasion. The hearer's own inferential machinery installs the false belief — the speaker never states it.

key_findings.claim: Philosophy of language has a worked-out lying/misleading distinction the framework can adopt wholesale
key_findings.detail: The traditional definition of lying (SEP, Mahon) has four conditions: statement, believed-false content, addressee, intent to deceive. Misleading-without-lying deceives via what is IMPLICATED rather than what is SAID (classic example: 'Valentino's been sick' — true, but arranged to hide the affair). Jennifer Saul's 'Lying, Misleading, and What is Said' (OUP 2012) gives the fullest treatment: the distinction is linguistically real (it turns on the notion of 'what is said') even though she argues it is morally insignificant. Related accounts: Carson/Saul's 'warranting context', Stokke's common-ground account, Fallis's norm-violation account, Sorensen's bald-faced lies (false assertion without intent to deceive — a dominance move, not a deception).

key_findings.claim: Paltering is the peer-reviewed name for the owner's 'verisleight' — active use of truthful statements to mislead
key_findings.detail: Rogers, Zeckhauser, Gino, Norton & Schweitzer, 'Artful Paltering: The Risks and Rewards of Using Truthful Statements to Mislead Others', Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 2017, 112(3), 456–473. Defines paltering as a third deception category distinct from lying by commission (false statements) and lying by omission (passive withholding). Over half of 184 surveyed business executives admitted paltering in negotiations. Palterers claim more value but raise impasse rates and suffer reputational damage when discovered; conflict is fueled by asymmetric construal — palterer: 'I told the truth'; target: 'I was misled'. Targets judge palters harsher when given in response to direct questions.

key_findings.claim: Presupposition smuggles claims because it PROJECTS and gets ACCOMMODATED — and both properties are testable in text
key_findings.detail: Presuppositions triggered by definite descriptions, factives ('regret that'), change-of-state verbs ('stopped'), clefts, and iteratives ('again') survive negation and questioning — 'Have you stopped X?' commits both yes and no answers to having done X. Lewis-style accommodation means unchallenged presupposed content silently enters common ground. Experimental work (Singh et al., Cognitive Science 2016) shows accommodation is automatic when content is plausible but breaks on implausible content — i.e., smuggling works best for claims the hearer half-believes already. Rhetorically, question presuppositions constrain the interlocutor's possible replies and impose new commitments when unshared.

key_findings.claim: Hedging has a formal semantics (Lakoff 1973) and a mature NLP detection tradition the open-source project can seed from
key_findings.detail: George Lakoff, 'Hedges: A Study in Meaning Criteria and the Logic of Fuzzy Concepts', Journal of Philosophical Logic 2 (1973), 458–508 (~1,850 citations), analyzed hedges ('sort of', 'technically', 'strictly speaking', 'regular') as operators on fuzzy-set membership (Zadeh) — crucially showing hedges are often LEGITIMATE expressions of genuine fuzziness, not always evasion. The CoNLL-2010 Shared Task ('Learning to Detect Hedges and their Scope') benchmarked hedge/weasel detection on BioScope and a Wikipedia weasel-tag corpus; Ganter & Strube (2009) 'Finding Hedges by Chasing Weasels' used Wikipedia {{weasel}} tags as free training data. Annotated corpora and lexicons exist and are reusable.

key_findings.claim: Agent deletion measurably shifts blame and money — the strongest experimental result behind the product's deleted-subject family
key_findings.detail: Fausey & Boroditsky, 'Subtle linguistic cues influence perceived blame and financial liability', Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 17 (2010), 644–650: agentive ('she toppled the candle') vs non-agentive ('the candle toppled') descriptions of identical accidents changed blame ratings and produced 30–50% higher requested financial damages under agentive framing — even for the well-known 2004 Super Bowl 'wardrobe malfunction' where participants had full visual knowledge. A preregistered direct replication (Tonković et al., Legal & Criminological Psychology 2022) reproduced the effect in English and Croatian. Political-language scholarship names the register: the 'past exonerative' (Schneider/Safire) — 'mistakes were made' traces from Grant 1876 through Ziegler 1973 to Reagan 1987, and journalism studies document the same pattern in police-killing headlines.

key_findings.claim: Euphemism theory gives the framework its 'loaded framing' backbone and a built-in evolution model
key_findings.detail: Allan & Burridge, 'Euphemism and Dysphemism: Language Used as Shield and Weapon' (OUP 1991) and 'Forbidden Words' (CUP 2006) establish the triad orthophemism (straight talk) / euphemism (shield) / dysphemism (weapon) — the same referent, three framings. William Lutz's doublespeak taxonomy adds four institutional types: euphemism, jargon, gobbledygook/bureaucratese, inflated language. Pinker's 'euphemism treadmill' (1994) explains technique EVOLUTION: concepts recontaminate each new label, forcing serial replacement — direct evidence that a technique database must be diachronic, with dated attestations per entry.

key_findings.claim: Frankfurt's 'On Bullshit' adds a truth-orientation axis orthogonal to true/false
key_findings.detail: Frankfurt (1986 essay; Princeton UP 2005): the liar is tethered to truth (must track it to conceal it); the bullshitter is INDIFFERENT to truth, aiming only at impression management — and is therefore 'a greater enemy of the truth than lies are'. For a taxonomy this means deceptive intent and truth-value are separate dimensions: bald-faced lies (false, no deception intended), palters (true, deception intended), bullshit (truth-value irrelevant). A framework that only models true/false misses two of the four quadrants.

key_findings.claim: DARVO and gaslighting are empirically studied DISCOURSE patterns, and naming them is protective — direct support for the product thesis
key_findings.detail: DARVO (Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender) coined by Jennifer Freyd (1997, Feminism & Psychology). Harsey, Zurbriggen & Freyd (2017, J. Aggression Maltreatment & Trauma) found ~72% of confronted perpetrators used DARVO components and exposure to DARVO increased victim self-blame; Harsey & Freyd's follow-up experiments showed DARVO exposure makes observers rate victims less believable and perpetrators less responsible — and that EDUCATING participants about DARVO beforehand reduced the perpetrator's believability. Abramson ('Turning up the Lights on Gaslighting', Philosophical Perspectives 28, 2014) analyzes gaslighting moves like 'that's crazy' as demands to see things the speaker's way rather than epistemic claims. Both are analyzable as sequences of marks on visible language, consistent with 'reads the language, never the mind'.

key_findings.claim: Deniability is the currency of indirect manipulation, and it has both a game-theoretic model and an operational linguistic test
key_findings.detail: Pinker, Nowak & Lee, 'The logic of indirect speech' (PNAS 2008) and Lee & Pinker's 'strategic speaker' theory (Psych Review 2010) model indirection (veiled threats, bribes, come-ons) as rational plausible-deniability strategy when interests conflict. Elisabeth Camp ('Insinuation, Common Ground, and the Conversational Record', OUP 2018) shows insinuation keeps content OFF the conversational record — but deniability collapses when no reasonable interpretation lacks the commitment. Operationally: implicatures are cancellable ('...but I don't mean X' is coherent), assertions are not, presuppositions survive negation — a text engine can literally test which channel a smuggled claim travels through.

key_findings.claim: The scientific floor, negative side: text-based lie detection does not work and the framework must refuse it explicitly
key_findings.detail: Bond & DePaulo's meta-analysis (Personality & Social Psychology Review 2006; 206 documents, 24,483 judges): humans achieve 54% lie/truth accuracy. SCAN (Sapir's 'Scientific Content Analysis', sold to police worldwide): Bogaard, Meijer, Vrij & Merckelbach (Frontiers in Psychology 2016; 117 participants, 234 statements, 12 criteria) found chance-level performance (49.6%/53% cross-validated) and concluded 'lacking empirical support, the application of SCAN in its current form should be discouraged'; ProPublica documented its unregulated global spread. Newman, Pennebaker et al.'s LIWC 'Lying Words' classifier (PSPB 2003): 61% overall, 67% topic-constant. CBCA and Reality Monitoring reach ~70% in lab settings but with base-rate sensitivity, criteria whose ABSENCE cannot indicate deception, and research-bias caveats (Oberlader et al. 2021). Nothing in this literature supports per-statement truthfulness verdicts.

key_findings.claim: Cross-linguistic variation is structural, not cosmetic: evidentiality-marking languages change which evasions are even possible
key_findings.detail: Aikhenvald ('Evidentiality', OUP 2004): languages including Quechua, Tariana, Tuyuca, Tibetan, Bulgarian, Turkish, and Korean grammatically mark information source (witnessed/inferred/hearsay), in several of them obligatorily — a bare unsourced claim is ungrammatical, so English-style overclaim ('everyone knows...') and source-vague weasel words work differently or must exploit evidential morphology itself. Turkish/English studies link evidential morphology to source memory. Fausey & Boroditsky's companion cross-linguistic work (English vs Spanish/Japanese eyewitness memory) shows agentive-framing defaults also differ by language. The six manipulation families are therefore language-parameterized, not universal constants.

key_findings.claim: Lakoff's framing work explains why marking loaded language helps even when users already 'know the facts'
key_findings.detail: 'Don't Think of an Elephant!' (2004): every word evokes a frame; NEGATING a frame activates it (Nixon's 'I am not a crook'); 'tax relief' smuggles a burden/hero/villain frame into apparently neutral vocabulary. Combined with Fausey & Boroditsky's finding that framing shifts judgments even about events people watched themselves, this grounds the product's 'loaded framing' family: frames operate below explicit belief, so a visible mark on the framing phrase is the right intervention level.

techniques.name: False implicature (misleading without lying)
techniques.definition: Installing a false belief via conversational implicature while every asserted sentence is true; exploits the hearer's presumption of cooperation (usually the Quantity or Relation maxim).
techniques.example: 'I've never been convicted of fraud' (implicating innocence, while charges were dropped on a technicality).
techniques.origin: Grice 1975 'Logic and Conversation'; Saul 2012 for the lying/misleading line
techniques.languages: Universal mechanism; strength of implicature varies with cultural directness norms

techniques.name: Paltering / verisleight
techniques.definition: The ACTIVE use of truthful statements to create a misleading impression — a third category beside lying by commission and lying by omission.
techniques.example: Seller asked if the house has flooded: 'This house has weathered every storm beautifully' (true; it flooded twice).
techniques.origin: Term revived by Schauer & Zeckhauser 2009; empirics in Rogers et al., JPSP 2017
techniques.languages: Documented in English-language negotiation studies; mechanism is Gricean, so expected cross-linguistically

techniques.name: Presupposition smuggling / loaded question
techniques.definition: Embedding a contested claim as a presupposition (via factives, change-of-state verbs, definites, clefts, 'again') so it projects through negation/questions and is accommodated unless explicitly challenged.
techniques.example: 'Have you stopped inflating the numbers?' — both answers concede the inflating.
techniques.origin: Frege/Strawson presupposition theory; Lewis 1979 accommodation; Karttunen projection
techniques.languages: Trigger inventories differ per language (e.g., Japanese 'no da', German modal particles); the projection/accommodation mechanics are cross-linguistic

techniques.name: Hedging (shields and approximators)
techniques.definition: Fuzzy operators ('sort of', 'basically', 'technically', 'I believe') that weaken commitment to the proposition or to its precision; legitimate for genuine uncertainty, manipulative when used to pre-build deniability.
techniques.example: 'We are broadly compliant with, essentially, the spirit of the regulation.'
techniques.origin: Lakoff 1973 (Journal of Philosophical Logic); Prince et al. 1982 split shields vs approximators; CoNLL-2010 for detection
techniques.languages: Hedge inventories are language-specific; BioScope (English) and multilingual weasel corpora exist

techniques.name: Weasel words (vague attribution)
techniques.definition: Attributing claims to unnamed or unverifiable sources so no one holds the commitment ('some say', 'experts agree', 'it is widely believed').
techniques.example: 'Many people are saying the audit was rigged.'
techniques.origin: Named in early-1900s American usage (popularized by Theodore Roosevelt); formalized as Wikipedia {{weasel}} tags; Ganter & Strube 2009 detection
techniques.languages: Universal strategy; realized via impersonal constructions, e.g. German 'man sagt', French 'on dit', Spanish 'se dice'

techniques.name: Agent deletion: passive voice and non-agentive framing
techniques.definition: Removing or demoting the doer via passives, intransitive alternations, or nominalization so blame has no landing site; measurably lowers assigned blame and damages by 30–50%.
techniques.example: 'Mistakes were made'; 'The gun discharged'; 'The costume ripped' vs 'He ripped the costume'.
techniques.origin: Fausey & Boroditsky 2010 (replicated 2022); 'past exonerative' coined by William Schneider; critical discourse analysis (Fowler, Fairclough; Billig on nominalization)
techniques.languages: Availability differs sharply: Spanish/Japanese prefer non-agentive frames for accidents by default, so the same form carries less evasive signal — detection weights must be language-specific

techniques.name: Nominalization
techniques.definition: Converting processes into agentless nouns ('the decision to terminate', 'the shooting') that hide who did what to whom and resist tense/agency questions.
techniques.example: 'Following the restructuring, headcount reductions occurred.'
techniques.origin: Halliday's grammatical metaphor; critical discourse analysis (Fairclough; Billig 2008 critique)
techniques.languages: Rich in bureaucratic registers of most literate languages

techniques.name: Euphemism (shield) and dysphemism (weapon)
techniques.definition: Substituting a milder/harsher expression for the same referent to steer affect; the orthophemism (neutral term) is the reference point that reveals the spin.
techniques.example: 'Collateral damage' vs 'civilian deaths' vs 'slaughter of innocents' — one referent, three X-phemisms.
techniques.origin: Allan & Burridge 1991, 2006
techniques.languages: Universal; taboo domains driving euphemism differ by culture (death, sex, disease, money, religion)

techniques.name: Doublespeak (jargon, gobbledygook, inflated language)
techniques.definition: Institutional register that distorts by technicality overload, bureaucratic fog, or importance inflation rather than by single-word substitution.
techniques.example: 'Negative patient care outcome' for death; 'revenue enhancement' for tax increase.
techniques.origin: William Lutz, 'Doublespeak' 1989, building on Orwell's 'Politics and the English Language' 1946

techniques.name: Loaded framing / frame evocation
techniques.definition: Choosing vocabulary whose frame imports unargued premises; negating the frame still activates it, so denial reinforces.
techniques.example: 'Tax relief' (taxes = affliction); 'I am not a crook.'
techniques.origin: Fillmore frame semantics; Lakoff 'Don't Think of an Elephant!' 2004; Tversky & Kahneman framing effects 1981
techniques.languages: Frames are culture-specific; metaphor inventories differ (Lakoff & Johnson 1980)

techniques.name: Bullshit (truth-indifferent assertion)
techniques.definition: Assertion produced without regard to truth value, aimed at impression management; distinct from lying, which requires tracking the truth to hide it.
techniques.example: Filler expertise-talk in a pitch: confident claims the speaker has never checked.
techniques.origin: Frankfurt 1986/2005; Ergo literature on 'indifference toward truth'

techniques.name: Bald-faced lie
techniques.definition: Asserting a known falsehood without intending anyone to believe it — a power/dominance or record-setting move, not a deception.
techniques.example: 'I didn't cheat', said to a dean who has the proof, forcing a process.
techniques.origin: Sorensen 2007; Carson 2006

techniques.name: DARVO
techniques.definition: Three-move discourse sequence by a confronted wrongdoer: Deny the behavior, Attack the confronter's credibility, Reverse Victim and Offender roles; measurably shifts observer credibility judgments; naming it inoculates.
techniques.example: 'That never happened, you're unstable, and honestly I'm the one being abused here.'
techniques.origin: Freyd 1997; Harsey, Zurbriggen & Freyd 2017; Harsey & Freyd 2020/2023
techniques.languages: Studied mainly in English; pattern defined at the discourse-move level, so portable

techniques.name: Gaslighting moves
techniques.definition: Utterances that attack the target's standing as a knower rather than the claim ('that's crazy', 'you're remembering it wrong') — demands to adopt the speaker's construal disguised as epistemic assessments.
techniques.example: 'You always do this — no one else thinks that happened.'
techniques.origin: Abramson 2014; subsequent epistemic-injustice literature (Spear 2019)

techniques.name: Insinuation / off-record indirection
techniques.definition: Communicating a risky content while keeping it off the conversational record for plausible deniability; deniability collapses only when no reasonable reading lacks the commitment.
techniques.example: 'Nice little restaurant you've got here; be a shame if the inspectors got interested.'
techniques.origin: Camp 2018; Pinker, Nowak & Lee 2008; Lee & Pinker 2010
techniques.languages: Universal; indirectness norms vary widely (high- vs low-context cultures)

techniques.name: Non-apology / minimization
techniques.definition: Apology-shaped utterances that delete the offense, the agent, or the harmed party ('if anyone was offended'), often combining past exonerative + conditional + hedge in one construction.
techniques.example: 'I regret that mistakes were made and that some may have felt hurt.'
techniques.origin: Speech-act analyses of apology (Austin/Searle felicity conditions); political-language commentary (Safire); non-apology scholarship
techniques.languages: Apology felicity conditions are language/culture-specific (e.g., Japanese apology register), so the minimization tells differ

framework_implications: Data model — three layers per technique entry: (1) surface trigger (lexical/syntactic pattern anchored to a visible phrase, as the product already does), (2) pragmatic mechanism (which Gricean maxim or commitment channel it exploits: said / presupposed / implicated / insinuated), (3) affordance (what the speaker gains — deniability, blame diffusion, frame import). The commitment hierarchy asserted > presupposed > implicated > insinuated (Saul, Camp) should be a first-class enum, because it predicts both deniability and the right challenge-question for the reader.

Engine — deniability is computable: implicatures are cancellable, presuppositions project through negation/questions, assertions do neither. The engine can classify which channel a claim travels through by applying transformation tests (negate the sentence, turn it into a question) and checking whether the marked content survives. This turns 'smuggled claim' from a vibe into a reproducible linguistic test, and each mark can ship with the concrete challenge question that surfaces the smuggled content ('Notice: this survives even if you answer no').

Hard scope wall, documented with citations: the framework must refuse truthfulness scoring the same way it refuses body-language reading. Put the negative results in the docs as the stated reason — humans 54% (Bond & DePaulo 2006), SCAN at chance (Bogaard et al. 2016) despite worldwide police adoption, LIWC 61–67%, CBCA/RM ~70% lab ceiling with 'absence of criteria is not evidence of deception' caveats. SCAN is the cautionary tale for governance: a criteria list that spread through practitioner training without validation. Never output a deception probability; output marks plus mechanism plus affordance.

Naming is the product: the DARVO inoculation results (Harsey & Freyd — pre-educating observers reduces the tactic's effectiveness) are direct experimental evidence for the 'lens of clarity everyone can learn' thesis. Design for teaching: every mark should link to the named technique, its mechanism, and its scholarly anchor, because knowing the name measurably blunts the trick.

Diachrony as schema, not prose: the euphemism treadmill and 'mistakes were made' lineage (Grant 1876 → Ziegler 1973 → Reagan 1987) show techniques and their surface forms evolve while mechanisms persist. Give each lexicon entry dated attestations, a stable mechanism ID, and a mutable surface-form list — origins and evolution then fall out of the data instead of needing essays.

Language-parameterized taxonomy: the six families are not universal constants. Grammatical evidentiality (Quechua, Turkish, Tariana...) changes what overclaim and source-vagueness even look like; Spanish/Japanese default to non-agentive accident framing, so a deleted agent is weaker evidence of evasion there; hedge/weasel inventories are per-language. Model families as universal MECHANISMS with per-language trigger packs and per-language baseline weights, and seed from existing corpora: BioScope, CoNLL-2010 hedge corpus, Wikipedia {{weasel}}/{{puffery}} tag dumps, multilingual weasel corpora.

Innocent-use baseline (orthophemism principle): Lakoff 1973 shows hedges legitimately express real fuzziness; passives are often just information structure; euphemisms can be kindness. Every detector needs a documented benign reading, and marks should be framed as 'this construction AFFORDS evasion — here is the question it dodges', never 'this is manipulation'. Consider surfacing the orthophemism (the neutral paraphrase) next to euphemism/dysphemism marks — the contrast is the lesson.

Governance: require at least one primary scholarly source per technique entry (the anti-SCAN rule), record effect sizes and replication status where they exist (e.g., Fausey & Boroditsky replicated 2022; DARVO effects replicated; SCAN failed), and adopt Frankfurt's insight structurally — model truth-orientation (lie / palter / bullshit / bald-faced lie) as an axis of the taxonomy's documentation even though the engine itself never adjudicates which one a given text is.

factChecks.claim: Grice's Cooperative Principle (1975, 'Logic and Conversation') posits four maxims — Quantity, Quality, Relation, Manner — implicatures are computed from presumed cooperation, and deception-by-implicature works by covertly violating a maxim while appearing to observe it (SEP implicature entry).
factChecks.evidence: SEP entry 'Implicature' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/implicature/) attributes the Cooperative Principle and the four maxims Quality/Quantity/Relation/Manner to Grice (1975: 26–30), 'Logic and Conversation', distinguishes covert violation from overt flouting, and explicitly discusses misleading-without-lying via implicature ('greater deniability', 'misleading Alan, but not lying'). The Quantity→half-truth / Relation→deflection / Manner→evasion mapping is the researcher's application, but each element is grounded in the entry's account of maxim exploitation.

factChecks.claim: SEP (Mahon) gives a four-condition traditional definition of lying; misleading-without-lying deceives via implicature ('Valentino's been sick'); Saul's 'Lying, Misleading, and What is Said' (OUP 2012) treats the distinction as linguistically real but argues it is morally insignificant; related accounts: Carson/Saul warranting context, Stokke common ground, Fallis norm-violation, Sorensen bald-faced lies.
factChecks.evidence: SEP 'The Definition of Lying and Deception' is by James Edwin Mahon (PhilPapers rec MAHTDO-6) and states four necessary conditions: statement, untruthfulness, addressee, intention that the addressee believe the statement true. The Valentino example appears there ('Valentino's been sick with mononucleosis for the past two weeks', from Coleman & Kay 1981 — Mary conceals her date with Valentino; 'the affair' is a fair gloss). Saul's book is Oxford University Press, 2012 (OUP catalogue 9780199603688); reviews (NDPR, EJoP) confirm she argues lying and misleading are 'on an equal footing in terms of act-evaluation' — the claim's 'morally insignificant' is a slightly flattened but recognized gloss (she allows misleading may indicate better character). The SEP entry covers Saul's warranting-context definition (L14, drawing on Carson), Stokke's common-ground account (L17), Fallis's norm-violation accounts (L15–L16), and Sorensen's bald-faced lies as assertion without intent to deceive.

factChecks.claim: Rogers, Zeckhauser, Gino, Norton & Schweitzer, 'Artful Paltering', JPSP 2017, 112(3), 456–473 (PubMed 27936834) defines paltering as a third deception category; over half of 184 surveyed business executives admitted paltering; palterers claim more value but raise impasse rates and suffer reputational damage; asymmetric construal ('I told the truth' vs 'I was misled'); palters judged harsher in response to direct questions.
factChecks.evidence: PubMed 27936834 confirms the exact citation: Rogers T, Zeckhauser R, Gino F, Norton MI, Schweitzer ME, 'Artful paltering: The risks and rewards of using truthful statements to mislead others', J Pers Soc Psychol 2017;112(3):456–473. The abstract confirms every element verbatim: paltering distinct from lying by omission (passive) and commission (false statements); the exact asymmetric-construal quotes ('I told the truth' / 'I was misled'); palters judged 'especially unethical when... used in response to direct questions'; palterers 'likely to claim additional value, but increase the likelihood of impasse and harm to their reputations'. HKS coverage of the study confirms 'more than half of 184 business executives surveyed admitted that they had paltered' (pilot study).

factChecks.claim: Presuppositions from definites, factives, change-of-state verbs, clefts, iteratives project under negation/questioning; Lewis-style accommodation lets unchallenged content enter common ground; Singh et al. (Cognitive Science 2016) show accommodation is automatic/easy for plausible content but breaks down for implausible content.
factChecks.evidence: Singh, R., Fedorenko, E., Mahowald, K., & Gibson, E. (2016), 'Accommodating Presuppositions Is Inappropriate in Implausible Contexts', Cognitive Science 40, 607–634, DOI 10.1111/cogs.12260 — exactly the claimed source URL. The paper's finding (via Wiley listing and secondary citations): accommodation cost is sensitive to contextual plausibility — accommodating is costlier than assertion / judged inappropriate only when the presupposed content is implausible, supporting the 'smuggling works best for half-believed claims' gloss. The trigger inventory (definites, factives like 'regret', change-of-state 'stopped', clefts, 'again') and projection under negation/questions ('Have you stopped X?') are standard, uncontroversial textbook linguistics (per SEP/linguistics literature).

factChecks.claim: George Lakoff, 'Hedges: A Study in Meaning Criteria and the Logic of Fuzzy Concepts', Journal of Philosophical Logic 2 (1973), 458–508 (~1,850 citations), analyzed hedges as operators on Zadeh fuzzy-set membership, showing hedges are often legitimate; CoNLL-2010 Shared Task benchmarked hedge/weasel detection on BioScope and a Wikipedia weasel corpus; Ganter & Strube (2009) 'Finding Hedges by Chasing Weasels' used Wikipedia weasel tags as training data.
factChecks.evidence: Crossref for DOI 10.1007/BF00262952 (the claimed Springer URL) confirms Lakoff, 'Hedges: A study in meaning criteria and the logic of fuzzy concepts', Journal of Philosophical Logic vol 2, issue 4, Oct 1973; PhilPapers and other indexes confirm pages 458–508. Citation count: Semantic Scholar shows exactly 1,882 — '~1,850' matches that database (note: count is database-dependent; Crossref shows 645, Google Scholar higher). The paper's fuzzy-set (Zadeh) basis and examples ('sort of', 'regular', 'strictly speaking') are confirmed by the indexed abstracts. ACL Anthology W10-3001 confirms 'The CoNLL-2010 Shared Task: Learning to Detect Hedges and their Scope in Natural Language Text' (Farkas, Vincze, Móra, Csirik, Szarvas) using the BioScope corpus plus Wikipedia weasel annotations, 23 participating teams. ACL Anthology P09-2044 confirms Ganter & Strube 2009, 'Finding Hedges by Chasing Weasels: Hedge Detection Using Wikipedia Tags and Shallow Linguistic Features' (ACL-IJCNLP 2009 Short Papers), using Wikipedia weasel tags as annotation.

factChecks.claim: Fausey & Boroditsky (Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 17 (2010), 644–650): agentive vs non-agentive descriptions changed blame and produced 30–50% higher requested financial damages, even for the 2004 wardrobe malfunction with full visual knowledge; Tonković et al. (Legal & Criminological Psychology 2022) preregistered replication reproduced the effect in English and Croatian; 'past exonerative' (Schneider/Safire) traces 'mistakes were made' from Grant 1876 through Ziegler 1973 to Reagan 1987.
factChecks.correction: Two fixes. (1) The flagship damages figure is 53% more in fines, not '30–50%': in the wardrobe-malfunction experiment, participants who read agentive 'ripped/tore the costume' levied 53% higher fines on Timberlake than those who read the non-agentive version (per Boroditsky's own summaries and Language Log's report of the paper) — the effect held even for participants who watched the video, so that part stands. (2) Tonković et al. 2022 did NOT reproduce the effect in Croatian: the preregistered direct replication ('Preregistered direct replication of the linguistic frame effect on perceived blame and financial liability', Legal & Criminological Psychology, DOI 10.1111/lcrp.12219) replicated the original findings in English, but Croatian results were mixed — a smaller agentive effect on blame only (not on the financial penalty) in Experiment 1 and no effect on the proposed fine in Experiment 2. Say 'replicated in English; partial/mixed in Croatian.'
factChecks.evidence: Crossref for DOI 10.3758/pbr.17.5.644 confirms Fausey & Boroditsky, 'Subtle linguistic cues influence perceived blame and financial liability', Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 17(5), 644–650, 2010. Language Log (languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu/nll/?p=2487) quotes the 53%-more-in-fines result and the video condition. Wiley (bpspsychub.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/lcrp.12219) confirms the Tonković et al. 2022 replication and its mixed Croatian results. Wikipedia 'Mistakes were made' confirms the lineage: Grant's Dec 5, 1876 message to Congress ('mistakes have been made, as all can see and I admit it'), Ziegler May 1, 1973, Reagan's Jan 27, 1987 State of the Union; William Schneider proposed 'past exonerative' and Safire called it 'passive-evasive' — that whole sub-claim is accurate.

findings.summary: The six captioneer families (hedging, deflection, deleted-subject, loaded framing, overclaim, minimizing) are functional universals, but their surface machinery is radically language-specific — and sometimes inverted. In the ~25% of languages with grammatical evidentiality (Turkish -mIş, Quechua =si, Aymara, Estonian -vat), the grammar forces a source-of-evidence declaration on every past statement, which creates a built-in deniability channel: experimentally, liars in four languages preferred indirect/hearsay marking at 3–21x odds when lying (preemptive reputation protection), Turkish readers treat evidential misuse as deception, and LLMs perform near chance on evidential trust reasoning that native speakers do robustly. Agent deletion — captioneer's passive-voice family — flips markedness across languages: English passives are a detectable choice, but in pro-drop Japanese/Chinese/Spanish subjectless sentences are the unmarked default (Spanish "se rompió" non-agentive framing measurably reduces blame and even memory for agents, per Fausey & Boroditsky), so the detector must key on agency-at-issue, not mere subject absence. Whole national ecosystems have evolved named manipulation machinery worth encoding as lexicon packs: Japanese sontaku (deniable anticipatory obedience, 2017 word of the year via the Moritomo scandal), aimai commitment-free formulas (zensho shimasu), non-apology "gokai wo maneita"; Chinese tifa watchwords (Qian Gang's deep-red-to-deep-blue frequency-tracked lexicon), chengyu allusive framing, and the homophone censorship-evasion lexicon (river crab/grass-mud horse, curated for years by China Digital Times); Cantonese HK-2019 euphemism plus loose romanization as anti-surveillance code; Soviet langue de bois (Thom's four diagnostics) and institutionalized whataboutism; German's jury-run Unwort des Jahres — a 30-year living public registry of manipulative coinages that is a ready-made governance model; French legal euphemism escalation (plan social → plan de sauvegarde de l'emploi by statute); and Arabic balagha, a 1000-year formal taxonomy of implicature and figuration (al-Jurjani's nazm) proving rhetoric taxonomies predate and exceed the Western canon. Engineering-wise, multilingual matching requires per-language analyzers (jieba/MeCab/mecab-ko), morpheme-level not surface-regex patterns (vowel harmony gives -mIş four allomorphs times person endings), Unicode NFC plus UTS #39 confusable skeletons (NFKC does not resolve confusables), and script-variant folding — and cross-linguistic deception research finds no universal cue set (pronoun cues flip direction between individualist and collectivist cultures), vindicating the not-a-lie-detector charter at the design level.

key_findings.claim: About a quarter of the world's languages grammatically mark evidence source, and in many it is obligatory — an unmarked statement is ungrammatical
key_findings.detail: Aikhenvald (2004, Evidentiality) documents obligatory evidential systems in Turkish, Quechua, Aymara, Tariana, Bulgarian, Tibetan and others, ranging from 2-way (firsthand/non-firsthand, Turkish) to 5-way (visual, nonvisual sensory, inferred, assumed, reported). Aymara (Hardman 1986) marks personal knowledge vs hearsay vs inference with =wa, -tay, siwa. Speakers of these languages must declare their evidence in the verb itself.

key_findings.claim: Liars across languages preemptively hedge with indirect/hearsay markers to protect reputation — whether the marker is lexical or grammatical
key_findings.detail: The 'Someone told me' study (Mahr & Csibra, PMC6481770) tested English/Italian (lexical markers) and Turkish -mIş / Estonian -vat (grammatical evidentials): when participants chose to lie, odds of using indirect marking rose 21.4x (EN), 7.8x (IT), 3.1x (TR), 8.4x (EE). Hearsay framing is a cross-linguistic deniability device: you win if believed, lose little if caught.

key_findings.claim: Evidential MISUSE itself reads as deception to native speakers — a manipulation tell that has no English equivalent
key_findings.detail: Eye-tracking study 'Eyes do not lie but words do' (Functions of Language) shows Turkish readers interpret mismatched evidentiality (e.g. direct -DI for information the speaker could only know by hearsay) as deceptive during reading. In evidential languages the hedging family partly moves INTO morphology: the tell is marker-context mismatch, not hedge-word presence.

key_findings.claim: LLMs are near chance at evidential source-trust reasoning that Turkish humans do robustly — a hard warning for the truth-caption feature in evidential languages
key_findings.detail: arXiv 2604.24665 (2026): 75 native speakers shifted -DI vs -mIş with source trustworthiness (67.7% -DI in high-trust contexts); across 10 LLMs and three paradigms, trust effects were inconsistent, often reversed, and near-chance after correction — models 'optimize surface plausibility' rather than track epistemic commitment.

key_findings.claim: Sontaku (忖度) is institutionalized deniability: manipulation that leaves NO textual trace because the order is never uttered
key_findings.detail: 2017 Japanese word of the year (Jiyu Kokuminsha, Dec 1 2017) from the Moritomo Gakuen scandal — state land sold at 134M yen vs 956M appraisal; Abe issued no order, officials 'anticipated his wishes'; the Finance Ministry later altered 14 documents removing Abe references (Carlson 2020, Public Administration and Policy). A framework about words must name the technique whose whole point is the absence of words.

key_findings.claim: Japanese aimai supplies stock commitment-free formulas that are literally untranslatable promises
key_findings.detail: Zensho shimasu (善処します, 'I will handle it appropriately') can mean anything from 'I'll act' to 'I will do nothing'; kentō shimasu ('I'll study it') conventionally means refusal. These are lexicalized non-commitments used routinely by politicians — hedging realized as fixed formula rather than scattered qualifiers, ideal for a phrase-level lexicon pack.

key_findings.claim: Agentive vs non-agentive framing measurably changes blame, fines, and even memory — and pro-drop languages make agent deletion the UNMARKED default
key_findings.detail: Fausey & Boroditsky (2010): 'tore the bodice' vs 'the bodice tore' produced 53% higher financial penalties; Spanish speakers describing accidents prefer 'se rompió el florero' and remember accidental agents worse than English speakers (same pattern vs Japanese). In Japanese/Chinese/Spanish, subjectless sentences are normal grammar — flagging every deleted subject would false-positive constantly; English passive-voice detection logic INVERTS.

key_findings.claim: Chinese official language runs on tifa (提法) — deliberately vague, trackable formulations whose FREQUENCY is the signal
key_findings.detail: Qian Gang (China Media Project) classifies party watchwords into deep red (legacy: 'class struggle'), light red (sanctioned: 'harmonious society'), light blue (tolerated), deep blue (banned: 'separation of powers'); term-frequency shifts in People's Daily and congress reports reveal power struggles (e.g. 'intra-party democracy' peaks 1956, 1987). A manipulation lexicon can be corpus-dated and frequency-tracked, not just listed.

key_findings.claim: Tone-rich Chinese enables an entire homophone-substitution code layer, curated for years as a public lexicon
key_findings.detail: River crab 河蟹 (héxiè) ≈ 'harmonized' 和谐 (censored), grass-mud horse 草泥马 ≈ an obscenity, 'aquatic products' replacing river crab when it too was censored; China Digital Times' Grass-Mud Horse Lexicon wiki distilled into the 'Decoding the Chinese Internet' ebook (2013; 2015 edition +25 terms; Time counted 71 'classics'). Cantonese adds its own layer: 送中 ('extradite to China' / 'see off a dying relative') pun drove 2019 framing.

key_findings.claim: Hong Kong 2019 produced euphemism-as-operational-security plus loose Cantonese romanization as an in-group cipher
key_findings.detail: 'Dreaming' (recounting illegal protest acts as dreams), 'shopping' (attending a protest), 'it's raining' (open umbrellas, pepper spray incoming), 'fire magic' 火魔法 (petrol bombs); phonetic Cantonese romanization deliberately unreadable to Mandarin-literate monitors — euphemism serving surveillance-evasion and identity-signaling simultaneously, the mirror image of state euphemism.

key_findings.claim: Soviet langue de bois has a four-point diagnostic checklist, and whataboutism is its institutionalized deflection arm
key_findings.detail: Françoise Thom (La langue de bois 1987 / Newspeak 1989; thesis 1983): abstraction avoiding the concrete, tautology, bad metaphor, Manichean good/evil division — a ready rubric. 'Langue de bois' itself traveled Russian→Polish→French (Clemenceau coinage 1919 claimed). Whataboutism ('And you are lynching Negroes') is Soviet-standardized tu quoque, popularized as a term by The Economist; Havel listed it among 'canonized demagogical tricks'.

key_findings.claim: Germany's Unwort des Jahres is a 30+ year, jury-governed, criteria-based public registry of manipulative coinages — a working governance template
key_findings.detail: Founded 1991 by linguist Horst Dieter Schlosser, later independent as Sprachkritische Aktion; jury of 4 linguists + 1 journalist; public submissions with justification by Dec 31; explicit criteria (violates human dignity or democratic principles, discriminates, euphemistic/obscuring/misleading). Winners: Entlassungsproduktivität 'layoff productivity' (2005), alternativlos 'without alternative' (2010, shuts down debate), Gutmensch (2015), freiwillige Ausreise 'voluntary departure' for deportation (2006), Remigration (2023).

key_findings.claim: French shows euphemism ESCALATION written into law: the euphemism itself got euphemized
key_findings.detail: 'Plan social' (social plan = mass layoffs) was already softening language; the 2002 loi de modernisation sociale renamed it 'plan de sauvegarde de l'emploi' (employment protection plan) — a treadmill where each coinage absorbs the stigma and is replaced, which a lexicon data model must capture as term lineage (predecessor/successor links with dates).

key_findings.claim: Arabic balagha is a millennium-old FORMAL taxonomy of exactly what the framework wants to build — proving the taxonomy should not be Western-canon-only
key_findings.detail: Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani (d. 1078, Dala'il al-I'jaz and Asrar al-Balagha) founded nazm theory — meaning arises from syntactic arrangement, not words alone — and systematized 'ilm al-ma'ani (pragmatics: word order, emphasis, omission, implicature), 'ilm al-bayan (figuration: metaphor, simile, metonymy), 'ilm al-badi' (embellishment). Categories like hadhf (deliberate omission) and taqdim/ta'khir (fronting for emphasis) map directly onto deleted-subject and loaded-framing families.

key_findings.claim: There is NO universal deception feature set: cue direction flips across cultures, so per-language validation is mandatory
key_findings.detail: Cross-linguistic studies (11 datasets, 5 languages: EN/NL/RU/ES/RO, 6 countries — arXiv 2505.13147; Cambridge NLE individualism/collectivism study) find deception cues volatile across genre and culture; first-person pronoun use DECREASES in lying individualist-culture speakers but INCREASES in collectivist contexts. English-derived cue lists systematically misclassify other languages — structural support for the 'reads the language, never the mind' charter.

key_findings.claim: Multilingual pattern-matching is an analyzer problem, not a regex problem: segmentation, morphology, and Unicode each break naive matching
key_findings.detail: Chinese/Japanese have no word boundaries (jieba for zh; MeCab/Juman++/KyTea/Sudachi for ja; MeCab-ko/Komoran for ko — Rust port Lindera compiles to WASM for client-side use). Agglutination defeats surface regex: Turkish -mIş surfaces as -mış/-miş/-muş/-müş by vowel harmony, stacked with person/number endings; Korean particles fuse to stems. On Unicode: NFKC normalization does NOT resolve visually confusable characters (Cyrillic а vs Latin a) — UTS #39 confusables.txt skeleton matching is a separate required pass; Chinese needs simplified↔traditional folding, Japanese half/full-width folding.

techniques.name: Reportative/hearsay evidential hedging
techniques.definition: Marking a claim as 'heard from others' via obligatory verb morphology, spreading information while grammatically declining responsibility for its truth — rumor with built-in deniability
techniques.example: Turkish 'gelmiş' (came, reportedly/inferentially) vs 'geldi' (came, I witnessed); Estonian -vat; Quechua =si; Aymara siwa
techniques.languages: Turkish, Quechua, Aymara, Estonian, Bulgarian, Tibetan, Tariana (~25% of world's languages)
techniques.origin: Grammaticalized over centuries, typically from perfect aspect or speech verbs (Aikhenvald 2004, 2021)

techniques.name: Evidential misuse (source laundering)
techniques.definition: Using the direct-witness evidential for hearsay to inflate certainty, or the indirect evidential for witnessed events to dodge commitment; native readers register the mismatch as deceptive
techniques.example: Reporting gossip with Turkish -DI (direct past) to present it as eyewitness fact
techniques.languages: Turkish (eye-tracking evidence); applicable to all evidential languages
techniques.origin: Documented experimentally in Functions of Language eye-movement study; Aikhenvald notes deliberate evidential choice in lying

techniques.name: Sontaku (忖度)
techniques.definition: Anticipatory obedience: subordinates execute a superior's unspoken wishes so the superior never issues a traceable order — manipulation via calculated silence
techniques.example: Moritomo Gakuen land sold at 1/7 of appraisal (2017); officials cited 'the prime minister's intention' though Abe gave no instruction
techniques.languages: Japanese (word exists; the maneuver appears in any hierarchy)
techniques.origin: Classical Chinese-derived term, obscure until the 2017 Moritomo scandal made it Japan's word of the year

techniques.name: Aimai commitment-free formulas
techniques.definition: Lexicalized vague responses that sound like assent or promise but commit to nothing, exploiting a politeness norm that treats directness as rude
techniques.example: Zensho shimasu 善処します ('I'll handle it appropriately' — possibly by doing nothing); kentō shimasu 検討します ('I'll study it' = conventional refusal)
techniques.languages: Japanese; analogous stock evasions exist in Korean formal register
techniques.origin: Japanese indirection culture (aimai 曖昧); notorious 1969 Sato–Nixon mistranslation of zensho shimasu as a real promise

techniques.name: Perception-blaming non-apology
techniques.definition: Apologizing for the misunderstanding the words 'invited' rather than for the act or content — relocating fault into the hearer's perception
techniques.example: Japanese 誤解を招いた(とすれば遺憾) 'gokai wo maneita' — 'it is regrettable if misunderstanding was invited'; English cousin: 'I'm sorry if anyone was offended'
techniques.languages: Japanese (formulaic); parallel formulas in English, Korean political speech
techniques.origin: Staple of postwar Japanese political crisis language

techniques.name: Honorific/passive distancing
techniques.definition: Using elevated honorific or passive morphology to blur who did what while sounding respectful; the honorific passive is formally identical to the plain passive, letting agency dissolve into deference
techniques.example: Japanese ~reru/rareru forms that read as either 'was done (by someone)' or 'the honored person did'; formal keigo layers that abstract the actor
techniques.origin: Grammaticalized deference systems; strategic exploitation documented in Korean politeness research (Wiley Handbook of Korean Linguistics)

techniques.name: Non-agentive accident framing (pro-drop agent deletion)
techniques.definition: Describing harmful events with intransitive/reflexive or subjectless constructions so no agent appears; in pro-drop languages this is the unmarked default, making the manipulation invisible
techniques.example: Spanish 'se rompió el florero' (the vase broke itself); Chinese/Japanese zero-subject sentences; English 'mistakes were made' is the marked cousin
techniques.languages: Spanish, Japanese, Chinese, Korean, Italian, Portuguese (pro-drop); English via passive
techniques.origin: Grammatical typology; blame/memory effects shown by Fausey & Boroditsky (2010)

techniques.name: Tifa (提法) official formulations
techniques.definition: Standardized, deliberately vague party phrases whose adoption, exact wording, and frequency are political signals; circular enough to fit any situation while enforcing orthodoxy
techniques.example: 'Harmonious society', 'socialism with Chinese characteristics'; Qian Gang's deep-red/light-red/light-blue/deep-blue classification of permitted-to-banned terms
techniques.languages: Mandarin Chinese (CCP discourse); structurally akin to Soviet langue de bois
techniques.origin: CCP discourse practice since Mao era; systematized analytically by Qian Gang, China Media Project (2012 'Watchwords' series)

techniques.name: Chengyu allusive framing
techniques.definition: Deploying four-character classical idioms whose embedded historical verdict frames an opponent or situation; the allusion smuggles the conclusion in as shared heritage
techniques.example: Diplomatic use of ancient idioms to cast rivals in stock villain roles; Mao's 'let a hundred flowers bloom' borrowed from Warring States literature
techniques.languages: Mandarin Chinese; parallel yojijukugo in Japanese, sajaseong-eo in Korean
techniques.origin: Literary Chinese; ~5,000+ common chengyu drawn from classical texts

techniques.name: Homophone substitution code
techniques.definition: Replacing censored or dangerous terms with near-homophones (tone shift or same pinyin), producing deniable text that native speakers decode instantly but filters miss
techniques.example: 河蟹 'river crab' for 和谐 'harmonize/censor'; 草泥马 'grass-mud horse' for an obscenity; 送中 'send to China'/'see off the dying' pun in HK 2019
techniques.languages: Mandarin (massive homophone space from tonal phonology), Cantonese (9 tones)
techniques.origin: Chinese internet, c. 2009 grass-mud horse meme; curated in CDT's Grass-Mud Horse Lexicon / 'Decoding the Chinese Internet' ebook

techniques.name: Protest euphemism + orthographic cipher
techniques.definition: Innocent everyday words repurposed as operational code, plus deliberately nonstandard romanization that excludes out-group readers — euphemism as counter-surveillance
techniques.example: HK 2019: 'dreaming' (recounting protest acts), 'shopping' (protesting), 'it's raining' (pepper spray incoming), 'fire magic' (petrol bombs); loose Cantonese romanization unreadable to Mandarin monitors
techniques.origin: 2019–2020 anti-extradition movement, LIHKG forum culture

techniques.name: Langue de bois (wooden language)
