techniques.definition: Ideological officialese diagnosed by four features: abstraction avoiding the concrete, tautology, dead/bad metaphor, and Manichean good-vs-evil division; supplants description with orthodoxy
techniques.example: Soviet formulas like 'the forces of progress' vs 'enemies of the people'; French political cant inherits the label
techniques.languages: Russian (origin), Polish, French, Romanian; generalizes to any bureaucratic register
techniques.origin: Term via Russian→Polish→French (1970s–80s); analyzed by Françoise Thom, La langue de bois (1987) / Newspeak (1989)

techniques.name: Whataboutism (institutionalized tu quoque)
techniques.definition: Answering an accusation by pivoting to the accuser's real or alleged sins, changing the subject while implying moral equivalence
techniques.example: Soviet retort 'And you are lynching Negroes' to any human-rights criticism; revived in post-2014 Russian state media
techniques.origin: Soviet propaganda from the 1930s; term popularized by The Economist; Havel called it a 'canonized demagogical trick'

techniques.name: Statutory euphemism escalation
techniques.definition: Renaming an unpleasant institution in law when the previous euphemism absorbs the stigma, creating a datable lineage of successive softenings (the 'euphemism treadmill' with legal force)
techniques.example: French layoffs: licenciement collectif → 'plan social' → 'plan de sauvegarde de l'emploi' (2002 loi de modernisation sociale)
techniques.languages: French (statutory example); corporate English parallel ('rightsizing', 'workforce optimization')
techniques.origin: French labor law 2002; euphemism-treadmill dynamic described by Pinker

techniques.name: Hadhf and taqdim (balagha omission/fronting)
techniques.definition: In classical Arabic rhetoric, deliberate ellipsis (hadhf) and word-order fronting (taqdim wa ta'khir) as codified meaning-manipulation devices — a formal pre-modern theory of framing by structure
techniques.example: Omitting the agent or object for effect; fronting a phrase to restrict or emphasize — catalogued in 'ilm al-ma'ani
techniques.origin: Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani (d. 1078), Dala'il al-I'jaz; nazm theory that arrangement, not words, carries meaning

techniques.name: Un-word coinage (dehumanizing technocratic euphemism)
techniques.definition: Compound coinages that process human harm into administrative or economic vocabulary; Germany's compounding morphology makes single-word versions especially potent and trackable
techniques.example: Entlassungsproduktivität 'layoff productivity' (2005), alternativlos 'without alternative' (2010), freiwillige Ausreise 'voluntary departure' for deportation (2006), Remigration (2023)
techniques.origin: Documented annually since 1991 by the Unwort des Jahres jury (founder Horst Dieter Schlosser)

framework_implications: Split the data model into two layers: a language-agnostic FAMILY taxonomy (function: evade commitment, delete agent, launder source, deflect, inflate, minimize) and per-language REALIZATION packs keyed by BCP-47 tag. Each pattern declares its match layer — surface-regex, lemma, morpheme-tag sequence, or construction — because Turkish -mIş has four vowel-harmony allomorphs times person endings and Korean particles fuse to stems; surface regex is only valid for isolating-ish languages like English and Chinese (post-segmentation).

Make family applicability per-language and allow inverted logic: deleted-subject detection must flag the marked construction in each language (passive in English; agentless framing of harm-events in pro-drop Japanese/Chinese/Spanish where zero subjects are the unmarked default — flag only when agency is at issue, or every sentence false-positives). Evidential-misuse is a family that simply does not exist for English and is core for Turkish/Quechua.

Engine pipeline: normalize (Unicode NFC, then UTS #39 confusable-skeleton pass — NFKC alone does NOT resolve confusables — plus simplified↔traditional Chinese folding and half/full-width folding) → segment/analyze with a pluggable per-language analyzer (jieba/zh, MeCab or Sudachi/ja, mecab-ko/ko; Lindera's Rust/WASM builds keep this client-side, preserving captioneer's no-server privacy stance) → match patterns against the token+morpheme stream, mapping every hit back to original character offsets so marks still point at visible phrases.

Lexicon entries need provenance and lineage fields: coinage date, coiner/first attestation, evolution notes, successor/predecessor links (plan social → plan de sauvegarde de l'emploi; 和谐 → 河蟹 → 水产), and citations. Three living registries prove this is maintainable by communities and are candidate data sources/partners: Unwort des Jahres (jury + published criteria), CDT's Grass-Mud Horse Lexicon (wiki + ebook), and China Media Project's tifa frequency tracking (corpus-dated watchwords).

Adopt the Sprachkritische Aktion governance model for the open-source lexicon: public submissions with justification and source, a small named review panel per language, and explicit inclusion criteria (euphemistic/obscuring/misleading; discriminates; anti-democratic) — this keeps 'manipulative' a defended editorial judgment rather than a crowd vote, and gives each language community ownership of its pack.

Encode the charter cross-culturally: indirection is not manipulation. Aimai vagueness, honorifics, and reportative evidentials are cooperative politeness by default; per-language packs should flag only mismatch-to-context (a lexicalized non-commitment where a commitment was requested, an evidential contradicting the speaker's known access, a perception-blaming apology formula) and captions must never score a language or culture as inherently evasive.

Do not port English cue lists or offer any universal 'lie score': cross-linguistic deception research (11 datasets, 5 languages) finds no universal feature set and cue directions flip between individualist and collectivist cultures (first-person pronouns). Every language pack ships with its own empirically justified tells and its own false-positive notes — this is the engineering-level enforcement of 'reads the language, never the mind'.

Gate the LLM truth-caption per language behind targeted evaluation: LLMs perform near chance on Turkish evidential trust reasoning that native speakers do robustly, so a first-person plain-meaning rewrite in an evidential or honorific language must demonstrably preserve source-marking and register meaning (e.g. render 'gelmiş' as 'I'm told he came', not 'he came') before that language's caption feature is enabled; include evidential/honorific preservation cases in the eval set.

Add a documented 'silence' boundary: sontaku shows the strongest manipulation can leave no textual trace (the order never uttered). The framework's educational content should teach absence-of-commitment and absence-of-order as patterns readers infer from context, while the engine honestly marks only what is present in the text — this belongs in the docs/curriculum layer, not the highlighter.

factChecks.claim: About a quarter of the world's languages grammatically mark evidence source, often obligatorily; Aikhenvald (2004) documents systems in Turkish, Quechua, Aymara, Tariana, Bulgarian, Tibetan, ranging 2-way to 5-way; Aymara (Hardman 1986) marks personal knowledge vs hearsay vs inference with =wa, -tay, siwa.
factChecks.correction: Core facts confirmed, three details need fixing. (1) The cited PDF is Aikhenvald 2007, 'Information source and evidentiality: what can we conclude?', Rivista di Linguistica 19.1:209-227 — not the 2004 book — and its obligatory-language list is Tariana, Matses, Makah, Hup, Quechua, Aymara; Turkish, Bulgarian and Tibetan are not named there (the 2004 book does treat them, but Turkish's choice is obligatory only in past-tense contexts and Aikhenvald classes it A2 'non-firsthand vs everything else', not A1 firsthand/non-firsthand). (2) The Aymara non-personal-knowledge marker is -tayna (Hardman's Chilean Aymara example uses -tin-: Saratinwa 'She had gone, but I didn't see her'), not '-tay'. (3) The marker-category mapping is crossed as written: -wa = personal knowledge, siwa/siw = hearsay ('they say'), -tayna = non-personal knowledge; inference proper is a separate marker (-pacha) in Hardman's five-way Aymara set.
factChecks.evidence: The cited PDF (linguistica.sns.it/RdL/19.1/10.aikhenvald.pdf, verified by downloading and extracting text) states verbatim: 'In about one quarter of the world's languages, marking information source is obligatory' and 'a clause without a marker of information source would not be acceptable to a native speaker' (citing Weber 1986 on Quechua: 'clause is ungrammatical, or the speaker incompetent'). It also confirms 'The maximum number of evidential terms in a system appears to be five' with parameters visual, (nonvisual) sensory, inference, assumption, reported, and confirms Eurasian 2-term catch-all 'non-firsthand' systems. WALS valueset 77A-aym exists: Aymara (Central), feature 77A Semantic Distinctions of Evidentiality, value 'Direct and indirect', source Hardman 1986. Hardman's own text (mason.gmu.edu 'Data source and person in Jaqi' PDF, extracted) gives: Sariwa 'She went (I saw her go)' = personal knowledge -wa; 'Sariw siw' 'She went, they say' = knowledge-through-language; Saratinwa 'She had gone (but I didn't see her)' = non-personal knowledge; Sarpachawa = deduced/inferential -pacha. Hardman 1986 'Data-source marking in the Jaqi languages' in Chafe & Nichols (eds.), Evidentiality, pp. 113-136 confirmed via PhilPapers.

factChecks.claim: The 'Someone told me' study (attributed to Mahr & Csibra, PMC6481770) tested English/Italian lexical markers and Turkish -mIş / Estonian -vat grammatical evidentials; when lying, odds of indirect marking rose 21.4x (EN), 7.8x (IT), 3.1x (TR), 8.4x (EE).
factChecks.correction: The authors are Francesca Giardini, Stanka A. Fitneva, and Anne Tamm — NOT Mahr & Csibra. Citation: Giardini, Fitneva & Tamm (2019), '"Someone told me": Preemptive reputation protection in communication', PLoS ONE 14(4): e0200883. (Mahr & Csibra have separate work on hearsay/commitment, which the researcher likely conflated.) Everything else checks out.
factChecks.evidence: PMC6481770 fetched directly: title '"Someone told me": Preemptive reputation protection in communication', authors Giardini, Fitneva, Tamm (2019); PLoS ONE 14(4):e0200883 confirmed via journals.plos.org search result. Languages/markers confirmed: English and Italian lexical ('someone told me'), Estonian indirect evidential -vat, Turkish -mIş vs unmarked direct. Odds ratios for choosing indirect marking when lying confirmed: English 21.4 (95% CI 8.1-56.3), Italian 7.8 (3.5-17.3), Turkish 3.1 (1.5-6.4), Estonian 8.43 (2.76-25.75) — the claim's '8.4x (EE)' rounds 8.43 correctly.

factChecks.claim: Eye-tracking study 'Eyes do not lie but words do' (Functions of Language) shows Turkish readers interpret mismatched evidentiality (e.g. direct -DI for hearsay-only information) as deceptive during reading.
factChecks.evidence: Article verified: Arslan, Tunalı, Çetin & Aydın, 'Eyes do not lie but words do: Evidence from eye-movement monitoring during reading that misuse of evidentiality marking in Turkish is interpreted as deceptive', Functions of Language 31(1), 2024, pp. 90-108 (benjamins.com URL 403'd but the article was verified via jbe-platform.com/content/journals/10.1075/fol.22061.ars and search). 40 native Turkish speakers; eye-movement monitoring during reading plus end-of-sentence deception-detection task; abstract: 'Readers had the tendency to judge stimulus material with source-evidentiality mismatch to be untruthful', with longer gaze durations at the critical verb in mismatch conditions. One nuance the researcher should carry forward: both mismatch directions were tested ('a direct or indirect evidential form either compatible or incompatible with the given information source'), and the abstract reports the INDIRECT evidential condition was detected as a lie more often than the direct condition — so the claim's -DI example is a tested mismatch type but not the one most often flagged as lying.

factChecks.claim: arXiv 2604.24665 (2026): 75 native Turkish speakers shifted -DI vs -mIş with source trustworthiness (67.7% -DI in high-trust); across 10 LLMs and three paradigms, trust effects were inconsistent, often reversed, near-chance after correction; models optimize surface plausibility rather than tracking epistemic commitment.
factChecks.evidence: Paper exists and all numbers check: arXiv:2604.24665v1 [cs.CL], 27 Apr 2026, 'Benchmarking Source-Sensitive Reasoning in Turkish: Humans and LLMs under Evidential Trust Manipulation'. Fetched full HTML: '75 unique participants who self-identified as native speakers of Turkish'; -DI proportion 0.677 in High-Trust contexts; 10 LLMs across three prompting paradigms (open gap-fill, explicit past-tense gap-fill, forced-choice A/B selection); LLM effects 'generally unstable, often reversed, and frequently overshadowed by output-compliance problems'; 'Acc% values remain close to chance for most models (roughly 50-58%)' and 'none remains significant after Holm correction across models'. The phrase 'optimize surface plausibility' appears in the paper's framing (whether models 'merely optimize surface plausibility or whether they track source-sensitive epistemic distinctions'), and its conclusion — models do not reliably reproduce human trust sensitivity — matches the claim's rendering.

factChecks.claim: Sontaku (忖度) was 2017 Japanese word of the year (Jiyu Kokuminsha, Dec 1 2017), arising from the Moritomo Gakuen scandal — land sold at 134M yen vs 956M appraisal; Abe issued no order; Finance Ministry altered 14 documents removing Abe references (Carlson 2020, Public Administration and Policy).
factChecks.evidence: All checkable specifics verified. Sontaku was selected as a 2017 grand-prize winner of Jiyū Kokuminsha's U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award, announced December 1, 2017 at Tokyo's Imperial Hotel (nippon.com 'The Winning Words'; Japan Times Dec 1 2017) — minor nuance: it shared the top prize with 'insuta-bae' (Instagrammable). Carlson, Matthew M. (2020), 'Sontaku and political scandals in Japan', Public Administration and Policy 23(1), pp. 33-45, fetched directly from emerald.com: 'Moritomo bought the land for only 134 million yens when it was appraised at 956 million yen'; 'The Asahi discovered dozens of deletions across a total of 14 documents' which 'purposely and systematically removed any mention or hints of political involvement' (the removed references included Abe and his wife Akie — slightly broader than 'Abe references'); sontaku framed as officials anticipating a superior's wishes without explicit orders.

factChecks.claim: Japanese aimai supplies lexicalized non-commitments: zensho shimasu ('I will handle it appropriately') can mean anything from 'I'll act' to 'I will do nothing'; kentō shimasu ('I'll study it') conventionally means refusal; used routinely by politicians.
factChecks.evidence: Well supported by multiple independent sources. Zensho shimasu: the famous 1969 Sato-Nixon textile-negotiations episode — Sato's 'zensho shimasu' was interpreted as 'I will do my best' while 'as used in Japanese political circles, [it] means nothing more than I'll think about it'; Washington and Tokyo 'spent the next two years squabbling over the meaning' (Washington Post 1991 'Japan's Master Interpreter'; languagehat.com; Kondo's interpreting-studies work in Asia Pacific Translation and Intercultural Studies). Kentō shimasu: multiple Japanese-communication guides confirm it 'often means the answer is no, but they're being polite' — a conventional soft refusal, though it can occasionally be genuine consideration, so 'conventionally means refusal' is a slight overstatement of a strong tendency. Both cited sources exist: the WordReference thread forum.wordreference.com/threads/zensho-shimasu.3610602/ (confirmed via search index; direct fetch bot-blocked with HTTP 418) and ResearchGate publication 340807974 'THE IMPORTANCE OF UNDERSTANDING MEANING AMBIGUITY IN JAPANESE (AIMAI)' (published April 2020, on aimai and kuuki yomenai — note it covers aimai generally; not verified that it discusses these two formulas specifically).

findings.summary: The open-source landscape has every ingredient for captioneer's vision but no assembled product: academic taxonomies of manipulation techniques are mature (SemEval-2023's 23 persuasion techniques in 6 families, span-annotated across 9 languages; DISARM's 106 CC-BY-4.0 disinformation TTPs at campaign level), yet the research code is abandoned one-offs (QCRI's flagship propaganda BERT untouched since May 2021, the main fallacy dataset unlicensed and frozen since 2023), the best annotated corpora are legally non-redistributable, the market-leading lexicon (LIWC) is proprietary and commercially enclosed via Receptiviti, and commercial media-literacy products (Ground News, AllSides, Ad Fontes, Otherweb) keep methodology closed or publish only opaque model weights — no maintained, community-governed, span-level, cross-language open lexicon of manipulation patterns exists; the niche of "Hunspell for manipulation" is genuinely empty. The governance playbook, however, is fully proven elsewhere over a decade-plus: SpamAssassin's corpus-gated rule promotion (rules ship only after mass-check shows they hit spam and not ham) is the direct anti-poisoning answer to adversarial pattern submissions; Wiktionary's attestation standard (3 independent, durably-archived uses spanning a year, with stricter fast-track rules for derogatory entries) is the evidence template; uAssets' issue-number provenance for every filter, CLDR's weighted per-language submission/vetting cycles, EasyList's published inclusion policy (and its 2017 DMCA attack) and Hunspell's engine/dictionary separation supply the rest. The recommended shape: Apache-2.0 engine, CC-BY-SA-4.0 pattern lexicon with stable DISARM-style technique IDs, every pattern entry carrying specimens plus counter-specimens and CI-measured false-positive rates on a benign "ham" corpus, per-language maintainer teams, and an RFV-style dispute process.

key_findings.claim: No direct competitor exists: nothing combines span-level close reading, an open redistributable pattern lexicon, historical origin/evolution, and cross-language comparison under community governance.
key_findings.detail: The pieces exist separately — SemEval taxonomies (papers only, data locked), Prta/Tanbih demo (closed backend, 2020 research demo by QCRI+MIT-CSAIL that highlights propaganda spans via API), DISARM (open but campaign-level, not sentence-level), LIWC (closed), and research datasets (abandoned). A 2026 search for open manipulation-language frameworks surfaces only benchmarks (MentalManip, CogManip, ExTax) — none is a maintained community lexicon. The gap captioneer targets is real and unoccupied.

key_findings.claim: The academic taxonomy backbone is ready-made: SemEval-2023 Task 3 defines 23 persuasion techniques in 6 families, span-annotated in 9 languages.
key_findings.detail: Families and techniques: Attack on Reputation (Name Calling, Doubt, Guilt by Association, Appeal to Hypocrisy, Questioning the Reputation); Justification (Appeal to Authority, Appeal to Popularity, Appeal to Values, Appeal to Fear/Prejudice, Flag Waving); Distraction (Straw Man, Red Herring, Whataboutism); Simplification (Causal Oversimplification, False Dilemma, Consequential Oversimplification); Call (Slogans, Appeal to Time, Conversation Killer); Manipulative Wording (Loaded Language, Repetition, Exaggeration/Minimisation, Obfuscation). Languages: EN, FR, DE, IT, PL, RU training + ES, EL, KA surprise. This is the lineage of SemEval-2020 Task 11 (18-technique inventory, merged to 14 classes, with span-identification + technique-classification subtasks; 250 teams registered) and SemEval-2021/2024 meme tasks. Captioneer's six families map cleanly onto subsets of this taxonomy.

key_findings.claim: Critical catch: the best span-annotated persuasion corpus is NOT open — SemEval-2023 data forbids redistribution and is limited to registered scientific use.
key_findings.detail: The task site states participants 'may not redistribute or share in part or full with any third party' and restricts use to scientific research. So the taxonomy (uncopyrightable ideas) can be adopted, but the framework must collect its own specimens under its own license. This is the single biggest data-supply gap the project must fill — and an opportunity, since a freely-licensed specimen corpus would itself be novel.

key_findings.claim: The open-source detection code that exists is largely abandoned research exhaust, not maintained infrastructure.
key_findings.detail: GitHub API checks (2026-07-07): QCRI/PropagandaTechniquesAnalysis-en-BERT on Hugging Face last modified 2021-05-19, 439 downloads, no license tag; causalNLP/logical-fallacy (the 2,453-example Logic dataset, ~10% noisy per community review) last pushed 2023-12-11, NO license, 92 stars; tmakesense/logical-fallacy frozen Oct 2022; SemEval entrant repos are one-shot. Argument-mining toolkits are alive but tiny and academic: arg-tech/oAMF (GPL-3.0, 15+ modules, pushed 2025-04, 12 stars), nlp-unibo/MAMKit (CC0, pushed 2025-09, 13 stars), Open-Argumentation/Canary (GPL-3.0, 2024, 13 stars). Nobody is running the 'EasyList of manipulation' — maintenance is the moat, not the model.

key_findings.claim: LIWC, the de-facto standard word-category lexicon, is proprietary and commercially enclosed — a cautionary tale and the strongest argument for a ShareAlike data license.
key_findings.detail: The LIWC-22 dictionary is proprietary; academic licenses (~$90, forever) are valid ONLY for university research and explicitly exclude research 'for, on behalf of, or in conjunction with any commercial entity'; Receptiviti holds exclusive commercial rights. Forty years of psycholinguistic lexicon work is thus fenced off from open tooling. An openly-licensed manipulation-cue lexicon would occupy the position LIWC monopolizes, and ShareAlike licensing prevents a Receptiviti-style enclosure of community contributions.

key_findings.claim: Commercial media-literacy products open-source essentially nothing that matters; Otherweb/Valurank is the partial exception but publishes weights, not inspectable patterns.
key_findings.detail: Ground News produces no original ratings — it averages AllSides + Ad Fontes + MBFC at publication level (never article spans). AllSides holds a patent on its multi-method bias rating (blind surveys + expert panels checking ~16 bias types); Ad Fontes uses paid left/center/right analyst panels then trained a private AI on their outputs. Otherweb (Valurank Corp, a public benefit corp) claims '20 AI models with source code and datasets open' and does publish ~33 models on Hugging Face (distilroberta-propaganda-2class, distilroberta-bias, clickbait, etc.), but these are document-level classifier weights — no curated pattern lexicon, no span-level explanation, no community contribution path. None of them does close reading of a user's own text.

key_findings.claim: DISARM is the closest governance-and-shape precedent: an open, MITRE-ATT&CK-style framework of manipulation techniques with stable IDs, a foundation, and CC-BY-4.0 licensing — but at the wrong altitude (campaigns, not sentences).
key_findings.detail: DISARM Red catalogs disinformation-creator TTPs: 106 top-level techniques (397 IDs with sub-techniques, T0xxx.yyy scheme) across 17 tactics, plus a Blue countermeasures framework. Governance: 'major changes are agreed on by the DISARM Foundation'; minor suggestions come via a public form; master data lives in a spreadsheet that regenerates all pages; STIX/MISP interop drove institutional adoption (NATO, EU trials). Repo active (pushed 2026-03). Lineage: Credibility Coalition MisinfosecWG (2018) → AMITT → merged with MITRE/FIU's SPICE (2022) → DISARM Foundation. It proves an open technique catalog with stable IDs and light central authority can survive and become a shared vocabulary — captioneer's framework should be its linguistic-level sibling.

key_findings.claim: SpamAssassin's rule lifecycle is the proven anti-poisoning mechanism: empirical corpus gating, where a rule ships only if nightly mass-checks show it hits spam and not ham.
key_findings.detail: Contributors file rules in Bugzilla WITH sample spam messages attached (headers intact). Rules start in a developer sandbox flagged 'tflags publish', then nightly MassCheck runs them against hand-classified spam/ham corpora contributed by multiple parties; RuleQA (ruleqa.spamassassin.org, still running in 2026) computes hit frequencies, and rules meeting promotion criteria graduate to the active set — others are automatically greyed out/demoted. Translated to a manipulation lexicon: every pattern must demonstrate, in CI, a high hit rate on attested manipulative specimens and a near-zero rate on a curated corpus of ordinary sincere speech drawn from across the political spectrum. A submitted pattern designed to flag opponents' ordinary speech fails the ham test mechanically — no editor debate required.

key_findings.claim: Wiktionary's Criteria for Inclusion supply the evidence standard: three independent, durably-archived uses spanning at least one year, with stricter fast-track rules for harm-adjacent entries.
key_findings.detail: Attestation requires 3 citations that are actual uses (not mentions), by different people, not quoting each other, spanning >1 year, from durable sources; disputes go through Requests for Verification (RFV) where entries die if evidence isn't produced; 'hot words' get a time-span exemption but not an evidence exemption; derogatory terms must attest within two weeks or face deletion. For a manipulation lexicon: every pattern requires ≥3 independent real-world specimens spanning time and sources; patterns implicating identifiable groups or political actors get the stricter derogatory-term track. This has kept the world's largest open dictionary honest for two decades.

key_findings.claim: uBlock Origin's uAssets shows minimal-bureaucracy provenance: every single filter must cite a formal issue number, and file ordering doubles as a decay-review queue.
key_findings.detail: CONTRIBUTING.md mandates that all added filters carry a comment linking the GitHub issue that motivated them ('this documents why a filter was added, and how to verify whether an old filter is still needed'); new filters append at the end so the oldest — most likely obsolete — sit at the top for re-verification. This is provenance and staleness-review baked into the data format itself, at near-zero process cost. Every lexicon pattern should likewise embed its justification-issue URL and be periodically re-verified against fresh specimens.

key_findings.claim: EasyList demonstrates both the license split for pattern data (dual GPLv3 + CC-BY-SA 3.0) and the fact that a widely-deployed pattern list WILL be attacked legally and socially, not just technically.
key_findings.detail: EasyList (3,039 stars, commits daily since 2005-era origins) is dual-licensed GPLv3/CC-BY-SA-3.0+ and governed by a published Policy page: abusive ad servers 'blocked without warning', filters not removed on a site's promise ('both can change'), removal requesters bear the burden of argument, harassment not tolerated. In Aug 2017 anti-adblock firm Admiral used a DMCA §1201 'circumvention' claim to force removal of its domain functionalclam.com from EasyList via GitHub — the community answered with BarbBlock (auto-blocking DMCA'd domains) and clarified inclusion policy. A lexicon that flags powerful actors' rhetoric should expect takedown pressure: publish clear inclusion criteria in advance, keep specimens as short fair-use quotations with citations, and mirror the data.

key_findings.claim: Adblock Plus's CVE-2019-11593 warns that an expressive pattern DSL becomes an attack surface: the $rewrite filter option let malicious filter lists inject arbitrary code into pages for 100M+ users.
key_findings.detail: In April 2019 Armin Sebastian showed filter-list maintainers (or anyone who compromised a list) could exploit $rewrite to execute code on sites like Google services, with short-TTL malicious lists making attacks nearly undetectable; three CVEs issued, the feature was removed. Lesson for the framework: keep the pattern language declarative and non-Turing-complete (regex/morphology/dependency templates, no callbacks, no URL fetches), sandbox evaluation, and sign lexicon releases — because auto-updating pattern data is a supply chain.

key_findings.claim: Unicode CLDR is the governance template for the cross-language dimension: cyclical submission/vetting phases, organization-weighted voting, and a permissive data license purpose-built for data files.
key_findings.detail: CLDR gathers locale data through the Survey Tool roughly annually: a submission phase, then a formal Vetting Mode where new data is frozen and contributors adjust votes and argue in forums; votes are weighted (TC member orgs 6, regular orgs 4, individuals less), and the Technical Committee arbitrates. Data ships under Unicode-3.0, an OSI-approved MIT-like license that 'expressly covers data and data files.' For per-language manipulation-cue layers (hedging looks different in Japanese than English), CLDR proves the model: universal structure centrally governed, per-locale content vetted by native-speaker teams with weighted consensus.

key_findings.claim: Hunspell proves the engine/dictionary split scales for 20 years: one tri-licensed engine, per-language dictionaries owned and licensed by their own communities.
key_findings.detail: The Hunspell engine (LGPL/GPL/MPL tri-license, adopted 2006 specifically so Mozilla could ship it; still actively maintained, pushed 2026-07-05, 2,532 stars) powers LibreOffice, Firefox, Chrome, and macOS, while each language's dictionary is a separate artifact maintained by its own community under its own license and distributed through LibreOffice/Mozilla channels. ConceptNet shows the data-side counterpart: the knowledge graph is CC-BY-SA 4.0 because it ingests Wiktionary (CC-BY-SA), demonstrating how ShareAlike propagates through derived lexical data — a compatibility constraint captioneer must plan for if it ever ingests Wiktionary-derived material.

key_findings.claim: Recommended license split, grounded in decade-plus precedents: Apache-2.0 for the engine, CC-BY-SA 4.0 for the pattern lexicon, CC-BY 4.0 for specimen metadata with short quoted excerpts.
key_findings.detail: Engine as Apache-2.0 (patent grant, maximal embedding — the Hunspell tri-license solved the same adoption problem pre-Apache era). Lexicon as CC-BY-SA 4.0: CC 4.0 explicitly covers sui-generis database rights, ShareAlike blocks LIWC/Receptiviti-style enclosure of community work, and it is the license family already used by the neighboring ecosystem (Wiktionary, ConceptNet, EasyList's content half, DISARM's earlier releases; DISARM itself now CC-BY-4.0). ODbL is the heavier alternative (OpenStreetMap) but its contract-based share-alike complicates mixing; CC-BY-SA is sufficient for a lexicon. Specimens: store citation metadata + minimal fair-use quotes under CC-BY so researchers can build corpora without ShareAlike friction. Never leave data unlicensed — causalNLP/logical-fallacy's missing license is exactly why it can't be built upon.

techniques.name: Loaded Language
techniques.definition: Words/phrases with strong emotional charge (positive or negative) used to influence the reader beyond the propositional content.
techniques.origin: Institute for Propaganda Analysis lineage; formalized in Da San Martino et al. 2019 (PTC, 18 techniques) and SemEval-2020/2023 taxonomies
techniques.languages: Annotated in EN, FR, DE, IT, PL, RU (+ ES, EL, KA test) in SemEval-2023; the single most frequent technique in news corpora
techniques.example: "a disgusting betrayal of hard-working families"

techniques.name: Name Calling / Labeling
techniques.definition: Attaching a charged label to a person/idea so the audience judges the label instead of the claim.
techniques.origin: IPA seven devices (1937); SemEval family: Attack on Reputation
techniques.example: "the radical mob"

techniques.name: Doubt (Casting Doubt)
techniques.definition: Undermining credibility of a person/institution by questioning rather than asserting.
techniques.origin: SemEval-2020 Task 11; family: Attack on Reputation
techniques.example: "Can we really trust anything this agency says?"

techniques.name: Guilt by Association
techniques.definition: Discrediting a target by linking them to a despised person/group (Reductio ad Hitlerum is the classic case).
techniques.origin: PTC-2019 as Reductio ad Hitlerum; generalized in SemEval-2023

techniques.name: Appeal to Hypocrisy (tu quoque)
techniques.definition: Deflecting a criticism by charging the critic with the same fault.
techniques.origin: Classical fallacy catalog; added to SemEval-2023 taxonomy

techniques.name: Questioning the Reputation
techniques.definition: Pre-emptive smearing of a source so future statements are discounted.
techniques.origin: New in SemEval-2023 (Piskorski et al.)

techniques.name: Appeal to Authority
techniques.definition: Citing an authority's endorsement as if it settles the claim, without supporting evidence.
techniques.origin: Classical rhetoric (argumentum ad verecundiam); PTC-2019

techniques.name: Appeal to Popularity (Bandwagon)
techniques.definition: Arguing a claim is true/right because many people accept it.
techniques.origin: IPA 'Band Wagon' device (1937)

techniques.name: Appeal to Values
techniques.definition: Wrapping a claim in sacred values (freedom, family, faith) so rejecting the claim feels like rejecting the value.
techniques.origin: New in SemEval-2023

techniques.name: Appeal to Fear / Prejudice
techniques.definition: Building support by projecting threat or exploiting existing prejudice rather than evidence.
techniques.origin: IPA lineage; PTC-2019

techniques.name: Flag Waving
techniques.definition: Justifying a position via group identity/patriotism rather than argument.
techniques.origin: IPA lineage; PTC-2019

techniques.name: Straw Man
techniques.definition: Refuting a distorted substitute for the opponent's actual position.
techniques.origin: Classical fallacy; span-annotated since PTC-2019

techniques.name: Red Herring
techniques.definition: Introducing irrelevant material to divert from the issue at hand.
techniques.origin: Classical fallacy; PTC-2019

techniques.name: Whataboutism
techniques.definition: Discrediting a criticism by accusing the critic's side of worse, without addressing the criticism.
techniques.origin: Cold-War-era term; formalized in PTC-2019
techniques.languages: 9 SemEval-2023 languages; culturally salient in RU-adjacent media

techniques.name: Causal Oversimplification
techniques.definition: Asserting a single cause for an outcome that has many.
techniques.origin: PTC-2019; family: Simplification

techniques.name: False Dilemma / Black-and-White
techniques.definition: Presenting exactly two options (or one 'no choice' path) when more exist.
techniques.origin: Classical fallacy; PTC-2019 as Black-and-White Fallacy

techniques.name: Consequential Oversimplification (Slippery Slope)
techniques.definition: Claiming an action will inevitably cascade into extreme consequences without establishing the chain.
techniques.origin: Classical slippery slope; added SemEval-2023

techniques.name: Slogans
techniques.definition: Brief striking phrases with emotional pull substituting for argument.
techniques.origin: PTC-2019; family: Call

techniques.name: Appeal to Time (Kairos)
techniques.definition: Claiming 'the moment demands it' — urgency as justification.
techniques.origin: Classical kairos; added SemEval-2023

techniques.name: Conversation Killer (Thought-terminating Cliché)
techniques.definition: Stock phrases that shut down critical discussion ('it is what it is').
techniques.origin: Robert Lifton (1961) 'thought-terminating cliché'; PTC-2019; renamed in SemEval-2023

techniques.name: Repetition
techniques.definition: Repeating a message/phrase until familiarity substitutes for evidence (illusory-truth effect).
techniques.origin: IPA lineage; PTC-2019

techniques.name: Exaggeration / Minimisation
techniques.definition: Representing something as far larger/worse or far smaller/less important than warranted — directly matches captioneer's overclaim + minimizing families.

techniques.name: Obfuscation / Intentional Vagueness
techniques.definition: Deliberately unclear or ambiguous wording so the audience fills in the meaning — cousin of captioneer's deleted-subject/passive family.

techniques.name: DISARM TTP catalog (framework-level, not a wording technique)
techniques.definition: 106 top-level techniques / 397 IDs across 17 tactics describing how disinformation campaigns are planned, produced, amplified and sustained (e.g. T0046 Search Engine Optimization) — the operations layer above captioneer's linguistic layer, with stable MITRE-style IDs.
techniques.origin: MisinfosecWG/Credibility Coalition 2018 → AMITT → merged with MITRE/FIU SPICE 2022 → DISARM Foundation; CC-BY-4.0
techniques.languages: English master data; used internationally via STIX/MISP interop

techniques.name: MentalManip taxonomy (interpersonal manipulation)
techniques.definition: Three-dimension scheme for conversational manipulation — presence, technique (e.g. gaslighting, guilt-tripping), and targeted vulnerability — the interpersonal register captioneer's users paste most often, distinct from news propaganda.
techniques.origin: Wang et al., ACL 2024 dataset of movie-dialogue manipulation

framework_implications: Split the project into three separately-licensed artifacts, Hunspell-style: engine (Apache-2.0), pattern lexicon (CC-BY-SA 4.0 — ShareAlike specifically to prevent LIWC/Receptiviti-style commercial enclosure of community contributions; CC 4.0 covers database rights), and a specimen-citation corpus (CC-BY 4.0 metadata with short fair-use quotes). Never ship unlicensed data — the field's best fallacy dataset is unusable precisely because it has no license.

Give every technique a stable DISARM/MITRE-style ID (e.g. MW.LOAD for loaded language) with a two-layer data model: universal technique nodes (definition, origin, history, cross-references to SemEval/DISARM/fallacy names) and per-language cue-pattern layers underneath, CLDR-style, each owned by a native-speaker maintainer team with weighted vetting. Adopt the SemEval-2023 23-technique taxonomy as the seed ontology (ideas are free) but collect fresh specimens — the SemEval corpus itself is non-redistributable.

Make every pattern entry a self-verifying record: id, technique, language, pattern (declarative DSL only — regex/morphology templates, no executable options; ABP's $rewrite CVE shows expressive filter languages become code-injection vectors), >=3 independent real-world specimens spanning >=1 year with source URLs and dates (Wiktionary CFI standard), counter-specimens it must NOT flag, and a link to the proposal issue (uAssets provenance rule).

Gate promotion empirically, SpamAssassin-style: CI runs every proposed pattern against two versioned corpora — attested manipulative specimens ('spam') and a politically-balanced corpus of ordinary sincere speech ('ham'). A pattern ships only above a precision threshold; a submission crafted to flag one faction's ordinary speech fails the ham test mechanically, which is the primary poisoning defense and removes most need for editorial judgment calls.

Run a Wiktionary-style RFV dispute process: anyone can challenge a pattern; challenged patterns are frozen (still visible, marked disputed) and deleted if attestation isn't reproduced in a fixed window. Patterns whose specimens target identifiable groups, living persons, or named political actors get the stricter fast-track standard (Wiktionary's derogatory-term rule: attest quickly or it goes).

Publish an EasyList-style inclusion policy BEFORE opening contributions: what qualifies as a manipulation cue, the explicit charter line that a mark describes the language and never asserts the speaker's intent or deception (this is also the legal shield), that entries are never removed in exchange for promises or payment, and that removal requesters bear the burden of evidence. Expect legal pressure — EasyList lost a domain to a DMCA §1201 claim in 2017 — so keep specimens as short cited quotations, sign releases, and mirror the lexicon across hosts.

Treat the lexicon, not model weights, as the ground truth: Otherweb/Valurank shows that publishing 33 classifier checkpoints is not an inspectable, correctable, teachable framework. ML models (a fine-tuned multilingual XLM-R-style tagger is the proven architecture from SemEval) should be derived artifacts trained from the lexicon+specimens and rebuilt on release, so every flag traces back to a human-readable pattern with attested specimens.

Add the maintenance layer nobody else has: uAssets-style decay review (oldest patterns re-verified against fresh specimens on a schedule) and SpamAssassin-style nightly re-scoring as language drifts — the landscape audit shows abandoned research code is the default failure mode, so budget governance for a 10-year horizon: a lightweight foundation or fiscal sponsor holding the trademark and final say on major taxonomy changes (DISARM Foundation model), with day-to-day merges by per-language teams.

Design for interop from day one: JSON/STIX-compatible export of technique IDs and marked spans so newsrooms, moderation pipelines, and researchers can embed the lexicon — DISARM's STIX/MISP compatibility is what got it adopted by institutions; a documented API/schema is the difference between a website and a framework.

Position honestly against the landscape: the historical-origin and cross-language-evolution dimensions (IPA 1937 devices → Lifton 1961 → PTC 2019 → SemEval 2023 lineage; technique salience differing by language community, e.g. whataboutism) exist nowhere as structured open data — encoding origin/evolution metadata on each technique node is captioneer's genuinely novel contribution and should be a first-class schema field, not documentation prose.

factChecks.claim: Claim 1: No direct competitor exists; the pieces exist separately — Prta/Tanbih (closed-backend 2020 QCRI+MIT-CSAIL demo highlighting propaganda spans via API), DISARM (open but campaign-level), LIWC (closed), abandoned research datasets; 2026 benchmarks (MentalManip, CogManip, ExTax) are not maintained community lexicons.
factChecks.evidence: Every checkable sub-fact verified: Prta is the ACL 2020 demo paper (aclanthology.org/2020.acl-demos.32) by Da San Martino, Shaar, Zhang (QCRI), Seunghak Yu (MIT CSAIL), Barrón-Cedeño (U. Bologna), Nakov (QCRI); it highlights propaganda technique spans and offers a web interface plus an API at tanbih.org/prta, with no released system code (only the underlying BERT model on HF). DISARM Foundation states the framework is published under CC-BY-SA-4.0 and documents influence operations at the campaign/TTP level (MITRE ATT&CK-style), not sentence spans. LIWC is proprietary (see claim 5). MentalManip exists (arXiv 2405.16584, ACL 2024, 4,000 annotated movie dialogues); ExTax exists (arXiv 2605.27045, submitted 2026-05-26, LLM-based taxonomy framework); CogManip exists (arXiv 2606.06099, a 2026 benchmark of manipulative LLM behavior across 1,000 multi-turn scenarios — note it lives at 2606.06099, not among the claim's cited URLs). All three are benchmarks/eval frameworks, not maintained community lexicons. The overall 'no direct competitor' statement is a negative claim that cannot be exhaustively proven, but nothing surfaced contradicting it and all its supporting evidence is accurate.

factChecks.claim: Claim 2: SemEval-2023 Task 3 defines 23 persuasion techniques in 6 families, span-annotated in 9 languages (EN/FR/DE/IT/PL/RU training + ES/EL/KA surprise); lineage from SemEval-2020 Task 11 (18-technique inventory merged to 14 classes, SI+TC subtasks, 250 teams registered) and SemEval-2021/2024 meme tasks.
factChecks.evidence: Task site (propaganda.math.unipd.it/semeval2023task3/) confirms 23 fine-grained techniques in 6 categories with span-level annotations for gold-label datasets. The overview paper (aclanthology.org/2023.semeval-1.317) confirms 9 languages: EN, FR, DE, IT, PL, RU training plus surprise Spanish, Greek, Georgian (ES/EL/KA). The six families and technique-to-family mapping match the published taxonomy (Attack on Reputation: Name Calling, Guilt by Association, Casting Doubt, Appeal to Hypocrisy, Questioning the Reputation; Justification: Flag Waving, Appeal to Authority/Popularity/Values/Fear; Distraction: Strawman, Red Herring, Whataboutism; Simplification: Causal Oversimplification, False Dilemma, Consequential Oversimplification; Call: Slogans, Conversation Killer, Appeal to Time; Manipulative Wording: Loaded Language, Obfuscation, Exaggeration/Minimisation, Repetition) — minor naming variants only (e.g. 'Doubt' = 'Casting Doubt', 'False Dilemma' = 'False Dilemma or No Choice'). SemEval-2020 Task 11 paper (arXiv 2009.02696 / aclanthology 2020.semeval-1.186) confirms: annotators worked with the 18-technique schema of Da San Martino et al. 2019, rare techniques were merged (Red Herring+Straw Man+Whataboutism; Bandwagon+Reductio ad Hitlerum) and Obfuscation dropped, yielding 14 classes; subtasks were Span Identification and Technique Classification; '250 teams signed up to participate and 44 made a submission'. SemEval-2021 Task 6 (Detection of Persuasion Techniques in Texts and Images, arXiv 2105.09284) and SemEval-2024 Task 4 (Multilingual Detection of Persuasion Techniques in Memes, aclanthology 2024.semeval-1.275) both exist.

factChecks.claim: Claim 3: SemEval-2023 Task 3 data is not open — the task site forbids redistribution ('may not redistribute or share in part or full with any third party') and restricts use to registered scientific research.
factChecks.evidence: Fetched propaganda.math.unipd.it/semeval2023task3/ directly. Verbatim: 'The dataset may include content which is protected by copyright of third parties. It may only be used in the context of this shared task, and only for scientific research purposes. The dataset may not be redistributed or shared in part or full with any third party.' Plus: 'You may not share you passcode with others or give access to the dataset to unauthorised users. Any other use is explicitly prohibited.' The claim's quote is a near-verbatim active-voice rendering of the actual passive-voice sentence; substance identical. The inference (taxonomy adoptable as uncopyrightable ideas, but specimens must be self-collected) follows.

factChecks.claim: Claim 4: Existing OSS detection code is abandoned research exhaust — QCRI HF model last modified 2021-05-19 with 439 downloads and no license tag; causalNLP/logical-fallacy (2,453-example Logic dataset, ~10% noisy) pushed 2023-12-11, no license, 92 stars; tmakesense/logical-fallacy frozen Oct 2022; arg-tech/oAMF GPL-3.0 15+ modules pushed 2025-04 12 stars; nlp-unibo/MAMKit CC0 pushed 2025-09 13 stars; Open-Argumentation/Canary GPL-3.0 2024 13 stars.
factChecks.correction: The Logic dataset has 2,449 examples, not 2,453 (Jin et al., arXiv 2202.13758: 'a dataset of 2,449 samples of 13 logical fallacy types', Table 2: 1,849 train / 300 dev / 300 test; LogicClimate is 1,079). The '~10% noisy per community review' figure could not be sourced — the causalNLP/logical-fallacy repo has zero GitHub issues mentioning noise/label quality; treat that percentage as unverified. Everything else is exact.
factChecks.evidence: Verified via Hugging Face and GitHub APIs on 2026-07-07. QCRI/PropagandaTechniquesAnalysis-en-BERT: lastModified 2021-05-19T11:27:07Z, downloads 439 (exact match), tags contain no license. causalNLP/logical-fallacy: 92 stars, license None, pushed_at 2023-12-11T18:36:37Z. tmakesense/logical-fallacy: pushed_at 2022-10-31T23:04:32Z (frozen Oct 2022). arg-tech/oAMF: GPL-3.0, pushed 2025-04-07, 12 stars, created 2025-01; README says 'over 15 AM modules' (elsewhere '17+ Open-Source AM Modules'). nlp-unibo/mamkit: CC0-1.0, pushed 2025-09-17, 13 stars. Open-Argumentation/Canary: GPL-3.0, pushed 2024-04-27, 13 stars. All counts/dates/licenses match the claim except the two corrected items.

factChecks.claim: Claim 5: LIWC-22 is proprietary; academic licenses (~$90, forever) are valid only for university research and explicitly exclude research 'for, on behalf of, or in conjunction with any commercial entity'; Receptiviti holds exclusive commercial rights.
factChecks.correction: The '(~$90, forever)' price/duration detail could not be verified for LIWC-22: current pricing is only visible inside the FastSpring checkout (liwcsoftware.onfastspring.com) and is not publicly listed; $90 is documented only for the older LIWC2007. The FAQ's 'The duration of your LIWC-22 license begins at the time of purchase' suggests term-based rather than perpetual licensing. Treat the specific price and 'forever' as unsupported. Also, the FAQ says Receptiviti, Inc. 'holds the non-academic rights to LIWC' — functionally the sole commercial rights holder, though the word 'exclusive' is not used verbatim.
factChecks.evidence: liwc.app/buy states verbatim: 'LIWC-22 cannot be used for research being conducted for, on behalf of, or in conjunction with any commercial entity' and limits web-store licenses to academics/students for purely academic research in university settings, directing all other use to a commercial license via Receptiviti. liwc.app/help/faq: 'The company that holds the non-academic rights to LIWC is Receptiviti, Inc.' and academics doing non-academic work (consulting/advising) need a commercial license. Core substance of the claim (proprietary, enclosed, commercial-entity exclusion quote, Receptiviti gatekeeping) is confirmed; only the price/perpetuity parenthetical is unverified.

factChecks.claim: Claim 6: Ground News averages AllSides + Ad Fontes + MBFC at publication level (no original ratings); AllSides holds a patent on its multi-method bias rating (blind surveys + expert panels, ~16 bias types); Ad Fontes uses paid balanced analyst panels then trained a private AI; Otherweb (Valurank Corp, PBC) claims '20 AI models with source code and datasets open' and publishes ~33 document-level classifier models on Hugging Face.
factChecks.evidence: ground.news/rating-system confirms Ground News does no original analysis, averaging available ratings from AllSides, Ad Fontes Media, and Media Bias/Fact Check, and states 'The analysis is done at the publication level' (not articles); the cited CJR article (cjr.org 'The Business of Balance') independently confirms the three-source reliance. AllSides describes its 'patented media bias ratings system' using Blind Bias Surveys plus politically balanced expert Editorial Review panels (allsides.com/media-bias/media-bias-rating-methods), and publishes the '16 Types of Media Bias' framework (allsides.com/media-bias/how-to-spot-types-of-media-bias) — note the 16 types are an educational guide; 'panels checking ~16 bias types' is a slight gloss. Ad Fontes (adfontesmedia.com): since Oct 2020 employs 40+ paid analysts in politically balanced pods of at least three (one left, one center, one right), and sells human-plus-AI article ratings to business customers — the AI is proprietary/private. SEC Form C filings confirm Otherweb, Inc. (formerly Valurank Corp) is a Delaware public benefit corporation (organized 2021-09-12) whose materials state '20 cutting-edge models, with source code and datasets open to the public'. Hugging Face API shows the valurank org hosts exactly 33 models including distilroberta-propaganda-2class, distilroberta-bias, and distilroberta-clickbait — all document-level classifiers, no curated pattern lexicon.

gaps.title: Abuse cases and legal exposure of the tool itself (weaponized labels, dual-use cookbook, regulation)
gaps.why: All six dimensions treated threats as external (poisoned contributions, DMCA, flak), but none studied captioneer as an attack surface or regulated object. Users will paste an ex's texts or a boss's email and wave the marked-up output as a verdict; the lexicon of techniques doubles as a manipulation cookbook; and marking a named person's public statement 'loaded framing' has defamation and EU AI Act/DSA exposure. Findings would change output wording, feature gates (private correspondence, named individuals), terms of service, hosting jurisdiction, and how the charter disclaimer is legally framed — none of which the current design addresses.
gaps.research_prompt: Context: captioneer.io is a live tool that highlights manipulation-affording phrases in pasted text (hedging, deflection, passive-voice agent deletion, loaded framing, overclaim, minimizing) plus an opt-in LLM plain-meaning rewrite; it is being grown into an open-source framework/lexicon of manipulation techniques. Its charter says it reads the language, never the mind — explicitly not a lie detector. Research the abuse cases and legal exposure of such a tool. Cover: (1) Weaponization of analytic labels in interpersonal and political conflict — empirical work on the implied truth effect (Pennycook et al. 2020: unlabeled content gains credibility when some content is labeled), the tainted truth effect, warning fatigue, the liar's dividend (Chesney & Citron), and documented misuse of therapeutic/analytic vocabularies like 'gaslighting' and 'DARVO' in custody disputes, HR complaints, and online harassment — what happens when a tool gives such labels machine authority? (2) Dual-use cookbook risk — evidence for and against the claim that publishing detailed persuasion-technique catalogs with examples gives attackers uplift (inoculation literature says naming helps defenders; check security-community debates around MITRE ATT&CK publication, offensive-technique disclosure norms, and any studies of persuasion-training increasing manipulative skill). (3) Regulatory classification — under the EU AI Act (2024), does a rhetoric-annotation tool risk being read as emotion recognition (Art. 5/Annex III) or face GPAI/transparency obligations, and how does its Art. 5 ban on manipulative AI interact with a tool that documents manipulation? Also DSA implications if integrated into platforms, and GDPR issues when users paste third parties' private messages (data-subject rights of the quoted person). (4) Defamation and opinion privilege — case law and legal analyses on ratings/labels as protected opinion: NewsGuard and Ad Fontes disputes, media-bias raters, credit-rating-agency First Amendment precedents, UK/EU honest-opinion defenses; what output phrasing ('this construction affords evasion' vs 'this is manipulative') keeps annotations inside opinion protection? (5) Precedents from adjacent tools — Grammarly tone detection, Perspective API misuse and bias findings, fact-checker legal threats. Deliver: a concrete threat model for the tool (who abuses it, against whom, via which feature), recommended output-wording constraints, feature gates and consent flows for private-text analysis, ToS/disclaimer language patterns with legal grounding, and any jurisdictional choices for hosting the lexicon.

gaps.title: Learning science of the lens: transfer, cynicism backfire, and validated measurement of 'discernment'
gaps.why: The teaching layer currently rests almost entirely on inoculation theory (Bad News, Jigsaw videos). But there is a direct empirical challenge nobody examined: Stanford's civic-online-reasoning work found close reading INFERIOR to lateral reading for evaluating information, and several 2023-2025 studies find manipulation-technique training raises indiscriminate skepticism — people start distrusting accurate, sincere text too. If the lens breeds cynicism rather than discernment, the curriculum design, mark density, and even the product's core close-reading premise need rework. No dimension covered how to measure whether a user actually acquired the lens.
gaps.research_prompt: Context: an open-source framework ('captioneer') teaches people to close-read text for manipulation techniques — six families (hedging, deflection, deleted agent/passive, loaded framing, overclaim, minimizing) marked as highlights on visible phrases, with per-technique micro-lessons planned on the inoculation-theory model (Bad News game, Jigsaw prebunking videos). Research the learning science of teaching this 'lens', with special attention to failure modes. Cover: (1) The close-reading critique — Stanford History Education Group / Wineburg's civic online reasoning research showing professional fact-checkers read laterally (leaving the text) while close/vertical readers get fooled; also 'critical ignoring' (Kozyreva, Wineburg, Hertwig, Lewandowsky 2023). Does this critique apply to rhetoric-level analysis of a statement whose source is already known (a boss's email, a politician's apology), or only to source-credibility tasks? Where exactly is close reading of language the right tool? (2) Backfire and skepticism spillover — studies where inoculation/media-literacy interventions reduced belief in TRUE content as much as false (Modirrousta-Galian & Higham 2023 meta-analysis of gamified inoculation; Hoes et al.; van der Meer et al.; Guess et al. India replication failure), danah boyd's 'Did Media Literacy Backfire?' argument, and any evidence on interventions that improved discernment specifically (signal-detection d-prime gains vs mere criterion shifts). (3) Measurement — validated instruments: MIST (Misinformation Susceptibility Test, Maertens et al. 2024), technique-recognition tests from Roozenbeek/van der Linden, signal detection analysis conventions in this literature; what would a validated 'lens acquisition' assessment for six rhetoric families look like? (4) Durability and dosage — inoculation decay curves and booster studies (Maertens et al. longevity work), spacing effects, age-appropriateness evidence for rhetoric instruction. (5) Reader-side effects of in-text highlighting itself — implied truth effect (unmarked spans read as endorsed), over-warning/alarm fatigue, and any HCI studies of inline credibility/rhetoric annotations changing reader judgment. Deliver: concrete design guidance — how the framework should sequence and dose lessons, whether/how the UI should pair close-reading marks with lateral-reading prompts, what outcome metric (discernment, not distrust) its curriculum should publish, and which claims about efficacy the project can honestly make.

gaps.title: Non-Western classical taxonomies of manipulation (Nyaya, Mohist, Han Feizi, balagha, Talmud)
gaps.why: The origins dimension was exclusively Greco-Roman/European (sophists → Aristotle → Rome → trivium → Renaissance → Schopenhauer). For a framework whose charter includes cross-language origins and evolution, this is a structural gap, not a content nicety: India's Nyaya tradition and China's Mohists built fallacy/disputation catalogs independently of Greece, and Han Feizi wrote a persuasion-difficulty treatise centuries before Machiavelli. Independent parallel lineages force a different genealogy schema (multiple unconnected roots with convergence edges, not one tree), provide evidence for which techniques are human universals versus Greek artifacts, and determine whether non-European contributors see their traditions in the framework.
gaps.research_prompt: Context: an open-source framework catalogs verbal-manipulation techniques with 'origin and evolution' as first-class data — each technique carries dated naming events (name, language, namer, work, year, quoted definition). The historical layer currently covers only the Western lineage (sophists, Aristotle's 13 fallacies, Rhetorica ad Herennium, Quintilian, medieval trivium, Renaissance figure manuals, Schopenhauer). Research pre-modern NON-Western taxonomies of verbal manipulation, fallacy, and persuasion, with primary sources, dates, and openly licensed translations. Cover: (1) Indian: the Nyayasutra's debate-flaw catalog — chala (quibbling, 3 types), jati (sophistical rejoinders, 24 types), nigrahasthana (points of defeat, 22 types), plus hetvabhasa (fallacious reasons); later Buddhist logic (Dignaga, Dharmakirti) and the vada/jalpa/vitanda debate typology; dating controversies and best English translations (public-domain Vidyabhusana? GRETIL availability). (2) Chinese: Mohist Canons on bian (disputation) and their named argument flaws; School of Names paradoxes; Han Feizi chapter 12 'Shui nan' (Difficulties of Persuasion) as audience-psychology manipulation theory; the Guiguzi as an explicit manual of manipulative rhetoric (its chapter-level taxonomy of techniques like bai he opening-and-shutting); Zhanguoce persuasions; availability via Chinese Text Project and licensing of standard translations. (3) Arabic/Islamic: balagha in depth — al-Jurjani's nazm theory, the ilm al-ma'ani / bayan / badi' division, taxonomies of kinaya (indirection/implicature) and majaz, and scholarship comparing them to Gricean implicature; also Ibn Rushd's commentary on Aristotle's Sophistical Refutations as a transmission bridge. (4) Hebrew: named argument moves and disqualified inferences in Talmudic dialectics (e.g., kal va-chomer misuse, pilpul critiques). (5) Anything comparable in Persian adab, Japanese, or documented African oral-rhetoric scholarship with formal catalogs. For each tradition: which of these six families appear independently (hedging, deflection, agent deletion, loaded framing, overclaim, minimizing) — convergent-discovery evidence; techniques with NO Western equivalent; exact texts, dates, and open-licensed editions/translations usable in a CC BY-SA database. Deliver: a comparative table (tradition x technique-family, with source citations) and schema implications for representing multiple independent origin lineages with later contact/transmission edges.

gaps.title: Evaluation infrastructure: the benign 'ham' corpus, achievable annotator agreement, and truth-caption faithfulness metrics
gaps.why: The governance design's central anti-poisoning mechanism (SpamAssassin-style promotion gating) presumes a politically balanced, openly licensed corpus of ordinary sincere speech to measure false positives against — no dimension checked whether such a corpus exists, how to build one, or how balance would be audited. Likewise nobody established what inter-annotator agreement is realistically achievable on span-level rhetoric marks (SemEval's own gamma values were modest), or how to evaluate the LLM rewrite's meaning preservation, which currently ships with no metric at all. If the ham corpus and agreement protocol can't be specified, the promotion gate and community annotation model collapse; this gap determines whether the framework's quality claims are testable.
gaps.research_prompt: Context: an open-source manipulation-pattern lexicon ('captioneer') plans SpamAssassin-style empirical gating: a proposed detection pattern ships only if CI shows high precision on attested manipulative specimens and a low false-positive rate on a benign corpus of ordinary sincere speech; the project also has an LLM 'truth caption' that rewrites a statement in plain first-person meaning, and it wants community span-level annotation. Research the evaluation infrastructure this requires. Cover: (1) Benign baseline ('ham') corpus construction — openly licensed, register-diverse, politically balanced corpora of ordinary sincere text: evaluate concrete candidates with licenses (CORE register-balanced web corpus, Europarl, US Congressional Record/Hansard, EDGAR filings, public-domain presidential speeches, Wikipedia talk vs article namespaces, CC Reddit dumps, OpenSubtitles, apology/complaint corpora) across the registers captioneer sees (workplace email, political statement, PR/crisis apology, personal message); how did SpamAssassin's mass-check, Jigsaw Perspective, and moderation research assemble and audit ham corpora, and what does the Perspective-API bias literature (false positives on AAVE, identity terms) teach about auditing political/dialect skew in a 'sincere speech' baseline? (2) Achievable inter-annotator agreement for span-level rhetoric annotation — published agreement numbers and protocols: PTC/SemEval propaganda-technique gamma, MAFALDA, BioScope hedge-scope kappa, CoNLL-2010, hate-speech and toxicity span tasks; expert vs crowd annotation, guideline length, adjudication designs that raised agreement; what precision/agreement thresholds are defensible for a community lexicon's promotion gate, and which of the six families (hedging, deflection, deleted agent, loaded framing, overclaim, minimizing) are known to be hard cases. (3) Faithfulness evaluation for meaning-preserving rewrites — metrics and human protocols from style transfer and paraphrase research (content preservation vs style strength trade-off), NLI/entailment-based factual-consistency checks, SARI, QA-based faithfulness metrics from summarization (QuestEval-style), and any work specifically on 'neutralizing' biased text (e.g., Pryzant et al. neutralizing subjective bias) — how to test that the rewrite preserves commitments (including hedges and evidential meaning) rather than strengthening them. (4) A positive target register for the rewrite — plain-language standards usable as an operational spec: ISO 24495-1:2023, US Plain Writing Act / plainlanguage.gov guidelines, and whether any are open enough to encode as checkable rules. Deliver: a publishable evaluation plan — recommended ham-corpus recipe with licenses, an annotation protocol with realistic agreement targets per family, CI gate thresholds with precedent, and a truth-caption eval suite design.

gapFindings.dimension: gap:Abuse cases and legal exposure of the tool itself (weaponized labels, dual-use cookbook, regulation)
gapFindings.summary: Captioneer is not just a lens — it is an authority-conferring labeling machine, a publishable technique catalog, and a processor of other people's words, and each of those roles has documented failure modes. The empirical record says labels leak beyond their targets: Pennycook et al. (Management Science 2020) show warning a subset implies the unwarned rest is clean; Freeze et al. (Political Behavior 2020) show invalid warnings taint true content; Schiff/Schiff/Bueno (APSR) show 'that's misinformation' claims measurably help liars evade accountability (the Chesney–Citron liar's dividend); and automation-bias research shows people defer to machine output even against contrary signals — so a captioneer mark will be waved as a verdict in exactly the arenas where therapy-speak ('gaslighting', 'narcissist', DARVO, 'parental alienation') is already weaponized in custody, HR, and harassment contexts. On dual use, the balance of evidence favors publication: inoculation research (Roozenbeek & van der Linden's Bad News line), the persuasion-knowledge model (Friestad & Wright 1994), and security-community norms around MITRE ATT&CK and full disclosure all support naming techniques for defenders, with the contested line being generative capability (working 'exploit code' = a make-this-more-evasive mode), not the taxonomy. Legally, the tool sits in a well-litigated safe harbor if and only if its outputs stay evaluative, span-anchored, and methodology-disclosed: NewsGuard (Consortium News, SDNY 2025), Stossel v. Meta (2022), and Jefferson County v. Moody's (10th Cir. 1999) all won as protected opinion, while Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank v. Morgan Stanley (2009) shows how privately-commissioned, fact-implying ratings lose that protection; UK Defamation Act 2013 s.3's honest-opinion defense is satisfied almost by construction if every mark indicates its textual basis. Under the EU AI Act, text-only rhetoric annotation escapes the emotion-recognition prohibition/high-risk class (which requires biometric data) and the Art. 5(1)(a) manipulation ban (which targets AI that manipulates, not AI that describes manipulation), but LLM captions carry Art. 50 disclosure duties and any drift into voice/video input or workplace-screening use flips the classification. GDPR's household exemption covers a user privately analyzing an ex's texts but dies on publication (Lindqvist), making captioneer's client-side architecture and the absence of share-links containing third-party private text load-bearing compliance features, not implementation details.

key_findings.claim: Partial labeling backfires: the implied truth effect means marking some phrases certifies the unmarked rest
key_findings.detail: Pennycook, Bear, Collins & Rand, 'The Implied Truth Effect' (Management Science 66(11):4944–4957, 2020): attaching warnings to a subset of false headlines significantly increased perceived accuracy of unwarned false headlines; the effect is eliminated (slightly reversed) only when verified-true items are also explicitly tagged. For captioneer: any statement returned with few marks reads as machine-certified clean; the six-family scope means the tool must visibly say 'unmarked is unchecked, not clean' and disclose coverage, or it becomes a laundering device for manipulation outside its taxonomy.

key_findings.claim: False positives are weapons, not noise: the tainted truth effect shows invalid warnings discredit true content
key_findings.detail: Freeze et al., 'Fake Claims of Fake News: Political Misinformation, Warnings, and the Tainted Truth Effect' (Political Behavior, 2020): wrongly labeling accurate news reduces its credibility and impairs political memory; warned individuals discard authentic information from the 'discredited' source wholesale. A captioneer false positive on an honest speaker's hedge ('I think', 'perhaps') doesn't merely mislabel a phrase — it degrades trust in the whole statement and its author. False-positive rate is therefore a harm metric, not a quality metric.

key_findings.claim: The liar's dividend: the tool's existence helps bad actors dismiss true accusations
key_findings.detail: Chesney & Citron coined the term (Deep Fakes, California Law Review 2019); Schiff, Schiff & Bueno (APSR, 'The Liar's Dividend: Can Politicians Claim Misinformation to Evade Accountability?') found experimentally that false claims of misinformation RAISE politician support and outperform silence or apology as scandal responses. Courtroom analogues exist (Guy Reffitt's Jan-6 'deepfake defense'; Tesla arguing Musk statements could be deepfakes). Applied here: 'I ran her texts through captioneer and it flagged manipulation' becomes a DARVO accelerant, and conversely 'that tool is junk, it flags everyone' becomes a universal dismissal of genuine marks.

key_findings.claim: Analytic vocabularies are already weaponized in custody, HR and interpersonal conflict — captioneer adds machine authority to that arsenal
key_findings.detail: Merriam-Webster made 'gaslighting' its 2022 word of the year on a 1,740% lookup increase while clinicians documented its dilution to cover ordinary disagreement; therapists describe 'weaponized therapy speak' used to control, dismiss, or avoid accountability; Psychiatric Times documents false abuse allegations as standard custody-battle leverage; BWSS documents 'parental alienation' claims deployed against DV survivors; Harsey & Freyd's DARVO research (J. Aggression, Maltreatment & Trauma 2020; 'Defamation and DARVO', J. Trauma & Dissociation 2022) shows both that DARVO exposure lowers victim credibility and that accused perpetrators extend DARVO through defamation suits. A marked-up screenshot with six clinical-sounding family labels is precision ammunition in every one of these arenas.

key_findings.claim: Automation bias makes machine labels weigh more than identical human claims
key_findings.detail: Alon-Barkat & Busuioc (J. Public Administration Research & Theory 33(1), 2023, N=605) and the broader literature: people, including experts, defer to algorithmic outputs even against contradicting warning signals, and perceived objectivity increases overreliance; training does not reliably eliminate it. So the same sentence — 'this phrasing deflects' — lands harder from captioneer than from a person, which is precisely why output wording, confidence display, and 'reads language, not minds' framing are safety features rather than copy.

key_findings.claim: Dual-use evidence favors publishing the taxonomy: technique-naming measurably helps defenders and no study shows attacker uplift from prebunking
key_findings.detail: Inoculation research (McGuire 1960s; Roozenbeek & van der Linden's Bad News game; Basol et al., J. Cognition 2020; Traberg, Roozenbeek & van der Linden, ANNALS 2022; Royal Society Open Science 2022 technique-based inoculation) shows exposing people to named manipulation techniques improves discernment, driven by decreased perceived reliability of manipulative content — even though Bad News deliberately puts players in the attacker role. The persuasion-knowledge model (Friestad & Wright, J. Consumer Research 21(1), 1994) predicts a 'detachment effect': tactic recognition discounts the tactic, structurally favoring defense. No published study documents prebunking increasing participants' manipulative skill; the honest caveat is replication is mixed on effect size ('Mixed News about the Bad News Game', J. Cognition).

key_findings.claim: Security-community disclosure norms draw the dual-use line at generative capability, not description — the ATT&CK analogy supports an open lexicon
key_findings.detail: MITRE ATT&CK has published a full adversary-technique taxonomy openly since 2015 with industry consensus that it is net-defensive (a 'common language' for defenders); the decades-old full-disclosure debate (Schneier 2007; OWASP disclosure norms) treats discussing concepts/techniques as legitimate while publishing weaponized exploit code remains contested. Mapped to captioneer: the lexicon with weakened, annotated examples = ATT&CK (publish); a mode that rewrites text to be MORE evasive/persuasive, or ready-to-paste manipulation templates = working exploit code (do not ship; explicitly refuse in the engine).

key_findings.claim: EU AI Act: text-only rhetoric annotation is outside the emotion-recognition prohibition and high-risk class — because those require biometric data — but the boundary is a design constraint
key_findings.detail: Art. 3(39) defines emotion recognition systems as inferring emotions/intentions 'on the basis of their biometric data'; Art. 5(1)(f) (in force 2 Feb 2025, Commission guidelines 4 Feb 2025) prohibits it only in workplace/education, and elsewhere it is Annex III high-risk. FPF and Commission guidance confirm text sentiment analysis without biometrics is out of scope. Captioneer's 'emotional register' line is safe ONLY while inputs are text: adding voice-tone or facial-video analysis instantly creates a biometric emotion-recognition system (high-risk everywhere, prohibited in workplace/education). Also note Art. 5(1)(f) exposure is use-context-dependent: an employer running staff messages through an emotion-inferring tool is the canonical banned scenario — a reason to contractually and technically discourage HR-screening use.

key_findings.claim: EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(a) bans AI that manipulates, not AI that documents manipulation — and the Feb 2025 Commission guidelines make the three-element test explicit
key_findings.detail: The prohibition requires cumulatively: a subliminal/purposefully manipulative/deceptive technique deployed BY the system, material distortion of behavior impairing informed decision-making, and significant harm. An annotation tool that surfaces manipulation to the reader's conscious attention is the inverse of a subliminal technique. Residual obligations: captioneer as an app built on an LLM API is a downstream 'provider of an AI system' (not a GPAI provider); Art. 50(1) requires disclosing AI interaction, and Art. 50(4) requires labeling AI-generated text 'published to inform the public on matters of public interest' absent human editorial responsibility — relevant if truth captions get embedded in public commentary or platform integrations. Repurposing toward Annex III uses (employment screening, essay grading in education) would flip it high-risk under Art. 25.

key_findings.claim: GDPR: the household exemption covers the private paste but dies on publication — Lindqvist controls the share feature
key_findings.detail: CJEU C-101/01 Lindqvist: publishing colleagues' personal data on a website is not a 'purely personal or household activity' because it makes data available to an indefinite number of people; C-212/13 Ryneš: the exemption is interpreted narrowly. A user privately analyzing an ex's texts is plausibly within the exemption, but generating a shareable marked-up artifact of a third party's private messages is not — and the quoted person holds access/erasure/rectification rights against whoever controls that processing. Captioneer's client-side analysis is therefore its strongest GDPR posture (the service never becomes controller of the pasted text); any server-side feature needs no-retention/no-training defaults and share-links must not embed third-party private text.

key_findings.claim: US defamation safe harbor for raters is real and recent: NewsGuard, Science Feedback, and Moody's all won on protected opinion — with known conditions
key_findings.detail: Consortium News v. NewsGuard (SDNY, Judge Failla, March 2025, dismissed with prejudice): a rating 'nutrition label' is 'inherently subjective' and 'incapable of being proven false', likened to a restaurant critic; 'anti-US' has no precise, falsifiable meaning; actual-malice pleading failed. Stossel v. Meta (N.D. Cal. 2022): a 'fact-check' label 'does not mean that the assessment itself is an actionable statement of objective fact'; anti-SLAPP motions granted (California's statute did real work). Jefferson County School Dist. No. R-1 v. Moody's, 175 F.3d 848 (10th Cir. 1999): 'negative outlook' protected under Milkovich because no provably false factual connotation. The safe harbor's conditions: evaluative not fact-implying language, disclosed methodology/basis, general publication.

key_findings.claim: The safe harbor has a documented failure mode: fact-implying, privately-commissioned, or knowingly-false ratings lose First Amendment protection
key_findings.detail: Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank v. Morgan Stanley (SDNY 2009, Judge Scheindlin): rating-agency First Amendment defense rejected because ratings were distributed to a limited group of investors and evidence suggested the ratings 'misstated the opinions or beliefs held' by the agencies (i.e., not honestly held); summary judgment denied 2012, settled 2013. Milkovich v. Lorain Journal is the governing line: opinion implying provably false facts is actionable. Mapped to captioneer: 'this is manipulative' / 'X is lying' imputes a provable mental state (actionable territory); 'this construction affords evasion' + the highlighted span + linked methodology stays evaluative. Paid private analyses of named individuals would replicate the exact posture that sank the rating agencies.

key_findings.claim: UK/EU: honest-opinion defense (Defamation Act 2013 s.3) is satisfiable by construction — every mark already 'indicates the basis of the opinion'
