key_findings.detail: S.3 conditions: (1) statement of opinion, (2) statement indicates, in general or specific terms, the basis of the opinion, (3) an honest person could have held it on facts existing at publication; defeated only by showing the opinion wasn't honestly held. Captioneer's charter rule that 'every mark points at a visible phrase in the text' is literally condition (2) implemented in software — a legal design pattern worth documenting. S.1's serious-harm threshold adds a further filter. This makes span-anchoring a hard invariant of the data model, not a UX nicety.

key_findings.claim: Adjacent-tool record: Perspective API's dialect bias shows how an annotator becomes a discrimination engine; Grammarly shows the safe scope; fact-checkers show the flak level
key_findings.detail: Sap et al., 'The Risk of Racial Bias in Hate Speech Detection' (ACL 2019): African-American English tweets flagged toxic at substantially higher rates due to lexical-cue overreliance — a rhetoric annotator tuned on standard English will over-mark dialect and L2 speakers, and in weaponized contexts (HR complaints, custody exhibits) those false positives become discriminatory evidence. Grammarly's tone detector (launched 2019, ~18 tones) has drawn no regulatory action — but it analyzes the AUTHOR's own drafts for the author, never issuing verdicts on third parties; that scope difference is the whole game. Poynter/IFCN meanwhile runs a legal defense fund (up to $40,000 per case) because annotating others' speech attracts lawsuits regardless of merit, and in June 2025 the FTC sent civil investigative demands to media-rating firms including NewsGuard and Ad Fontes — flak also arrives from regulators, not just plaintiffs.

key_findings.claim: Concrete threat model: five abuser-target-feature triples cover most of the risk surface
key_findings.detail: (1) Ex-partner/co-parent pastes private texts, exports marked-up screenshot as 'evidence' in custody or divorce (features: paste + share/screenshot; victim: the quoted person; amplifiers: automation bias, therapy-speak arenas). (2) Manager/HR runs an employee's messages to justify discipline (feature: paste; victim: employee; amplifiers: dialect false positives, EU workplace emotion-recognition line). (3) Political operative selectively runs an opponent's statement, publishes marks stripped of scope disclaimer (feature: public-statement analysis; victim: named individual; amplifiers: implied truth on unmarked rivals, defamation exposure for the operative AND subpoena/flak exposure for the tool). (4) Harasser runs a target's posts repeatedly to build a 'manipulation profile' (feature: repeated analysis; victim: target; amplifier: aggregation turning text-marks into a person-verdict). (5) Manipulation student mines the lexicon's examples as templates (feature: open lexicon; victim: everyone downstream; mitigations: weakened examples, no generator).

techniques.name: Verdict laundering (machine-authority appeal)
techniques.definition: Presenting a tool's linguistic annotations as an objective verdict on a person — 'the AI confirmed he's manipulative' — exploiting automation bias to convert span-level opinion into character evidence.
techniques.example: A marked-up screenshot of an ex's apology text entered in a custody dispute as proof of abusiveness.
techniques.origin: Automation-bias literature (Alon-Barkat & Busuioc 2023); direct analogue of misused polygraph and 'AI lie detector' outputs.
techniques.languages: Universal; hits dialect and L2 speakers hardest wherever the underlying detector is biased (Sap et al. 2019).

techniques.name: Implied-clean certification
techniques.definition: Running one's own or an ally's statement through the tool and brandishing the sparse output as certification of honesty, exploiting the implied truth effect on unmarked content.
techniques.example: 'I ran my statement through captioneer — zero manipulation flags' as a press-release credibility ritual.
techniques.origin: Pennycook et al. 2020 implied truth effect, transposed from fact-check labels to rhetoric marks.
techniques.languages: Universal; worse for languages the lexicon covers thinly, where under-marking is systematic.

techniques.name: Tainted-truth flak
techniques.definition: Deliberately generating or publicizing the tool's false positives on plainly honest text to discredit the tool and, by extension, all of its genuine findings.
techniques.example: A columnist runs the Gettysburg Address or a hostage-negotiation transcript through the tool and mocks the hedging flags to argue every mark is meaningless.
techniques.origin: Freeze et al. 2020 tainted truth effect; standard delegitimization play against fact-checkers.
techniques.languages: Universal; ceremonial/formal registers (legalese, diplomatic language) are rich false-positive bait.

techniques.name: Liar's-dividend dismissal
techniques.definition: Invoking the existence of manipulation-detection to wave away authentic accusations or authentic marks — 'everything gets flagged by these tools' — gaining credibility from public awareness of the tool's fallibility.
techniques.example: A politician responds to a captioneer-annotated speech with 'AI smear tools flag everyone; this is automated defamation.'
techniques.origin: Chesney & Citron 2019; Schiff, Schiff & Bueno APSR experiments showing misinformation claims outperform apology.

techniques.name: DARVO-with-tooling
techniques.definition: An abuser runs the victim's messages (often distress-driven, hedged, or accusatory) through the analyzer and uses the resulting marks to reverse victim and offender.
techniques.example: 'Look — HER texts are full of loaded framing and overclaim; the tool proves she's the manipulator.'
techniques.origin: Freyd's DARVO (1997); Harsey & Freyd 2020 showing DARVO exposure lowers victim credibility; 'Defamation and DARVO' 2022.
techniques.languages: Universal; trauma-affected speech patterns (fragmented, hedged) are systematically mark-prone, biasing the tool against victims.

techniques.name: Selective-span screenshotting
techniques.definition: Cropping the tool's output to show only the marks (dropping scope disclaimers, coverage notes, and the 'affordance not verdict' framing) before redistribution.
techniques.example: A tweet showing only the red-highlighted phrases of a rival's statement with the caption 'caught.'
techniques.origin: Standard decontextualization play documented across fact-check label misuse; analogous to quote-mining.

techniques.name: Aggregation into person-profiles
techniques.definition: Running many texts by one author and compiling mark densities into a 'manipulation score' for the person, converting text-level annotation into a character rating the tool never made.
techniques.example: A harassment campaign publishing 'X's messages average 4.2 manipulation flags per paragraph.'
techniques.origin: Same move that turned Perspective API toxicity scores into journalist-built 'most toxic user' rankings.

techniques.name: Label dilution / semantic inflation
techniques.definition: Community overuse stretches the lexicon's precise terms ('deflection', 'gaslighting-adjacent framing') to cover ordinary disagreement, destroying their diagnostic value and harming genuine victims' credibility.
techniques.example: 'Gaslighting': 1,740% lookup spike, Merriam-Webster WOTY 2022, now applied to any disputed memory.
techniques.origin: Documented trajectory of therapy-speak (gaslighting, narcissist, trauma, boundaries) 2016–2024.
techniques.languages: Documented in English; parallel inflations exist in other languages (e.g., loanword adoption of 'gaslighting' into German, Spanish, Japanese usage).

techniques.name: Cookbook harvesting
techniques.definition: Mining the open lexicon's technique definitions and examples as ready-made templates for constructing evasive or manipulative text, or as a checklist for evading detection.
techniques.example: Rewriting a corporate apology against the lexicon until zero flags remain while preserving agent deletion ('mistakes were made' variants the taxonomy doesn't yet catch).
techniques.origin: Exploit-code side of the full-disclosure debate; adversarial-evasion literature against toxicity classifiers.
techniques.languages: Universal; cross-language technique entries (how deflection works in Japanese vs English) would be the highest-uplift content if published as templates.

techniques.name: Litigation and regulatory flak against the annotator
techniques.definition: Rated or marked parties suing the tool (defamation, tortious interference) or triggering regulator action, independent of merit, to impose cost and chill operation.
techniques.example: Consortium News' $13M suit against NewsGuard (dismissed 2025); Stossel v. Meta/Science Feedback (anti-SLAPP, 2022); FTC CIDs to NewsGuard and Ad Fontes (June 2025); IFCN legal-defense fund existing at all.
techniques.origin: Fact-checker and media-rater litigation record 2021–2025.
techniques.languages: Jurisdiction-dependent: US anti-SLAPP states are safest; England (low serious-harm bar pre-2013, libel tourism history) and jurisdictions without opinion privilege are riskiest.

framework_implications: Make span-anchoring a hard invariant of the data model, and document it as legal architecture: every mark MUST reference a visible quoted span plus a lexicon entry with disclosed methodology. This is UK Defamation Act 2013 s.3 condition 2 ('indicates the basis of the opinion') and the Milkovich 'disclosed basis' requirement implemented in the schema. A mark object without a span reference should fail validation.

Ship canonical output strings inside the lexicon, not the app: each technique entry carries an approved 'affordance phrasing' field ('this construction affords evasion', 'the agent is deleted here') and a banned-verdict list ('manipulative person', 'lying', 'gaslighter'). Localizations must translate the affordance framing, not just the label — verdict-drift in translation is a defamation vector per locale. Never emit statements about intent, honesty, or mental state; that is the exact line between Consortium News v. NewsGuard (won) and Abu Dhabi v. Morgan Stanley (lost).

Counter the implied truth effect in the output contract: every result must carry machine-readable coverage metadata (which families were checked, which weren't) and the UI must render 'unmarked ≠ clean' adjacent to any low-mark result. Prohibit a single numeric 'manipulation score' and any per-person aggregation endpoint — annotate texts, never people. Consider an explicit 'this tool cannot certify honesty' string on zero-mark outputs, mirroring Pennycook's finding that only verifying-the-true removes the effect.

Adopt the security-community dual-use line explicitly in governance: the taxonomy, origins, evolution, and cross-language entries are ATT&CK-equivalent (publish openly, with a written defensive-purpose rationale citing the inoculation literature as both ethical and legal shield); anything generative in the manipulative direction is exploit-code-equivalent (the engine's rewrite is one-way toward plain meaning only; a 'make this more persuasive/evasive' mode is a permanent non-goal in the charter). Publish examples in 'weakened dose' form — short, annotated, dated fragments — never as reusable templates, mirroring Bad News's microdosing design.

Gate private-correspondence analysis: keep analysis of pasted text client-side (this is the GDPR compliance architecture, per Lindqvist/Ryneš — the service never becomes controller of third-party personal data), add a consent interstitial for share/export ('You are publishing someone else's words with labels attached; the labels describe wording, not the writer'), and never mint share-URLs that embed third-party private text by default. Watermark exported images with the scope disclaimer so selective screenshotting carries the caveat with it.

Gate named-individual public-statement analysis differently from private text: require a source link, render the full statement (no cropped-context analysis), and stamp outputs with date-of-analysis and lexicon version — this supports the honest-opinion defense (facts existing at the time) and creates an audit trail against 'the tool said X' fabrications.

Keep the framework text-only by schema: input type = text is a hard rule, because under the EU AI Act biometric inputs (voice tone, facial video) would convert the register line into an emotion-recognition system (Annex III high-risk; prohibited in workplace/education under Art. 5(1)(f)). Encode intended-purpose restrictions in the license/ToS: not for employment screening, education assessment, credit, or legal proceedings — both to stay out of Annex III via Art. 25 repurposing and because those are the documented weaponization arenas (custody, HR).

Comply with AI Act Art. 50 on the LLM caption path: label the truth caption as AI-generated (50(1)/50(4)), and require downstream integrators (DSA-covered platforms embedding captioneer) to carry the label through — if a platform uses captioneer marks in moderation decisions it owes Art. 17 DSA statements of reasons, so the framework should emit machine-readable rationale objects (span + technique + lexicon version) that platforms can cite.

Treat false positives as harms in CI: a published false-positive corpus (formal registers, apologies, trauma-affected speech, dialect and L2 samples per Sap et al. 2019) with regression gates before any lexicon rule ships; bias audits across dialects are a release requirement, not research. Track and publish FP rates per technique family — the tainted truth effect means each FP damages a real speaker and the tool's whole evidentiary standing.

Choose jurisdiction and ToS deliberately: host and incorporate where opinion privilege and anti-SLAPP statutes are strong (California anti-SLAPP disposed of Stossel; SDNY applied robust opinion doctrine for NewsGuard); ToS should (a) characterize all outputs as subjective evaluative opinions about text construction based solely on the quoted spans, (b) prohibit use as evidence in legal, employment, or custody proceedings and for harassment, (c) reserve takedown of abusive shared artifacts, and (d) include a data-subject contact route for quoted third parties. Budget for flak: the IFCN fund ($40k/case) and the 2025 FTC CIDs to raters show annotation tools attract both suits and regulator demands regardless of merit — an open-source foundation/fiscal host with legal-defense reserves is part of the architecture.

Add 'label dilution' monitoring to governance: the therapy-speak trajectory (gaslighting's 1,740% spike and semantic bleaching) predicts the lexicon's own terms will inflate in community use; version the lexicon semantically, define each technique with inclusion AND exclusion criteria ('this is NOT deflection when...'), and publish counter-examples — exclusion criteria are the framework's main defense against its vocabulary being stretched into a weapon.

gapFindings.dimension: gap:Learning science of the lens: transfer, cynicism backfire, and validated measurement of 'discernment'
gapFindings.summary: The learning-science literature delivers a sharp two-part verdict on captioneer's pedagogy. First, the Stanford lateral-reading critique (Wineburg & McGrew 2019; Kozyreva et al. 2023) is real but scoped: close/vertical reading fails at SOURCE-CREDIBILITY tasks on unfamiliar web sources, where fact-checkers succeed by leaving the page; it does not indict rhetoric-level analysis of a statement whose author is already known (a boss's email, a politician's apology) — but the tool must never present close reading as a verification method, and should hand off to lateral-reading prompts whenever a checkable factual claim or unknown source appears. Second, and more dangerous: the signal-detection re-analyses (Modirrousta-Galian & Higham 2023 JEP:General; Graham et al. 2023 four-team replication; Seabrooke et al. 2025 India replication) show the flagship inoculation games (Bad News, Go Viral!) mostly induce a conservative response criterion — blanket skepticism that lowers belief in TRUE content nearly as much as false (d=0.36–0.58 vs 0.56–1.23) — with no ROC sensitivity gain; Hoes et al. 2024 (N=6,127, 3 countries) found the same spillover for fact-checks, literacy tips, and misinformation coverage, echoing danah boyd's 2017 warning and the 1941 cynicism critique that helped kill the Institute for Propaganda Analysis, the direct ancestor of technique-family curricula. The fixes are known: matched manipulative/neutral twin stimuli, post-lesson FEEDBACK exercises (Leder et al. 2024: six experiments where feedback converted criterion shifts into genuine d′ gains, mostly by improving real-news accuracy), memory-targeting boosters on a ~10–30-day cadence (Maertens et al. 2025 Nature Comms: game effects die by day 9, memory boosters retain 100% of effect), and evaluation that reports discernment plus distrust bias, on the MIST's V/r/f/d/n model (Maertens et al. 2024) and the Guay et al. 2023 standard of always testing true-and-false item sets. In-text highlighting itself carries a documented hazard — the implied truth effect (Pennycook et al. 2020): unmarked spans read as endorsed unless the UI positively marks clean/plain spans — plus habituation to repeated identical warnings. The framework should therefore publish a "sincerity-preservation" metric (belief in sincere text unchanged) as its headline efficacy claim, not raw manipulation-detection rates.

key_findings.claim: The Stanford close-reading critique is about source-credibility tasks on unfamiliar sources, not rhetoric analysis of known-source statements
key_findings.detail: Wineburg & McGrew (Teachers College Record, 2019) had professional fact-checkers, PhD historians, and Stanford undergraduates evaluate unfamiliar websites; fact-checkers 'read laterally' — leaving the page to vet the source elsewhere ('taking bearings') — and were faster and far more accurate, while historians and students read vertically and were fooled by polished design and on-page features. The failure mode is using textual/close analysis to infer TRUSTWORTHINESS OF AN UNKNOWN SOURCE. Captioneer's core case (parsing the rhetoric of a statement whose author is known) is outside that critique — but the moment a user is evaluating whether to BELIEVE checkable claims or an unfamiliar source, close reading is demonstrably the wrong first tool.

key_findings.claim: 'Critical ignoring' (Kozyreva, Wineburg, Lewandowsky, Hertwig 2023) reframes attention itself as the scarce resource — deep reading of bad text is a cost, not a virtue
key_findings.detail: Current Directions in Psychological Science paper defines critical ignoring as 'choosing what to ignore and where to invest one's limited attentional capacities', with three strategies: self-nudging (removing temptations from one's digital environment), lateral reading (vetting the source elsewhere), and do-not-feed-the-trolls. Implication for a close-reading tool: inviting users to spend deep attention on every manipulative text is itself a failure mode; the lens should include an explicit 'this may not deserve your attention' outcome.

key_findings.claim: Signal-detection re-analysis shows gamified inoculation raises indiscriminate skepticism, not discernment
key_findings.detail: Modirrousta-Galian & Higham (Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 152(9), 2411–2437, 2023) re-analyzed Bad News / Go Viral! studies with ROC analysis: no improvement in discrimination between true and fake headlines, only a conservative response-bias shift (rating everything as less reliable). This is the direct empirical challenge to the pre/post mean-rating evidence base that Bad News-style curricula cite.

key_findings.claim: Independent four-team replication confirmed: Bad News reduced belief in TRUE tweets almost as much as false ones, with zero sensitivity gain
key_findings.detail: Graham et al. ('Mixed News about the Bad News Game', Journal of Cognition, 2023; N=353 undergraduates, Tetris control, 32 tweets with 8 true items): belief in false tweets dropped (d=0.56–1.23) but belief in true tweets also dropped (d=0.36–0.58), no significant true/false difference; ROC AUC discrimination unchanged (p=.93); significant conservative bias (p<.001), BF=8.43 against a sensitivity improvement.

key_findings.claim: The India replication failed: no discrimination improvement at all (d_z=0.04)
key_findings.detail: Seabrooke, Modirrousta-Galian & Higham (Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 2025; preregistered, N=150 Indian participants, Indian headlines) found no pre/post discrimination gain and only an item-artifact-attributable bias shift, contradicting Iyengar et al. 2023. Combined with Guess et al.'s weaker India result, cross-cultural transfer of technique-training is unproven — relevant to captioneer's cross-language ambitions.

key_findings.claim: Skepticism spillover is general across intervention types, not a quirk of games
key_findings.detail: Hoes, Aitken, Zhang, Gackowski & Wojcieszak ('Prominent misinformation interventions reduce misperceptions but increase scepticism', Nature Human Behaviour, 2024; N=6,127 in US, Poland, Hong Kong) tested fact-checking, media-literacy tips, and news coverage of misinformation: all reduced belief in false claims but also damaged credibility of factual information (e.g., US Accountability fact-check β=−0.352 on misperceptions; Contextualized coverage β=+0.132 on true-news skepticism); only fact-checking improved discernment in most contexts. A parallel 2024 study found a health media literacy intervention increased skepticism of both inaccurate AND accurate cancer news. danah boyd's 2017 essay 'Did Media Literacy Backfire?' is the cultural-level version: teaching doubt without teaching trust feeds tribal epistemology.

key_findings.claim: This exact backfire killed captioneer's 1930s ancestor: the Institute for Propaganda Analysis
key_findings.detail: The IPA (1937–1942, Clyde R. Miller) taught the 'seven propaganda devices' — the first device-spotting curriculum and the direct ancestor of six-family technique marking. In a 1941 Public Opinion Quarterly exchange, Bruce L. Smith argued propaganda-device education fostered cynicism that could push students toward authoritarianism; combined with political pressure, the IPA folded in 1942 (documented in Sproule, 'Propaganda and Democracy', 1997). An 85-year-old warning that device-spotting without a trust-building counterweight curdles into cynicism.

key_findings.claim: Discernment CAN be improved — the fix is feedback with true/sincere items, not more warnings
key_findings.detail: Leder et al. ('Feedback exercises boost discernment of misinformation for gamified inoculation interventions', JEP: General 153(8), 2068–2087, 2024): across six experiments, adding a brief post-game assessment WITH performance feedback (after Bad News and Harmony Square) produced genuine signal-detection discernment gains lasting 1 week+, primarily by improving accuracy on REAL news. Guess et al. (PNAS 2020) similarly showed Facebook's 'Tips to Spot False News' improved discernment +26.5% (US) and +17.5% (India, educated sample) even though it lowered perceived accuracy of both classes. Discernment gains come from practice-plus-feedback on mixed item sets, not from exposure to technique taxonomies alone.

key_findings.claim: There is now a methodological standard: report discernment on mixed true/false item sets, decomposed by signal detection
key_findings.detail: Guay, Berinsky, Pennycook & Rand ('How to think about whether misinformation interventions work', Nature Human Behaviour 7, 1231–1233, 2023) argue evaluations must include both true and false content and analyze discernment between them, because the normative goal is accuracy maximization, not distrust. The SDT convention in this literature: sensitivity (d′ or ROC AUC) = discernment; criterion (c) = skepticism shift. An intervention that only moves criterion is not media literacy — it is distrust training.

key_findings.claim: MIST is the validated template for what a 'lens acquisition' instrument should look like
key_findings.detail: Maertens, Götz, Golino, Roozenbeek et al. (Behavior Research Methods 56(3):1863–1899, 2024; N=8,504 across 7 samples) built the Misinformation Susceptibility Test with GPT-2-generated fake items + Reuters/AP real items, validated via factor analysis, IRT, and exploratory graph analysis; versions MIST-20/16/8 (binary judgments, 50/50 real/fake, <2 min); scoring 'Verification Done' framework: V (veracity discernment), r (real-news detection), f (fake-news detection), d (distrust bias), n (naïveté bias), with US/UK population norms; CC-BY 4.0, materials on OSF. Its five-score schema is exactly what lets you distinguish a user who acquired the lens from one who merely became cynical (rising f with falling r and rising d).

key_findings.claim: Durability: inoculation decays in days-to-weeks; game effects die fastest (~9 days); memory-targeting boosters restore 100% of the effect
key_findings.detail: Maertens et al. ('Psychological booster shots targeting memory increase long-term resistance against misinformation', Nature Communications, 2025; N=11,759, five preregistered longitudinal experiments): text- and video-based inoculation stayed significant ~30 days (video d=0.230 at T30), Bad News-style game effects lost significance by day 9; a memory-focused booster restored the full original effect (d=0.440 at T30, '100% retention'), while threat/motivation-only boosters did little — memory, not motivation, drives longevity. Earlier work (Maertens et al. 2021, JEP:Applied, three longitudinal experiments) showed decay beginning within days and effects gone within ~2 months without boosting. Dosage design: one-shot lessons are near-worthless; spaced recall of technique names/examples is the active ingredient.

key_findings.claim: The booster study also models the RIGHT outcome measure for a rhetoric tool: manipulative vs neutral versions of the same story
key_findings.detail: Its video experiments measured discernment as manipulativeness ratings of matched manipulative/neutral rewrites of identical news stories — a rhetoric-level (not truth-level) discernment task that eliminates topic confounds. This maps one-to-one onto captioneer's six families: the correct test is 'same content, with and without the hedge/deflection/loaded frame', not true-vs-fake headlines. Roozenbeek et al.'s technique-based work (Royal Society Open Science, 2022, 'Technique-based inoculation against real-world misinformation') similarly measures technique recognition on real-world items.

key_findings.claim: The implied truth effect: marking some spans certifies the unmarked ones — unless clean spans get positive marks
key_findings.detail: Pennycook, Bear, Collins & Rand (Management Science, 2020): attaching warnings to a subset of false headlines INCREASED perceived accuracy of untagged false headlines (readers infer unmarked = checked); crucially, adding verification tags to true items 'eliminates, and in fact slightly reverses' the effect. For an in-text highlighter this is direct: in a partially-marked document, unmarked sentences will read as endorsed. The mitigation is a positive affordance for clean spans (e.g., 'plain speech' marking or an explicit coverage statement), not silence.

key_findings.claim: Warning habituation and generalization limit mark density
key_findings.detail: The warning-label literature (Current Opinion in Psychology 2023 review: labels 'widely effective' but with modest effect sizes) plus security-warning habituation research shows repeated identical stimuli lose effect through learning, and habituation to one warning type generalizes to visually similar warnings. A page saturated with identical six-color highlights will train users to stop seeing them; effects of labels also decay over time.

key_findings.claim: Age-appropriateness: technique instruction works down to teens with classroom evidence; a junior variant exists for ages 8–10
key_findings.detail: Bad News is designed for 15+; 'Bad News Junior' targets ages 8–10 in ten languages; a 2024 study of Swedish upper-secondary civics classrooms ('Bad News in the civics classroom', J. Research on Technology in Education) found improved discernment of manipulation techniques in social media posts; cross-national replication of technique-based games (Roozenbeek et al.) shows d≈0.37 across Sweden, Germany, Greece, Poland. But almost all school studies measure technique-recognition, not veracity discernment — the criterion-shift critique has rarely been run on minors.

techniques.name: Lateral reading
techniques.definition: Evaluating information by leaving the text: open new tabs, search what other sources say about the author/organization/claim before investing attention in the page itself ('taking bearings').
techniques.origin: Coined by Wineburg & McGrew (Stanford History Education Group), 2017/2019, from observation of professional fact-checkers
techniques.example: A fact-checker landing on minimumwage.com immediately searches the site name and discovers it is run by a PR firm for the restaurant industry — something no amount of on-page close reading reveals
techniques.languages: Validated mainly in US English; German and Dutch classroom adaptations exist via the 'boosting' program (scienceofboosting.org)

techniques.name: Critical ignoring
techniques.definition: Deliberately choosing what NOT to read: self-nudging (removing low-quality feeds from the environment), lateral reading, and do-not-feed-the-trolls, treating attention as the scarce resource manipulators hijack.
techniques.origin: Kozyreva, Wineburg, Lewandowsky & Hertwig, Current Directions in Psychological Science, 2023
techniques.example: Declining to close-read outrage bait at all, rather than analyzing its rhetoric

techniques.name: Technique-based (prebunking) inoculation
techniques.definition: Forewarning plus weakened exposure: teach the manipulation technique via a micro-dose example before encountering it in the wild, on the vaccine analogy.
techniques.origin: McGuire's inoculation theory (1961); operationalized as Bad News (Roozenbeek & van der Linden, 2019: six techniques — impersonation, emotion, polarization, conspiracy, discredit, trolling), Go Viral!, Harmony Square, Cat Park, and Jigsaw's prebunking videos
techniques.example: Bad News players run a fake-news empire deploying each technique, then rate real tweets
techniques.languages: Bad News in multiple languages; replications in Sweden, Germany, Greece, Poland (d≈0.37); India replications failed

techniques.name: Post-lesson feedback exercises
techniques.definition: A short scored quiz with performance feedback immediately after technique training; the only manipulation shown to convert inoculation's criterion shift into genuine signal-detection discernment gains, chiefly by improving accuracy on sincere/real items.
techniques.origin: Leder, Schellinger et al., JEP: General, 2024 (six experiments on Bad News and Harmony Square)
techniques.example: After the hedging micro-lesson, user classifies 8 passages (4 manipulative, 4 sincere) and sees which they got wrong and why

techniques.name: Memory-targeting booster shots
techniques.definition: Spaced follow-up micro-interventions that rehearse the memory of the technique (not re-scare the user); restore up to 100% of decayed inoculation effect at 30 days.
techniques.origin: Maertens, Roozenbeek et al., Nature Communications, 2025 (N=11,759)
techniques.example: A 30-second recall prompt at day 10: 'Which family was in the CEO apology you read last week?'

techniques.name: Signal-detection / ROC evaluation (d-prime vs criterion)
techniques.definition: Decomposing pre/post rating changes into sensitivity (ability to tell manipulative from sincere) and response criterion (blanket skepticism); the field's convention for distinguishing discernment from distrust.
techniques.origin: Classical SDT applied to misinformation by Modirrousta-Galian & Higham, JEP: General, 2023; endorsed as standard by Guay, Berinsky, Pennycook & Rand, Nature Human Behaviour, 2023
techniques.example: Bad News: AUC unchanged (p=.93) but criterion shifted conservative (p<.001) — skepticism, not skill

techniques.name: MIST (Misinformation Susceptibility Test)
techniques.definition: Psychometrically validated 20/16/8-item binary test scoring five dimensions: Veracity Discernment (V), real-news detection (r), fake-news detection (f), distrust bias (d), naïveté bias (n), with population norms.
techniques.origin: Maertens et al., Behavior Research Methods, 2024; items GPT-2-generated (fake) + Reuters/AP (real); CC-BY 4.0, materials on OSF
techniques.languages: Validated in US and UK English; translations in progress by third parties

techniques.name: Matched-twin stimuli (manipulative vs neutral rewrites)
techniques.definition: Test items built as two versions of the same content — one with the manipulation technique, one plain — eliminating topic/veracity confounds; the correct outcome measure for rhetoric-level (not truth-level) training.
techniques.origin: Used in Jigsaw/Cambridge prebunking video experiments and Maertens et al. 2025 booster studies
techniques.example: Same layoff announcement written with and without deleted-agent passives; learner must rate manipulativeness of each

techniques.name: Implied-truth mitigation via positive verification marks
techniques.definition: Counteracting the implied truth effect (unmarked content read as endorsed) by explicitly marking verified/clean content, which eliminates and slightly reverses the effect.
techniques.origin: Pennycook, Bear, Collins & Rand, Management Science, 2020
techniques.example: In-text UI shows 'plain speech' shading on clean spans instead of leaving them blank

techniques.name: Seven propaganda devices (historical ancestor)
techniques.definition: Name-calling, glittering generalities, transfer, testimonial, plain folks, card stacking, bandwagon — the first mass-taught technique-spotting taxonomy; its curriculum was criticized in 1941 for breeding cynicism and folded in 1942.
techniques.origin: Institute for Propaganda Analysis (Clyde R. Miller), 'How to Detect Propaganda', 1937; critique by Bruce L. Smith, Public Opinion Quarterly, 1941; history in Sproule, Propaganda and Democracy, 1997

framework_implications: Scope the lens explicitly in the charter and UI: close reading is for the RHETORIC of a known-source statement; it is not a verification method. Whenever the engine detects a checkable factual claim or the user indicates the source is unfamiliar, render a lateral-reading handoff prompt ('Who is behind this? What do other sources say?' — the three Civic Online Reasoning questions) alongside the marks, and include a 'this may not deserve your attention' outcome (critical ignoring) as a first-class verdict.

Data model: every technique fixture must be a matched twin pair — the same content written with and without the technique (manipulative/neutral rewrites, per the Nature Comms 2025 booster stimuli). The corpus schema should require sincere counterparts for each of the six families (e.g., honest epistemic hedging vs weasel hedging), because teaching and testing without sincere twins is what produces criterion shift instead of discernment.

Ship a validated 'Lens Acquisition Test' as a core open-source artifact, modeled on MIST: 6-family item bank of twin pairs, binary or Likert judgments, scored with signal detection into five published numbers per learner — overall discernment (AUC/d-prime), manipulative-detection rate, sincere-recognition rate, distrust bias, naïveté bias. License it CC-BY with items and scoring scripts on a public repo, and publish population norms as data accumulates.

Adopt the Guay et al. (2023) evaluation standard as governance: any PR adding a technique family, detector rule, or micro-lesson must include matched sincere items and report discernment (not just hit rate); CI should fail if a detector's false-positive rate on the sincere twin corpus exceeds a published threshold. Make 'sincerity preservation' (no drop in trust of plain honest text) the project's headline efficacy metric.

Curriculum sequencing per family: (1) micro-dose example, (2) immediate mixed practice set (half sincere), (3) scored feedback — feedback is the single manipulation proven to convert skepticism into discernment (Leder et al. 2024, six experiments); (4) memory-targeting booster prompts at ~day 10 and ~day 30 (game-style effects die by day 9; memory boosters retain 100% of effect). Never ship a lesson as one-shot exposure without practice+feedback.

Anti-cynicism instrumentation: track each user's marking/judgment behavior for rising distrust bias (flagging sincere passages, rating everything manipulative) and surface a calibration lesson when detected — explicitly teach that hedging is often epistemic honesty and passives are often innocent. Include 'clean read' example texts in every lesson so the trained category is 'manipulative vs plain', never 'text vs trap'. This is the 1941 IPA lesson encoded in product.

UI of marks: counteract the implied truth effect by giving unmarked spans a positive state — either a subtle 'plain speech' affordance or an explicit coverage note ('spans without marks were analyzed and no technique family matched; absence of marks is not endorsement'). Cap mark density per viewport and vary mark styling/interaction to slow habituation; expose a density slider ('show only strongest marks') because saturation trains blindness.

Honest efficacy claims policy (README + site): the project may claim improved recognition of the six technique families and shifted manipulativeness ratings (effect sizes in this literature run d≈0.2–0.5 and decay within weeks without boosters); it may NOT claim users get better at detecting lies, judging truth, or resisting persuasion generally — cross-cultural transfer is unproven (two India replication failures) and gamified-only training shows no discernment gain in ROC re-analyses. Pre-register any efficacy study and report both classes of items.

Cross-language roadmap caution: because technique-training effects failed to replicate on Indian headlines with Indian participants, treat each language/culture port as requiring its own twin-pair corpus and its own discernment validation, not just translated lesson text — budget for per-locale item banks in the data model (locale field on every fixture, norms table per locale).

Age gating: default curriculum for 15+, with a simplified variant possible down to ~8–10 (Bad News Junior precedent); for minors, publish only technique-recognition outcomes and be explicit that criterion-shift effects in children are unstudied.

gapFindings.dimension: gap:Non-Western classical taxonomies of manipulation (Nyaya, Mohist, Han Feizi, balagha, Talmud)
gapFindings.summary: At least four fully independent classical lineages built formal taxonomies of verbal manipulation, and they differ not just in content but in analytical stance: India's Nyayasutra (core redaction ~150 CE, parts far older) is a PROCEDURAL-DEFEAT catalog (3 chala quibbles, 24 jati sham rejoinders, 22 nigrahasthana defeat conditions, 5 hetvabhasa pseudo-reasons — with an even earlier 44-item debate manual in Caraka Samhita Vimanasthana 8 and a 7th-century Buddhist meta-critique in Dharmakirti's Vadanyaya); China splits into a diagnostic semantics of disputation (Mohist Canons' bian, kuang ju "wild picking," the Xiaoqu's named ways analogical inference breaks; Xunzi's "three delusions" of naming = loaded framing theorized ~250 BCE) and manipulator's-eye manuals (Han Feizi ch. 12 "Shui nan," d. 233 BCE — audience psychology, prescribed magnify/minimize, the fatal "reverse scale"; Guiguzi's chapter-level toolkit of bai he, fan ying, fei qian, chuai/mo — elicitation techniques with no Greek counterpart); Arabic balagha is SEMANTIC-COMPOSITIONAL and is the tradition closest to captioneer's own method — al-Jurjani's nazm (d. 1078/81) analyzes word-order fronting, ellipsis/agent omission (Arabic literally names the passive "built-for-the-unknown"), and the 3-type kinaya taxonomy of deniable implicature that modern scholarship (Ali 2000) reads as proto-Gricean, standardized by al-Sakkaki (d. 1229) into ma'ani/bayan/badi' and vernacularized into Persian through a documented Raduyani→Watwat→Shams-i Qays chain; Talmudic dialectics contributes INFERENCE-GOVERNANCE (the dayo rule capping a fortiori overclaim, the gezerah-shavah received-tradition restriction on analogy, the internal pilpul-critique literature). Cross-checking captioneer's six families: overclaim and loaded framing are named in 4+ unconnected lineages (strong human universals), deflection in 3 (chala is precisely deflection-by-misconstrual), hedging/minimizing appear mostly as PRESCRIBED craft in the manuals, while agent deletion as a flagged manipulation is essentially unique to Arabic among classical taxonomies — and is language-relative, since pro-drop languages make deleted subjects the unmarked case. The genealogy must therefore be a multi-root DAG with typed contact edges (Sophistici Elenchi→Syriac→3 Arabic versions→Ibn Rushd; Dignaga→Xuanzang→Japanese inmyō/rongi; Arabic badi'→Persian manuals), and the CC BY-SA seed data must be built from public-domain translations (Vidyabhusana 1913, Rodkinson 1903, ctext originals) with fresh original glosses where the standard translations (Graham 1978, Watson 1964, Wu/Swearingen 2016, Steinsaltz CC BY-NC) are license-incompatible.

key_findings.claim: The Nyayasutra contains a complete, Greece-independent adversarial-language flaw taxonomy with exact counts: 3 chala, 24 jati, 22 nigrahasthana, 5 hetvabhasa
key_findings.detail: Chala (quibbling, NS 1.2.10-14) has three named types: vak-chala (verbal quibble on an ambiguous word), samanya-chala (deflecting by over-generalizing the claim to absurdity), upacara-chala (taking figurative speech literally). Jati (NS 5.1) lists 24 sham rejoinders founded on 'mere similarity or dissimilarity' (sadharmya-sama, vaidharmya-sama, utkarsa-sama, apakarsa-sama, etc.). Nigrahasthana (NS 5.2) lists 22 procedural defeat conditions (shifting the thesis, incoherence, repetition, silence, evasion, conceding tacitly...). Hetvabhasa (NS 1.2.4-9): savyabhicara (erratic), viruddha (contradictory), prakaranasama (question-begging), sadhyasama (unproved), kalatita (mistimed). Dating is contested: composition estimates span 6th c. BCE to 2nd c. CE with core redaction ~150 CE — the schema needs date intervals, not years.

key_findings.claim: A public-domain English translation of the full Nyaya lists exists: Vidyabhusana's The Nyaya Sutras of Gotama (Sacred Books of the Hindus vol. 8, 1913; 1930 reprint on archive.org)
key_findings.detail: Everything published before 1931 is US public domain in 2026, so Vidyabhusana's sutra-by-sutra translation (and his 1921 History of Indian Logic) can be quoted verbatim into a CC BY-SA database — this is the single cheapest high-value seed source for the non-Western layer. Sanskrit e-text is on GRETIL (Göttingen), but GRETIL files carry per-file headers rather than a blanket CC license — verify per file before ingestion.

key_findings.claim: India's debate taxonomy predates/parallels Nyaya in a medical text: Caraka Samhita Vimanasthana 8 is a 44-category debate manual (~1st-2nd c. CE)
key_findings.detail: CaS Vim. 8.15-26 covers sambhasa (colloquy, friendly vs hostile) and 8.27-66 covers vada (disputation) in 44 categories (vada-marga), including quibble, false rejoinder, fallacies of reason, and points of defeat that later get 'independent categorical status in the Nyayasutras.' Also the canonical debate typology: vada (truth-seeking), jalpa (win-at-any-cost — where chala/jati/nigrahasthana are deployed as weapons), vitanda (pure demolition, no counter-thesis). Shows the taxonomy arose from professional practice (physicians defending diagnoses at court), not philosophy seminars.

key_findings.claim: Buddhist logic produced the first meta-taxonomy dispute: Dharmakirti's Vadanyaya (7th c. CE) is a whole treatise attacking the Nyaya list of defeat conditions
key_findings.detail: Dignaga (5th-6th c.) and Dharmakirti reformed debate theory; Vadanyaya's central theme is 'the nature and classification of nigrahasthanas,' rejecting most of Nyaya's 22 as illegitimate and reducing defeat to essentially two grounds. Traditions argue about the catalog itself — the framework should model taxonomy-critiques as first-class nodes, not just techniques.

key_findings.claim: The Mohist Canons (late 4th-mid 3rd c. BCE) built an independent semantics of disputation with named failure modes
key_findings.detail: Bian (disputation) = contending over which of two complementary terms 'fits' (Canon A74); named flaws include kuang ju 狂舉 'wild picking' (arbitrary citing of features, B66) and the Xiaoqu (Lesser Selection)'s catalog of how the four argument forms — pi (illustrating), mou (parallelizing), yuan (citing precedent), tui (inferential pushing) — go wrong: things may be 'so in one case, not in another' (shi er ran / shi er bu ran). Xunzi's Zhengming chapter (~250 BCE) adds the 'three delusions' (san huo): using names to confuse names, using actualities to confuse names, using names to confuse actualities — the earliest systematic theory of loaded framing via naming. Chinese originals are public domain on ctext.org; the standard English of the dialectical chapters (A.C. Graham, Later Mohist Logic, 1978) is copyrighted, so the framework needs original glosses.

key_findings.claim: Han Feizi ch. 12 'Shui nan' (Difficulties of Persuasion, before 233 BCE) is an audience-psychology manipulation treatise ~1,750 years before Machiavelli
key_findings.detail: Its thesis: the difficulty of persuasion is 'knowing the mind of the persuaded so as to fit my words to it.' It prescribes magnifying what the ruler is proud of and minimizing what he is ashamed of (overclaim and minimizing as TECHNIQUES, not flaws), flattery calibration, framing self-interest as public virtue, and warns of the ni lin 'reverse scale' — the one topic that kills the persuader. Full translations: Liao 1939 (US PD in 2035) and Watson 1964 (copyrighted); Chinese original PD on ctext.

key_findings.claim: The Guiguzi is an explicit manipulator's manual with a chapter-level technique taxonomy — closer to modern social engineering than to Greek rhetoric
key_findings.detail: Warring States-Han text (compiled ~4th c. BCE-1st c. CE, attribution contested); chapters name techniques: bai he (Open-Shut: alternately drawing out and strategically withholding), fan ying (Reflect-Respond: echo-probing to elicit disclosure, 'casting nets'), nei jian (Affect-Fortify), di xi (Mend-Break), fei qian (Captivate-Capture: praise as a trap), wu he (Resist-Reconcile), chuai (Weighing hidden feelings), mo (Gauging/stroking), quan (Assessing), mou (Deploying schemes), jue (Deciding). Aimed at one powerful counterpart, not a public audience. First full critical English translation: Wu & Swearingen 2016 (SIU Press, copyrighted); Chinese original PD on ctext. Elicitation-by-provocation has NO named Greek equivalent.

key_findings.claim: Arabic balagha is the classical tradition closest to captioneer's own analytical stance: meaning-effects of construction choices, including agent deletion, theorized by al-Jurjani ~1078
key_findings.detail: Al-Jurjani's (d. 1078/1081) nazm theory (Dala'il al-I'jaz, Asrar al-Balagha) holds that eloquence lives in syntactic arrangement: taqdim wa-ta'khir (fronting/postponing = emphasis framing), hadhf (rhetorically motivated ellipsis, including omission of the agent), qasr (restriction). Arabic grammar literally names the passive voice al-mabni lil-majhul, 'built for the unknown [agent]' — the construction is NAMED for agent deletion, eight centuries before Anglophone passive-voice critiques. Al-Sakkaki's Miftah al-'Ulum (d. 626/1229) standardized the tripartite ma'ani (sentence-level pragmatics) / bayan (figuration: haqiqa vs majaz, isti'ara, kinaya) / badi' (embellishments) division; al-Qazwini's Talkhis al-Miftah (d. 1338) made it the madrasa canon. Arabic originals PD; major English studies copyrighted.

key_findings.claim: Kinaya is a formal taxonomy of deniable implicature, explicitly compared to Grice in modern scholarship
key_findings.detail: Balagha divides kinaya (indirection) into three types — kinaya 'an sifa (of an attribute: 'much ash on his hearth' = generous), 'an mawsuf (of the thing described), 'an nisba (of an attribution) — with the classical doctrine that kinaya is 'more eloquent than plain statement' (ablagh min al-tasrih) precisely because it is deniable. Mohamed M. Yunis Ali, Medieval Islamic Pragmatics: Sunni Legal Theorists' Models of Textual Communication (Routledge 2000), maps usul al-fiqh's wad' (conventional meaning) vs isti'mal (contextual use) and kinaya/majaz machinery onto and against Gricean implicature — ready-made scholarly bridge between a classical taxonomy and the framework's modern semantics layer.

key_findings.claim: The Arabic tradition carries BOTH an independent root and the documented Greek contact edge — one tradition, two roots
key_findings.detail: Balagha grew from Quranic i'jaz debates and grammar (Heinrichs on the genesis of the haqiqa/majaz dichotomy), independent of Aristotle. In parallel, Aristotle's Sophistici Elenchi reached Arabic via Syriac (Athanasius of Balad, 7th c.) in three 9th-10th c. Arabic versions (Yahya ibn Adi, d. 974; his student Ibn Zur'a, d. 1008; preserved in MS Paris BnF ar. 2346), then Ibn Sina's Kitab al-Safsata (in al-Shifa) and Ibn Rushd's middle commentary — feeding back to Latin Europe. So the genealogy schema must allow a single tradition multiple roots plus typed contact edges; 'Arabic rhetoric' is not one lineage.

key_findings.claim: Talmudic dialectics contributes inference-GOVERNANCE: named rules that cap or license argument moves, plus an internal anti-sophistry critique literature
key_findings.detail: The dayo principle (Bava Kamma 25a: 'it is sufficient for the conclusion to be like the premise') is a named anti-overclaim rule — a kal va-chomer (a fortiori) may never yield a conclusion stronger than its source. Gezerah shavah (verbal analogy) 'may not be reasoned on one's own' — it must be received from tradition: a governance restriction on arbitrary analogy. Fallacy-discovery moves are named (teshuvah/pirka = objection/refutation). Pilpul is the tradition's own contested-sophistry category: distinguished as truth-seeking analysis vs far-fetched skill display, condemned by 16th-c. authorities (e.g., Maharal). Licensing: the William Davidson/Steinsaltz Talmud on Sefaria is CC BY-NC — NOT CC BY-SA compatible; the PD option is Rodkinson (1903, partial and weak) or original-language quotation with fresh translation.

key_findings.claim: Persian gives a clean, dated vernacularization chain — the perfect test case for transmission edges
key_findings.detail: Ibn al-Mu'tazz's Kitab al-Badi' (887 CE, first badi' figure catalog, ~17-18 figures) → Raduyani's Tarjuman al-balagha (first Persian manual, written 1088-1114) → Rashid al-Din Watwat's Hada'iq al-sihr fi daqa'iq al-shi'r (d. 1182/83, the standard Persian textbook) → Shams-i Qays Razi's al-Mu'jam (completed ~1232-33). Each step adapts the Arabic figure inventory to Persian poetics — 'borrowed taxonomy, adapted inventory,' distinct from both independent origin and pure translation.

key_findings.claim: Japan's inmyō shows transmission can preserve a taxonomy while inverting its function (adversarial → ceremonial)
key_findings.detail: Indian hetuvidya (Dignaga's school) was translated by Xuanzang in 7th-c. China and carried to Japan with the Hossō school; medieval Japanese rongi debate ritualized it in Heian/Kamakura monastic examinations — 'hardly had defining experiences' of real inter-religious contest, unlike India. Edge type: institutional-transmission with functional drift. It briefly re-weaponized in Meiji-era Buddhist polemics against Christianity.

key_findings.claim: Documented African formal systems exist but as ethnographically recorded oral catalogs: Ethiopian wax-and-gold and Akan okyeame indirection
key_findings.detail: Amharic/Ge'ez sam-enna warq ('wax and gold', rooted in church qene poetry): institutionalized double-meaning verse where the surface (wax) hides the real meaning (gold); Levine (Wax and Gold, 1965) documents its social functions — deniable insult, criticism of authority, privacy defense. Akan (Ghana): Yankah's Speaking for the Chief (Indiana UP, 1995) documents the okyeame — royal speech is REQUIRED to pass through an orator-intermediary (institutionalized agent-displacement/liability buffering), plus akutia (veiled innuendo) and formal proverb praxis. Schema consequence: oral traditions need 'practice origin' (unknown/interval) separated from 'documentation event' (Levine 1965, Yankah 1995).

key_findings.claim: Comparative matrix (tradition x captioneer's six families): overclaim and loaded framing are named in 4+ independent lineages; agent deletion is flagged only in Arabic — and is language-relative
key_findings.detail: HEDGING: prescribed in Guiguzi (bai he withholding), enabled by kinaya's deniability, institutionalized in wax-and-gold — 3 lineages, mostly as craft. DEFLECTION: Nyaya chala (deflection-by-misconstrual) + 24 jati (pseudo-refutation); Mohist critique of Gongsun Long's word-twisting; Talmudic sham-pirka — 3 lineages as flaw. AGENT DELETION: only Arabic names it (hadhf; al-mabni lil-majhul) — absent from Indian/Chinese/Talmudic catalogs, plausibly because Sanskrit debate was oral-procedural and Chinese is a null-subject language where deleted agents are unmarked grammar, not a tell. LOADED FRAMING: Xunzi's three delusions; Nyaya prakaranasama; balagha taqdim/qasr; Talmud's gezerah-shavah restriction — 4 lineages, strongest universal. OVERCLAIM: Mohist kuang ju; Nyaya savyabhicara + utkarsa-sama; Talmud dayo violations; Han Feizi prescribes magnification — 4 lineages. MINIMIZING: Han Feizi prescribes it; Nyaya apakarsa-sama; wax-and-gold's innocuous surface — 3 lineages. Convergent discovery is real but uneven: the six families are not equally universal.

techniques.name: chala (quibbling)
techniques.definition: Deflecting an assertion by willfully misconstruing it; three named types: vak-chala (exploiting a word's ambiguity), samanya-chala (over-generalizing the claim to refute a strawman), upacara-chala (taking figurative speech literally).
techniques.origin: Nyayasutra 1.2.10-14, Sanskrit, attrib. Gautama/Aksapada; redaction ~150 CE (composition window 6th c. BCE-2nd c. CE); PD English: Vidyabhusana 1913.
techniques.example: Speaker: 'the boy has a nava-kambala (new blanket)'; quibbler: 'he does not have nine (nava) blankets' — Vidyabhusana's classic vak-chala illustration.

techniques.name: jati (sham rejoinders, 24 types)
techniques.definition: A catalog of 24 futile counterarguments 'founded on mere similarity or dissimilarity' — a taxonomy of BAD REBUTTALS that mimic refutation (e.g., sadharmya-sama, vaidharmya-sama, utkarsa-sama overextension, apakarsa-sama understatement). Aristotle catalogs bad arguments; Nyaya uniquely catalogs bad counterarguments.
techniques.origin: Nyayasutra 5.1, Sanskrit, ~150 CE redaction.
techniques.example: Utkarsa-sama: 'if sound is like a pot (both produced), sound must also be visible like a pot' — overextending an analogy to force a false concession.

techniques.name: nigrahasthana (points of defeat, 22 types)
techniques.definition: 22 procedural conditions under which a debater loses: shifting the thesis (pratijnantara), self-contradiction (pratijnavirodha), incoherent or meaningless speech (nirarthaka, aparthaka), repetition (punarukta), silence (ananubhasana), evasion (viksepa), tacit concession (matanujna), and using chala/jati themselves.
techniques.origin: Nyayasutra 5.2; critiqued and mostly rejected in Dharmakirti's Vadanyaya (7th c. CE).
techniques.example: Viksepa: breaking off the debate on a pretext ('I have business elsewhere') when losing — evasion codified as automatic defeat.

techniques.name: hetvabhasa (pseudo-reasons, 5 types)
techniques.definition: Reasons that look probative but are not: savyabhicara (erratic — proves too much), viruddha (contradicts one's own tenet), prakaranasama (question-begging), sadhyasama (as unproved as the conclusion), kalatita (mistimed).
techniques.origin: Nyayasutra 1.2.4-9; parallel list in Caraka Samhita Vim. 8 (~1st-2nd c. CE).

techniques.name: vada / jalpa / vitanda (debate typology)
techniques.definition: Three-way typology of dialogue by intent: truth-seeking discussion (vada), win-at-any-cost wrangling where tricks are weapons (jalpa), and pure demolition with no counter-thesis (vitanda) — an intent-layer classification captioneer lacks.
techniques.origin: Nyayasutra 1.2.1-3 and Caraka Samhita Vimanasthana 8 (sandhaya vs vigrhya sambhasa, friendly vs hostile colloquy).

techniques.name: kuang ju (wild picking)
techniques.definition: Arbitrarily citing features as grounds for classifying things together or apart — overclaiming category membership; the Mohist name for reckless analogical generalization.
techniques.origin: Mohist Canons B66, Chinese, late 4th-mid 3rd c. BCE; standard study A.C. Graham 1978 (copyrighted); original PD on ctext.org.

techniques.name: Xiaoqu inference pathologies
techniques.definition: The Lesser Selection names four argument forms — pi (illustrating), mou (parallelizing), yuan (citing precedent), tui (pushing an inference) — and warns each 'becomes fallacious when extended': things are 'so in one case, not in another' (shi er ran / shi er bu ran); predicates apply 'in one respect, not in all.'
techniques.origin: Mohist dialectical chapters (Xiaoqu), Chinese, 3rd c. BCE.
techniques.example: 'Her brother is a handsome man, but loving her brother is not loving a handsome man' — parallel form, non-parallel inference.

techniques.name: san huo (three delusions of naming)
techniques.definition: Xunzi's taxonomy of framing manipulation: (1) using names to confuse names, (2) using actualities to confuse names, (3) using names to confuse actualities — loaded framing analyzed as misuse of the naming system itself (zhengming, rectification of names).
techniques.origin: Xunzi ch. 22 'Zhengming', Chinese, ~250 BCE; original PD on ctext.org.

techniques.name: ni lin (the reverse scale)
techniques.definition: Han Fei's name for the persuadee's fatal taboo: the dragon is tame, but one inverted scale under its throat kills whoever touches it — audience-psychology hazard mapping as a named persuasion concept.
techniques.origin: Han Feizi ch. 12 'Shui nan' (Difficulties of Persuasion), Chinese, before 233 BCE; trans. Liao 1939, Watson 1964.

techniques.name: shui nan doctrine (fit words to the mind)
techniques.definition: Persuasion succeeds by profiling the target: magnify what he is proud of, minimize/erase what he is ashamed of, dress his private interest as public virtue — overclaim and minimizing PRESCRIBED as techniques, with named failure modes (appearing to probe secrets, contradicting his self-image).
techniques.origin: Han Feizi ch. 12, before 233 BCE.

techniques.name: bai he (opening and shutting)
techniques.definition: Guiguzi's master technique: alternately drawing the counterpart out (kai/bai — express, invite, encourage) and shutting down (he — withhold, conceal, stay silent) to control disclosure asymmetry.
techniques.origin: Guiguzi ch. 1, Chinese, Warring States-Han compilation (~4th c. BCE-1st c. CE); trans. Wu & Swearingen 2016 (copyrighted); original PD on ctext.org.

techniques.name: fan ying (reflect-respond / echo probing)
techniques.definition: Eliciting information by echoing, baiting, and 'casting nets': say little, provoke the other to speak, compare their words against their reactions — a formal elicitation technique (modern analog: social-engineering elicitation), no Greek counterpart.
techniques.origin: Guiguzi ch. 2.

techniques.name: fei qian (captivate-capture / praise as trap)
techniques.definition: 'Flying and clamping': inflate the target with calibrated praise until they open up, then clamp — flattery formalized as an acquisition device; overclaiming the target's merits instrumentally.
techniques.origin: Guiguzi ch. 5.

techniques.name: chuai / mo (gauging and stroking)
techniques.definition: Paired techniques for reading concealed inner states: chuai (weigh the counterpart's circumstances and desires when emotions peak) and mo (subtle probing touches to test reactions) — pre-persuasion target modeling.
techniques.origin: Guiguzi chs. 7-8.

techniques.name: kinaya (deniable indirection, 3 types)
techniques.definition: Stating an attribute's concomitant instead of the attribute, keeping literal deniability; taxonomized as kinaya of the attribute, of the thing described, and of the attribution (nisba); doctrine: ablagh min al-tasrih — 'more eloquent than declaration.' Modern scholarship reads it as a proto-Gricean implicature theory.
techniques.origin: Arabic balagha; systematized from al-Jurjani (d. 1078/81, Dala'il al-I'jaz) through al-Sakkaki's Miftah al-'Ulum (d. 1229) and al-Qazwini's Talkhis (d. 1338); Grice comparison in M.M.Y. Ali, Medieval Islamic Pragmatics (2000).
techniques.example: 'Much ash beneath his cooking-pot' = he is hospitable — assertable and deniable at once.
techniques.languages: Arabic (vernacularized into Persian, Ottoman Turkish, Urdu rhetoric)

techniques.name: hadhf + taqdim/ta'khir + al-mabni lil-majhul (agent deletion and order framing)
techniques.definition: Nazm-theory analysis of construction choices: hadhf (rhetorically motivated omission, including the agent), taqdim wa-ta'khir (fronting/postponement for emphasis), qasr (restriction); Arabic grammar names the passive 'built for the unknown [agent]' — agent deletion encoded in the construction's very name.
techniques.origin: Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani, Dala'il al-I'jaz and Asrar al-Balagha, Arabic, d. 1078/1081 (Arabic originals PD).

techniques.name: majaz vs haqiqa (figurative vs literal)
techniques.definition: The load-bearing dichotomy of bayan: when may speech be taken non-literally, who bears the burden, and how figurative reclassification can be abused — later famously attacked wholesale by Ibn Taymiyya (a taxonomy-critique event).
techniques.origin: Genesis traced by W. Heinrichs, 'On the Genesis of the Haqiqa-Majaz Dichotomy' (Studia Islamica); mature form in al-Jurjani and al-Sakkaki.

techniques.name: dayo principle (anti-overclaim cap)
techniques.definition: 'It is sufficient for the conclusion to be like its premise' — a named rule that a kal va-chomer (a fortiori) inference may never output a stronger conclusion than the source case; violating it is a recognized argument flaw.
techniques.origin: Mishnah/Talmud, Bava Kamma 25a, Hebrew/Aramaic, redacted ~200-600 CE; hermeneutic lists: Hillel's 7 rules (~1st c. BCE), R. Ishmael's 13 middot (~2nd c. CE).

techniques.name: gezerah shavah restriction (governance of analogy)
techniques.definition: Verbal-analogy inference between passages sharing a term is valid ONLY if received from one's teacher — 'no one may reason a gezerah shavah on his own': a procedural license requirement preventing arbitrary loaded analogies.
techniques.origin: Talmudical hermeneutics; restriction discussed at Pesachim 66a and codified in the middot literature.

techniques.name: pilpul (contested hyper-dialectic)
techniques.definition: Sharp casuistic argumentation; the tradition itself split it into truth-seeking analysis vs display sophistry ('far-fetched analogies to demonstrate skill'), with a named critique literature (16th-c. condemnations, e.g., Maharal) — an internal anti-sophistry category.
techniques.origin: Medieval-early modern Ashkenazi Talmud study; critiques from 16th c.

techniques.name: sam-enna warq (wax and gold)
techniques.definition: Institutionalized double-meaning verse: the 'wax' surface meaning conceals the 'gold' true meaning; used for deniable insult, criticism of authority, humor, and privacy defense; formal types taught in church qene schools.
techniques.origin: Ge'ez qene tradition of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, carried into Amharic; documented by Donald Levine, Wax and Gold (1965).
techniques.example: A couplet praising a host's generosity whose homophonic reading accuses him of stinginess.

techniques.name: okyeame mediation + akutia (Akan)
techniques.definition: Royal speech must pass through the okyeame (orator-intermediary) who artistically reworks it — institutionalized agent-displacement/liability buffering; akutia is veiled innuendo targeting a hearer who cannot prove being targeted; formal proverb praxis (Yankah) governs deniable citation of authority.
techniques.origin: Akan oral tradition (Ghana); documented in Kwesi Yankah, Speaking for the Chief (Indiana UP, 1995) and The Proverb in the Context of Akan Rhetoric (1989).

techniques.name: inmyō / rongi (transmitted Buddhist debate logic)
techniques.definition: Japanese reception of hetuvidya (Dignaga's logic) via Xuanzang's 7th-c. Chinese translations; ritualized as rongi doctrinal debate in Heian/Kamakura monasteries — a taxonomy preserved by ceremony after losing adversarial function.
techniques.origin: India (5th-6th c.) → China (Xuanzang, 7th c.) → Japan (Hossō school, 7th-8th c.).

techniques.name: badi' catalog and its Persian vernacularization
techniques.definition: Catalog of rhetorical figures/embellishments founded by Ibn al-Mu'tazz's Kitab al-Badi' (887 CE, ~17-18 figures), expanded and adapted into Persian by Raduyani (Tarjuman al-balagha, 1088-1114), Watwat (Hada'iq al-sihr, d. 1182/83), and Shams-i Qays (al-Mu'jam, ~1232-33).
techniques.origin: Arabic, 887 CE; Persian chain 11th-13th c.

framework_implications: Model the genealogy as a multi-root DAG, not a tree: root nodes for Greek, Indian (Nyaya/Caraka), Chinese (Mohist + persuasion-manual), Arabic (balagha), Hebrew (middot) lineages, with typed edges — translation (SE→Syriac→Arabic), commentary (Ibn Rushd's Talkhis), vernacularization (Ibn al-Mu'tazz→Raduyani→Watwat→Shams-i Qays), institutional-transmission (Dignaga→Xuanzang→inmyō), critique (Dharmakirti→nigrahasthana; Ibn Taymiyya→majaz), and analytic-convergence (unconnected lineages naming the same move). Allow one tradition to carry multiple roots (Arabic = balagha + falsafa).

Extend the naming-event record to: term in original script + transliteration + language + work + fine-grained passage locator (sutra number, Canon number like B66, chapter, folio, daf) + DATE AS AN INTERVAL with an uncertainty flag (Nyayasutra spans -600 to +150; Guiguzi compilation contested) + catalog-count (3/24/22/5, 44, 3 kinaya types, 3 san huo, 13 middot) — counts are checkable claims contributors can verify against PD sources.

Add a per-source 'stance' field and separate technique from evaluation: the same move is PRESCRIBED craft in Guiguzi/Han Feizi/balagha manuals and PROSCRIBED flaw in Nyaya/Mohist/Talmud catalogs. Four stance values fall out of the data: procedural-defeat (India), semantic-compositional (Arabic), audience-psychology manual (China-legalist), inference-governance (Talmud); the Greek fallacy list is one stance among several, and captioneer's six families are surface-detection categories that cut across all four.

Make detection families explicitly language-relative in the engine: agent-deletion is a strong tell in English but unmarked grammar in null-subject/pro-drop languages (Mandarin, Japanese, Arabic verb morphology) — ship per-language detector configs, and surface the Arabic evidence (the passive is literally named 'built-for-the-unknown') in the UI as the historical anchor for that family.

The comparative matrix suggests candidate NEW families the six-family set misses, each with classical pedigree: elicitation (Guiguzi fan ying/chuai/mo — provoking disclosure), deniable indirection (kinaya / wax-and-gold / akutia — adjacent to hedging but functionally distinct: assert-and-deny), procedural evasion (nigrahasthana-type: thesis-shifting, non-response, repetition — visible in transcripts/threads, not single statements), and analogy-overextension (jati/kuang ju/dayo violations). Tag existing families with a 'universality' score: loaded framing and overclaim (4+ independent lineages) vs agent deletion (1 lineage, language-bound).

Licensing plan for a CC BY-SA seed: quote verbatim from PD sources — Vidyabhusana 1913/1930 (full English of all Nyaya lists), Rodkinson 1903 (partial Talmud), pre-1931 translations, Chinese/Sanskrit/Arabic originals (ctext.org originals are PD, but ctext's RDF data is CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 — incompatible, do not ingest; GRETIL files need per-file license checks). Write ORIGINAL English glosses for Mohist dialectics, Han Feizi ch. 12, and Guiguzi rather than reusing Graham 1978 / Watson 1964 / Wu-Swearingen 2016 (all copyrighted; Liao vol. 1 enters US PD in 2035); treat Sefaria's Davidson/Steinsaltz Talmud (CC BY-NC) as reference-only with fresh translation of quoted lines.

Separate 'practice origin' from 'documentation event' for oral traditions: Ethiopian sam-enna warq and Akan okyeame/akutia have unknown origin intervals but precise documentation events (Levine 1965, Yankah 1995) — a schema that only has 'named in year X by Y' would falsely credit 20th-century ethnographers as originators and erase the traditions' own priority.

Governance: recruit per-tradition maintainers and require original-script terms plus primary-source locators for new entries (the Nyaya/balagha/Talmud communities have living scholarly traditions that will audit this data); represent taxonomy-critiques (Vadanyaya vs nigrahasthana, pilpul condemnations, Ibn Taymiyya vs majaz) as first-class nodes so contributors can record that traditions disagree about their own catalogs — this is what makes non-European contributors see their traditions treated as intellectual history, not as exotic garnish on a Greek tree.

gapFindings.dimension: gap:Evaluation infrastructure: the benign 'ham' corpus, achievable annotator agreement, and truth-caption faithfulness metrics
gapFindings.summary: The gap is fillable, but only with realistic targets: (1) A politically balanced, openly licensed ham corpus can be assembled register-by-register — Enron (FERC public release, ~500k messages) for workplace email; Congressional Record (US-gov public domain, party metadata enables balance-by-construction), Europarl ("no known copyright restrictions") and UK Hansard (Open Parliament Licence v3.0) for political speech; Pryzant's 385k unchanged-neutral Wikipedia sentences (WNC) plus Wikipedia article namespace (CC BY-SA) for encyclopedic register; Civil Comments (CC0, ~2M comments, mostly non-toxic) for public comments — while Reddit/Pushshift (post-2023 legal grey) and OpenSubtitles (rights retained by opensubtitles.org) must be excluded; the truly private registers (personal messages) are solved the way SpamAssassin solved it, via federated mass-check where contributors run patterns locally and upload only hit logs. (2) Achievable span agreement is now well-bounded by precedent: binary "mark the manipulative span" with 3–7 raters and character-majority aggregation reaches Cohen's kappa ~0.55–0.61 (SemEval-2021 Toxic Spans); fine-grained technique labeling by independent annotators starts at gamma ~0.31 (PTC) and only reaches ~0.60 after a consolidation phase; 23-way fallacy labeling collapses to gamma ~0.13 even among experts (MAFALDA) — so captioneer's gate must be two-tier (crowd span marking, then expert family adjudication with disjunctive gold) and per-family (hedging/passive cues are tractable; deflection, minimizing, overclaim are pragmatic and hard). SpamAssassin's actual promotion numbers (S/O ≥ 0.95, ≥0.25% target hit, <1% non-target hit, pass lint, not too slow, vote override allowed) transfer almost directly. (3) Truth-caption faithfulness has no single metric but a defensible suite exists: directional NLI (source must entail rewrite — SummaC-style), QA-based checks (QAFactEval beats QuestEval), a claim-strength ladder classifier (Wright & Augenstein's exaggeration work: no-relation → correlational → conditional-causal → direct-causal) to catch hedge deletion/strengthening specifically, SARI against reference rewrites, and a human triad (meaning/style/fluency) with reported alpha per the TST-standardization literature. (4) The positive target register should be the US Federal Plain Language Guidelines (public domain, checkably concrete) — ISO 24495-1:2023 is the right citation but is paywalled ISO copyright and cannot be encoded verbatim in an open repo. The Perspective bias literature (Dixon 2018 identity-term false positives, Sap 2019 AAVE 2x offensive-labeling, Sap 2022 annotator politics) dictates that the ham FP gate be evaluated per-slice (register x party x dialect) with pinned template tests, never as a single aggregate number.

techniques.name: Federated mass-check (privacy-preserving ham federation)
techniques.definition: Contributors run the candidate ruleset locally against their own private ham/spam corpora and upload only per-message rule-hit logs (never text); a central QA app aggregates all logs as one virtual corpus and greys out rules failing promotion thresholds.
techniques.example: SpamAssassin nightly mass-check producing ham.log/spam.log consumed by ruleqa.spamassassin.org; for captioneer: users opt in to run the pattern pack over their own email archive and submit only per-family hit counts, covering the workplace-email and personal-message registers no open license can.
techniques.origin: Apache SpamAssassin project, early 2000s

techniques.name: S/O ratio promotion gate
techniques.definition: A rule ships only if the share of its hits that land on the target class (spam/manipulative) vs the benign class is at least 0.95, with minimum coverage (>=0.25% of target corpus) and a hard FP cap (<1% of ham), plus lint and runtime checks; a maintainer vote can override.
techniques.example: SpamAssassin RulesProjPromotion criteria
techniques.origin: Apache SpamAssassin RuleQA

techniques.name: Mathet's gamma for free-span categorical annotation
techniques.definition: Unified agreement measure handling unaligned spans with categories (alignment + chance correction), implemented in pygamma-agreement; the standard for propaganda-technique and fallacy span IAA.
techniques.example: PTC gamma ~0.31 pre-consolidation, ~0.6 vs gold post-consolidation; MAFALDA gamma avg 0.13
techniques.origin: Mathet et al. 2015, Computational Linguistics

techniques.name: Consolidation/adjudication phase
techniques.definition: After independent annotation, a designated consolidator (or third linguist) resolves discrepancies with the original annotators; empirically roughly doubles span-level agreement.
techniques.example: PTC (0.31-0.34 to ~0.6-0.74); BioScope and CoNLL-2010 Wikipedia weasels both used two independent linguists + third adjudicator
techniques.origin: BioScope 2008; Da San Martino et al. 2019

techniques.name: Character-majority crowd aggregation
techniques.definition: 3-7 raters mark free spans; the gold span is the maximal contiguous run of character offsets marked by a majority of raters; agreement computed as mean pairwise kappa over character offsets (binary toxic/non-toxic).
techniques.example: SemEval-2021 Task 5: kappa 0.61 (35 posts), >0.55 at up to 1,000 posts
techniques.origin: Pavlopoulos et al., SemEval-2021

techniques.name: Disjunctive gold labels
techniques.definition: The gold standard stores alternative acceptable annotations (disjunction of conjunctions of labels) and scoring counts a match with any alternative as correct — absorbs legitimate taxonomy overlap instead of punishing it as disagreement.
techniques.example: MAFALDA's P/R/F metric for 23 fallacy types
techniques.origin: Helwe et al., MAFALDA 2024

techniques.name: Priming/binary decomposition of taxonomy
techniques.definition: Ask crowds the reliable question (where is the span?) and reserve the unreliable one (which technique?) for trained annotators; or use category selection only as a priming exercise then collapse to binary.
techniques.example: Toxic Spans collapsed 5 category choices into one binary span label; recommended for captioneer: six parallel binary questions per span instead of one 6-way choice
techniques.origin: SemEval-2021 Task 5

techniques.name: Pinned template bias test sets
techniques.definition: Synthetic sentences from templates ('I am a <identity> person') swapped across identity/dialect/party terms; a detector must score all fills equivalently (pinned AUC / per-slice FP parity) before release.
techniques.example: Dixon et al. 2018 for Perspective; for captioneer: same proposition rendered in AAVE vs SAE, or with Democrat vs Republican actors, must trigger identical marks
techniques.origin: Dixon, Li, Sorensen, Thain, Vasserman — AIES 2018

techniques.name: Dialect priming of annotators
techniques.definition: Showing annotators the likely dialect/community of a text before rating significantly reduces false 'offensive/manipulative' judgments on minority dialects.
techniques.example: Sap et al. 2019: priming AAE dialect reduced offensiveness ratings on AAE tweets
techniques.origin: Sap et al., ACL 2019

techniques.name: Directional NLI faithfulness gate
techniques.definition: Run entailment in the source-entails-rewrite direction (sentence-pair aggregation a la SummaC): a hedged source ('may have contributed') does not entail a strengthened rewrite ('caused'), so strengthening is caught as non-entailment; the reverse direction catches dropped content.
techniques.example: SummaC benchmark aggregation; apply both directions and gate on the minimum
techniques.origin: Laban et al. 2022 (SummaC); Falke et al. 2019

techniques.name: QA-based faithfulness (QuestEval/QAFactEval)
techniques.definition: Generate questions from source commitments, answer them from the rewrite (and vice versa), compare answers with a learned answer-overlap metric; QAFactEval's tuned components beat QuestEval on SummaC, and QA+NLI combined beats either.
techniques.example: QAFactEval-NLI learned combination
techniques.origin: Scialom et al. 2021; Fabbri et al., NAACL 2022

techniques.name: Claim-strength ladder equality check
techniques.definition: Classify each claim's causal/epistemic strength on an ordinal scale (no relation -> correlational -> conditional causal -> direct causal, driven by modals/hedges/causal triggers) in source and rewrite; require equality to guarantee hedge and evidential preservation.
techniques.example: Wright & Augenstein exaggeration detection (EMNLP 2021), SPICED matched-paraphrase information change (EMNLP 2022)
techniques.origin: Copenhagen NLP (CopeNLU), building on Sumner et al. press-release exaggeration studies

techniques.name: SARI (add/keep/delete F1)
techniques.definition: Rewrite metric comparing output to both source and human references, scoring the words added, kept, and deleted — rewards minimal faithful edits rather than fluent paraphrase drift.
techniques.example: Standard in text simplification; fits truth-caption once 200-500 reference captions exist
techniques.origin: Xu et al., TACL 2016

techniques.name: TST evaluation triad with agreement reporting
techniques.definition: Evaluate rewrites on three separate axes — style/register strength (classifier acc), content preservation (sBLEU/SBERT), fluency (PPL/CoLA) — gate on the minimum axis, and report human-rater kappa/alpha for every human evaluation.
